Use affine coordinates with A=(0,0), B=(1,0), D=(0,1), and C=(1,1); then E=(1/2,0), O=(1/2,1/2), G=(1,g), and F=(1,f). Since GF/BC=7/14=1/2, f-g=1/2. Writing P on OG and EF with the same parameter t (their first coordinates force the parameters to be equal), the second coordinates give 1/2+t(g-1/2)=tf, so 1/2=t(f-g+1/2)=t, hence t=1/2. Thus P is the midpoint of both OG and EF. Triangle AEO is 1/8 of the parallelogram, and triangle EOP is 1/16, so the shaded region is 3/16 of its area. If θ is the angle between AB and AD, then AC=AB gives 25²=25²+14²+2(25)(14)cosθ, so cosθ=-7/25 and sinθ=24/25. Therefore the parallelogram’s area is 25·14·24/25=336, and the shaded area is (3/16)(336)=63. Final answer: 63

The image shows diagonal AC spanning 8 grid squares horizontally and diagonal BD spanning 6 grid squares vertically, so if O is their intersection, AO=4 and BO=3. In a rhombus, diagonal AC bisects ∠BAD, hence ∠BAD/2=∠BAO. Since the diagonals are perpendicular, triangle AOB is right, and tan∠BAO=BO/AO=3/4. Final answer: \(\frac{3}{4}\)

The figure shows a right triangle with legs AC=5 and BC=12, hypotenuse AB, and altitude CD perpendicular to AB, with P on segment CD. Since AB=√(5²+12²)=13, the altitude is CD=(AC·BC)/AB=60/13. Let CP=t. The distance from P to AB is PD=60/13−t, so tangency to AB gives 60/13−t=4 and t=8/13. To check the other sides, place C=(0,0), A=(5,0), and B=(0,12); since CD has direction (12,5), P=(12t/13,5t/13). Thus the distances from P to BC and AC are 12t/13 and 5t/13, respectively. Tangency to BC gives 12t/13=4, so t=13/3, which lies on CD because 13/3<60/13; tangency to AC would give t=52/5>60/13, which is impossible for P on CD. Final answer: 8/13 or 13/3

The diagram shows D on line l2 to the right of C, with E vertically below D on l1. Since l1 is y = −2x + 1, A = (0,1), so AB = 1 − (−2) = 3. The y-coordinate of C is −1, and −1 = −2x + 1 gives C = (1,−1); thus the line through B(0,−2) and C has slope 1, so l2 is y = x − 2. Let D = (t,t−2); the vertical line through D meets l1 at E = (t,−2t+1). Because D is above E as shown, DE = (t−2) − (−2t+1) = 3t−3. Therefore 3t−3 = 2AB = 6, giving t = 3 and D = (3,1). Final answer: (3,1)

The image shows B and C on the same horizontal grid line, while A is three grid squares to the right and three squares above B, so \(\overrightarrow{BA}=(3,3)\) and \(\overrightarrow{BC}=(2,0)\). Thus \(BA\) makes a \(45^\circ\) angle with the horizontal ray \(BC\), and \(\sin B=\sin 45^\circ=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\). Final answer: \(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\)

The diagram shows B, D, and C collinear with D between B and C, E on AC, and ∠ADE=40°. Since AB=AC and ∠ABC=40°, the other base angle ∠ACB is also 40°. Let ∠BDA=x; then ∠ADC=180°−x, so in triangle ADC, ∠DAC=180°−40°−(180°−x)=x−40°. Because E lies on AC, ∠DAE=x−40°, and therefore in triangle ADE, ∠AED=180°−40°−(x−40°)=180°−x. For triangle ADE to be isosceles, two of its angles must be equal: x−40°=40° gives x=80°, or x−40°=180°−x gives x=110°, while 40°=180°−x gives x=140°, which would make ∠BAD=0° in triangle ABD and force D=B, contrary to the condition. Final answer: 80° or 110°

The image shows A on the vertical wall, B on the horizontal ground, and the right-angle vertex of the isosceles triangle at B, with C above and to the right; hence AB ⟂ BC and AB = BC. Taking O = (0,0), the wall as the y-axis, and the ground as the x-axis gives A = (0,50) and B = (28,0), so vector BA = (−28,50). Rotating this vector 90° clockwise and preserving its length gives vector BC = (50,28), so C = (28,0) + (50,28) = (78,28). Therefore C is 28 cm above the ground. Final answer: 28 cm

The image shows square ABCD of side 2, with E and F moving on AD, AE = DF, G = CF ∩ BD, and H = BE ∩ AG; the displayed order of E and F is only one position, since no permanent order is stated. Set A = (0,0), D = (2,0), B = (0,2), C = (2,2), and let AE = DF = t, so E = (t,0), F = (2−t,0), where 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. Intersecting CF with BD gives G = (4/(t+2), 2t/(t+2)), so AG has equation y = tx/2, while BE has equation y = 2−2x/t; hence H = (4t/(t²+4), 2t²/(t²+4)). Writing H = (x,y), direct substitution gives x² + (y−1)² = 1, so H lies on the unit circle centered at O = (0,1). Since OD = √[(2−0)²+(0−1)²] = √5, the reverse triangle inequality gives DH ≥ OD−OH = √5−1. Equality occurs at the point of the circle on ray OD, corresponding to t = √5−1 ∈ [0,2], so it is attainable. Final answer: √5−1

The image shows D on BC, E on AC, AD intersecting BE, ∠1 = ∠BAD = 15°, and ∠2 as the acute angle between AD and BE. Let each side of equilateral triangle ABC have length s. In triangle ABD, ∠ABD = 60° and ∠BAD = 15°, so ∠ADB = 105°; by the sine rule, BD/sin15° = s/sin105°, giving BD = s(sin15°/sin75°) = s(2 − √3). Hence CE = s(2 − √3). Taking B = (0,0), C = (s,0), and A = (s/2, √3s/2), point E lies CE/CA = 2 − √3 of the way from C to A, so E = (√3s/2, (2√3 − 3)s/2). Therefore the inclination of BE to BC satisfies tan∠EBC = (2√3 − 3)/√3 = 2 − √3 = tan15°, so ∠EBC = 15°. Since ∠ADB = 105°, AD has inclination 180° − 105° = 75° to BC, and thus the acute angle between AD and BE is 75° − 15° = 60°. Final answer: 60°

The figure shows O, E, C, and B in order on the positive x-axis, with C = (x, 0), 2 < x < 4, and CD vertical. Since line AB through A(0, 2) and B(4, 0) has equation y = 2 − x/2, D = (x, 2 − x/2). Folding across the vertical line CD reflects B(4, 0) to E(2x − 4, 0). For a right angle at A, AD·AE = (x, −x/2)·(2x − 4, −2) = x(2x − 3), which is nonzero for 2 < x < 4; for a right angle at D, DA·DE = (−x, x/2)·(x − 4, (x − 4)/2) = −3x(x − 4)/4, also nonzero in this interval. Thus the right angle must be at E, so EA·ED = (4 − 2x, 2)·(4 − x, (4 − x)/2) = (4 − x)(5 − 2x) = 0. Since x ≠ 4, x = 5/2. Final answer: 5/2

The image shows A and B as the left and right x-intercepts, C as the y-intercept below the x-axis, D as C’s reflection above the x-axis, and BD as a descending line. Using the given vertex, the parabola is y=(1/2)(x−3/2)²−25/8=(1/2)x²−(3/2)x−2=(1/2)(x+1)(x−4), so A=(−1,0), B=(4,0), C=(0,−2), and D=(0,2). Thus line BD has equation y=−x/2+2. Let Q=(u,v). Since C,D,P,Q are consecutive vertices of a parallelogram, C+P=D+Q, so P=(u,v+4). Because Q lies on BD, v=−u/2+2, while P lies on the parabola, giving v+4=(1/2)u²−(3/2)u−2. Substitution yields (1/2)u²−u−8=0, hence u=1±√17 and v=(3∓√17)/2. Final answer: Q=(1+√17,(3−√17)/2) or Q=(1−√17,(3+√17)/2).

The image shows that B and C lie on the same horizontal grid line, and moving from C to A requires going 4 grid squares left and 2 grid squares up. Since CB is horizontal, \(\tan C\) equals the vertical change divided by the horizontal change along CA, so \(\tan C=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2}\). Final answer: \(\frac{1}{2}\)

The image shows a right triangle with the right angle at C, so AB is the hypotenuse, AC = 6 is adjacent to angle A, and BC = 8 is opposite angle A. By the Pythagorean theorem, AB = √(AC² + BC²) = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10. Therefore, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse = AC/AB = 6/10 = 3/5. Final answer: 3/5

The graph shows that the area reaches its maximum of 6 cm² when P arrives at B at time t=a, then decreases to 0 when P reaches C at t=a+4; thus the trip from B to C takes 4 s, so BC=1×4=4 cm. At P=B, triangle APC is triangle ABC, whose area is S=1/2·AB·BC=6, giving 1/2·AB·4=6 and hence AB=3 cm. Final answer: 3 cm

The image shows that y=k₁x+b₁ is the increasing line and y=k₂x+b₂ is the decreasing line, and they intersect at A(−2,1). Thus the two function values are equal when x=−2; to the right of A, the graph of y=k₁x+b₁ lies above that of y=k₂x+b₂, so k₁x+b₁>k₂x+b₂ when x>−2. Final answer: x>−2.

The figure shows that O is the center, AB is a chord of length 2√3, and C lies in the interior of AB. Let M be the midpoint of AB; then OM ⟂ AB and AM=√3. Using OA=2, OM=√(OA²−AM²)=√(4−3)=1. For an interior point C on AB, the distance from O satisfies OM≤OC<OA, so 1≤OC<2. The only integer in this interval is 1. Final answer: 1

The graph shows that l₁ and l₂ intersect at (−1,3), l₂ passes through the origin, and l₁ has positive slope. Since l₂ passes through (−1,3) and (0,0), k₂=(0−3)/(0−(−1))=−3, so k₂x>0 gives x<0. Also, the two lines are equal at x=−1, and because k₁>k₂, k₁x+b>k₂x holds for x>−1. Combining these conditions gives −1<x<0. Final answer: (−1,0)

The figure places the center P below the x-axis and to the left of the y-axis. Since the circle has radius 1 and is tangent to the x-axis from below, the center has y-coordinate −1. Substituting y = −1 into y = −(1/2)x² + 1 gives −1 = −(1/2)x² + 1, so x² = 4 and x = ±2. Because P is on the left side of the y-axis, x is negative. Final answer: −2

The figure shows D on AC with AD = 3 and E on AB such that DE is perpendicular to AB, so triangle ADE is right at E and ∠DAE = ∠CAB. In right triangle ABC, cos A = AC/AB = 4/5. Therefore, in triangle ADE, AE/AD = cos A = 4/5, giving AE = 3 × 4/5 = 12/5. Final answer: 12/5

The image shows an upward-opening parabola tangent to the x-axis at A, with A left of the y-axis, while a line through A meets the y-axis at C and the parabola again at B, and C is the midpoint of AB. Since y=ax²+2ax+1 has exactly one common point with the x-axis, ax²+2ax+1=0 has a repeated root, so its discriminant is zero: (2a)²−4a·1=4a(a−1)=0. Because a≠0 for a parabola, a=1. Thus A=(−1,0); the midpoint condition gives B=(1,4) and C=(0,2), which is consistent with the figure. Final answer: y=x²+2x+1=(x+1)².

The image shows ∠AOB = 120° with OC inside it, but it does not show or constrain OD to lie inside ∠AOB. Let ∠AOC = x; then ∠BOC = 2x, so 3x = 120° and ∠AOC = 40°. Writing ∠AOD = α and ∠BOD = β, the condition 2α = 3β gives α:β = 3:2. If OD is inside ∠AOB, then α + β = 120°, giving α = 72° and ∠COD = 72° − 40° = 32°. However, an exterior ray is also possible: in the other valid configuration, α + β = 360° − 120° = 240°, so α = 144° and β = 96°; OD then has direction 216° counterclockwise from OA, giving ∠COD = 216° − 40° = 176°. Final answer: 32° if OD lies inside ∠AOB; otherwise 176° is also possible, so the measure is not uniquely determined.

The image shows the right triangle AOB with O=(0,0), A=(0,4) on the y-axis, B=(4,0) on the x-axis, and hypotenuse AB given by x+y=4; the lines considered have slope −2. For y=−2x+b, its intersections with OA, OB, and AB are respectively (0,b), (b/2,0), and (b−4,8−b). The first lies on OA when 0≤b≤4, the second lies on OB when 0≤b≤8, and the third lies on AB when 4≤b≤8. Thus for 0<b<4 there are two intersections on OA and OB, for b=4 there are the two distinct intersections A and (2,0), and for 4<b<8 there are two intersections on AB and OB. At b=0 or b=8 the line touches the triangle only at O or B, respectively, so the endpoints are excluded. Final answer: 0<b<8

The figure shows A and B as the x-intercepts, C as the y-intercept, E on segment BC, and EF vertical to the x-axis. Factoring the parabola gives y=(3/4)(x−1)(x−4), so A=(1,0), B=(4,0), and C=(0,3), hence OC=3. The line through B and C is y=3−3x/4, so if E has x-coordinate x, then yE=3−3x/4, while the point F on the parabola has yF=3x²/4−15x/4+3. Thus EF=yE−yF=3x−3x²/4. Setting EF=OC gives 3x−3x²/4=3, or x²−4x+4=0, so (x−2)²=0. Final answer: 2

The image shows right triangle ABC with vertical dam height BC = 6 m, horizontal base AC, and inclined slope AB labeled 1:2, meaning BC:AC = 1:2. Thus AC = 2 × 6 = 12 m, and by the Pythagorean theorem, AB = √(BC² + AC²) = √(6² + 12²) = √180 = 6√5 m. Final answer: 6√5 meters

The figure shows D on the original side AB, E on the original side AC, the fold line DE, and the folded image A′ outside quadrilateral BCED; ∠1 is ∠BDA′ = 70°, while ∠2 is ∠DPC = 152° at P = DA′ ∩ EC. Let A₀ be the original position of A. Since DB and DA₀ are opposite rays, ∠A₀DA′ = 180° − 70° = 110°; folding across DE makes DE the angle bisector, so ∠A′DE = 55°. Because PE and PC are opposite rays, ∠DPE = 180° − 152° = 28°. Thus, in triangle DPE, ∠DEP = 180° − 55° − 28° = 97°. Since EA₀ and EC are opposite rays, ∠A₀ED = 180° − 97° = 83°, and folding gives ∠A′ED = 83°. Therefore, in triangle A′DE, ∠A′ = 180° − 55° − 83° = 42°; reflection preserves the original angle A. Final answer: 42°

The diagram shows A-E-F, B-F-G, C-G-H, and E-H-D collinear, while EF ⟂ FG because EFGH is a rectangle. Thus AF ⟂ BF, so right isosceles triangle AFB has AB = √(FA² + FB²) = √(8 + 8) = 4 and ∠ABF = ∠BAF = 45°. Since ABCD is a rhombus, BC = CD = 4; because BF lies inside ∠ABC = 60°, ∠FBC = 60° − 45° = 15°. Right triangle BGC therefore gives BG = 4 cos 15° = √6 + √2 and CG = 4 sin 15° = √6 − √2, so FG = BG − BF = √6 − √2. Also CD ∥ AB and CH ∥ AF, so ∠DCH = 45°; right triangle CDH is therefore isosceles with CH = 4/√2 = 2√2, giving GH = CH − CG = 3√2 − √6. Hence the rectangle’s area is FG·GH = (√6 − √2)(3√2 − √6) = 8√3 − 12. Final answer: 8√3 − 12

The image shows A and B as the intersections of the line and parabola, with B=(2,2), but it does not mark C or impose any further positional restriction. Since B lies on y=kx, 2=2k gives k=1; since B also lies on y=x²+c, 2=4+c gives c=−2. Thus the curves are y=x and y=x²−2, whose other intersection is A=(−1,−1). Let C=(t,t²−2). Using vectors B−A=(3,3) and C−A=(t+1,t²−1), the area is (1/2)|3(t²−1)−3(t+1)|=(3/2)|t²−t−2|. Setting this equal to 3 gives |t²−t−2|=2, so t²−t−2=2 or t²−t−2=−2. Hence t=(1±√17)/2, 0, or 1, and substitution into y=t²−2 gives the corresponding coordinates. Final answer: C=(0,−2), (1,−1), ((1+√17)/2,(5+√17)/2), or ((1−√17)/2,(5−√17)/2).

The image shows collinear bases AB=1, BC=2, and CD=3 with upward equilateral apices E, F, and G, respectively; segment AG crosses EB, BF, and FC at P, Q, and R, and the shaded regions are triangles PBQ and RCG. Set A=(0,0), B=(1,0), C=(3,0), and G=(9/2,3√3/2), so AG has equation y=x/√3. Intersecting it with EB, BF, and FC gives P=(3/4,√3/4), Q=(3/2,√3/2), and R=(9/4,3√3/4), hence BP=1/2, BQ=1, CR=3/2, and CG=3. The included angle at both B and C is 60°, so using area=(1/2)ab sin 60° gives [PBQ]=√3/8 and [RCG]=9√3/8. Their sum is 10√3/8=5√3/4. Final answer: 5√3/4

The figure shows OM drawn from the center O perpendicular to side AB at M, so OM is the apothem of the regular hexagon. Since a regular hexagon has central angle ∠AOB = 360°/6 = 60°, OM bisects it, giving a right triangle with hypotenuse OA = 1 and angle AOM = 30°. Thus OM = OA cos 30° = 1·(√3/2) = √3/2. Final answer: √3/2

The image shows that in the reassembled rectangle, AD and GH form the top side, AF lies along the diagonal, AG forms an outer vertical side, and GF is fitted against DF, so GF=DF. Let AD=x; since DF:AD=5:12, DF=5x/12, and the right triangle ADF gives AF=√(AD²+DF²)=13x/12. Thus the new rectangle has width AD+GH=x+6 and height AG=AF−GF=AF−DF=13x/12−5x/12=2x/3. Its diagonal has the same slope as AF, so height/width=DF/AD=5/12; therefore (2x/3)/(x+6)=5/12, giving 8x=5x+30 and x=10. Final answer: 10

The diagram shows that at the top-right vertex V of the larger hexagon, the top triangle has a right angle, while the inward segment passes through consecutive vertices X and Y of the smaller hexagon, with X between V and Y. A regular hexagon has interior angle 120°, so the angle at V in the adjacent triangle is 120° − 90° = 30°; therefore the congruent triangles are 30°-60°-90° triangles, whose side lengths are in the ratio 1:√3:2. Let the short leg be a. The larger hexagon’s side is the long leg, so L = √3a; also VX = a by congruence, while VY, the adjacent triangle’s hypotenuse, is 2a. Hence the smaller hexagon’s side is XY = VY − VX = 2a − a = a. The perimeter ratio is 6L/(6XY) = L/XY = √3. Final answer: √3

The figure shows that A lies on both the hyperbola and line CD, while EF is parallel to CD and shifted 2 units to the right. Since A=(1,3) lies on y=m/x, 3=m/1, so m=3; accordingly CD is x+y=4 and EF is x+y=6. The hyperbola segment below CD is (t,3/t) for 1≤t≤3, and reflection across x+y=4 maps it to (4−3/t,4−t). A reflected point would lie on EF only if (4−3/t)+(4−t)=6, giving t²−2t+3=0, whose discriminant is −8, so there is no common point, rather than exactly one. Thus the stated conditions are inconsistent. Final answer: no such m.

The figure shows right triangle ABC with BC vertical, AC horizontal, and a right angle at C; the waterfront slope AB has slope ratio BC:AC = 1:√3. Thus 4:AC = 1:√3, so AC = 4√3 m. Final answer: 4√3 m.

From A to B, the diagram shows a displacement of 3 units right and 1 unit up, while from A to C it shows 3 units right and 3 units up, so AB = (3,1) and AC = (3,3). For the angle A between two vectors, tan A = |AB × AC|/(AB · AC) = |3·3 − 1·3|/(3·3 + 1·3) = 6/12 = 1/2. Final answer: 1/2

The image shows A above B, D above C, M at the midpoint of BC, and P drawn on AB as one position along the path B-A-D; let B=(0,0), A=(0,6), C=(20,0), D=(20,6), and M=(10,0). If B is reflected to B′ across MP, then MB′=MB=10, so B′ must be a nontrivial intersection of the rectangle’s boundary with the circle (x−10)²+y²=100. These intersections are (2,6), (18,6), and C=(20,0), excluding the unchanged point B. Since MP is the perpendicular bisector of BB′, for B′=(2,6) its equation is x+3y=10, giving P=(0,10/3) and MP=√(10²+(10/3)²)=10√10/3; for B′=(18,6), the crease is 3x+y=30, giving P=(8,6) and MP=√(2²+6²)=2√10; for B′=C, the crease is x=10, giving P=(10,6) and MP=6. Thus the condition permits three crease lengths, with the pictured P-on-AB case corresponding to 10√10/3. Final answer: 6, 2√10, or 10√10/3.

The figure shows D moving along the hypotenuse AB of right triangle ABC, with AC = 2, BC = 4, and E obtained by rotating CD counterclockwise 90° about C. Set C = (0,0), A = (0,2), and B = (−4,0), and let t = AD/AB, where 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Then D = (−4t, 2−2t), and the 90° counterclockwise rotation gives E = (2t−2, −4t). Using the determinant area formula, [△BED] = 1/2|det(D−B, E−B)| = 2(1−t)(1+5t) = 2(1+4t−5t²). This concave quadratic is maximized when t = −4/[2(−5)] = 2/5. Since AB = √(AC²+BC²) = √20 = 2√5, AD = (2/5)AB = 4√5/5. Final answer: 4√5/5

The three parallel lines a, b, and c cut transversal l₁ at A, C, E and transversal l₂ at B, D, F, so corresponding intercepts are proportional: BD/DF = AC/CE = 3/4. Since BF = BD + DF, BD/BF = 3/(3 + 4) = 3/7. Final answer: 3/7

The image shows the increasing line I₁ and the decreasing line I₂ intersecting at P(a,2), with I₁ above I₂ to the right of P. Since P lies on I₁: y=x+1, we have 2=a+1, so a=1. Therefore x+1≥mx+n holds at and to the right of the intersection, giving x≥1. Final answer: [1,+∞)

The image shows right triangle ABC with ∠ACB = 90° and altitude CD perpendicular to hypotenuse AB at D. Since AC = 4 and BC = 3, the Pythagorean theorem gives AB = √(4² + 3²) = 5. From △ABC ∼ △ACD, corresponding sides satisfy AB/AC = AC/AD, so AD = AC²/AB = 4²/5 = 16/5. Final answer: 16/5

The graph is a decreasing line that intersects the y-axis at 2 and the x-axis at 3. Thus k=(0-2)/(3-0)=-2/3 and b=2, so kx+b≥0 becomes -2x/3+2≥0, which gives x≤3; equivalently, the line is on or above the x-axis for x≤3. Final answer: (-∞,3]

The figure shows that ABC is right-angled at C, AB=7 is the hypotenuse, D is the midpoint of AB, P lies on AB, and Q lies on the perpendicular bisector FG of CP. Therefore PQ=CQ, so PQ+QD=CQ+QD≥CD by the triangle inequality. Since D is the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle, CD=AB/2=7/2. Equality is attainable by taking P=D and Q as the midpoint of CD; then Q is on the perpendicular bisector of CP=CD and lies between C and D, giving CQ+QD=CD. Final answer: 7/2

The image shows A = (−3,0), B = (0,4), C = (0,c) with 0 ≤ c ≤ 4, and B′ on the positive x-axis. Since folding along AC reflects B to B′, points A and C on the fold line are equidistant from B and B′. Let B′ = (t,0). From AB = AB′, 5 = |t + 3|, so t = 2 or −8; the image and C ∈ OB imply t = 2. Then CB = CB′ gives 4 − c = √(2² + c²). Squaring yields 16 − 8c + c² = 4 + c², so c = 3/2. Final answer: (0, 3/2)

The figure shows E on AB and F on BC, with the first fold making AE equal to the rectangle’s height BC, so AE = 1, and the second fold placing CF onto EF, so CF = EF. Since BEF is an isosceles right triangle with the right angle at B, let BE = BF = x; then EF = x√2. Because BC = BF + FC, 1 = x + x√2, giving x = 1/(1 + √2) = √2 − 1. Therefore AB = AE + EB = 1 + (√2 − 1) = √2. Final answer: √2

The figure shows the six congruent squares in two staggered rows of three, with EH and FG parallel sides of small squares and EG forming a straight chain of four perpendicular small-square sides. Let x = DH and let y = DE; then the side EH has horizontal and vertical components x and y, so a perpendicular side directed down and right has components y horizontally and x vertically. Since EG consists of four such sides and spans the full horizontal width of ABCD, 4y = 10, giving y = 5/2. Following H to E, E to G, and G to F gives the full vertical height 10, consisting of two drops of y and four drops of x, so 2y + 4x = 10. Thus 5 + 4x = 10, giving x = 5/4. Final answer: 5/4
From the grid, take C=(0,0), B=(4,2), and A=(5,5). The slopes of AC and AB are 1 and 3, respectively, so the tangent of the angle between them is tan A=|(3−1)/(1+3·1)|=2/4=1/2. Final answer: 1/2

The image shows AB=2, BC=1, EF perpendicular to AB with E directly above F, and EG parallel to diagonal BD. Set A=(0,0), B=(2,0), C=(2,1), D=(0,1), and let F=(t,0), so E=(t,1). The figure shows A(−1,0) and B(2,3) on the parabola, with M lying on the arc above line AB and MA, MB forming adjacent sides of the parallelogram. The diagram shows E on AC, F on AB, D on BC, and EF is the crease mapping A to D, so every point on EF is equidistant from A and D. Set A=(0,0), C=(0,8), and B=(8,8); since AE=5, E=(0,5). The figure shows \(D\) on \(AB\), \(E\) on \(AC\), and \(F\) on \(BC\), with \(DE\parallel BC\) and \(EF\parallel AB\). Since \(AD=2BD\), \(AB=AD+BD=3BD\), so \(AD/AB=2/3\). The image shows that 199 of 301 women and 152 of 254 men approved the new design plan, giving sample proportions p̂W = 199/301 = 0.661 and p̂M = 152/254 = 0.598. Test H0: pW = pM against Ha: pW > pM using the pooled proportion p̂ = (199 + 152)/(301 + 254) = 351/555 = 0.632. The two-proportion z statistic is z = (p̂W − p̂M)/√[p̂(1 − p̂)(1/301 + 1/254)] = (0.661 − 0.598)/0.0411 ≈ 1.53, which gives a one-sided p-value of about 0.063. Because 0.063 > 0.05, the null hypothesis is not rejected. Final answer: At the 5% level, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the proportion of women who approve is higher than the proportion of men who approve.

The image shows the uniform conducting rod pivoted at its upper end, with its lower end sliding along the semicircular conductor; its small angular displacement θ=α is measured from the downward vertical, while the magnetic field B points perpendicular to the circuit plane and gravity acts downward. Rotation changes the enclosed area at the rate dS/dt=(ℓ²/2)θ̇, so the induced emf is ε=−(Bℓ²/2)θ̇ and the current is I=ε/R. The resulting magnetic torque opposes the motion and has magnitude B²ℓ⁴θ̇/(4R). Therefore ω²=ω₀²−β²=3g/(2ℓ)−[3B²ℓ²/(8mR)]². Substituting B=2 T, ℓ=0.1 m, m=0.05 kg, R=0.2 Ω, and g=9.81 m/s² gives β=1.5 s⁻¹ and ω²=147.15−2.25=144.9 s⁻². Final answer: 144.9 s⁻²

The image shows the slab parallel to the plates, with the upper plate carrying +σ, the lower plate carrying −σ, separation d, and the slab moving upward and rightward at θ = 30°. Since d ≪ s, edge effects are negligible, and after contact with either plate the conducting slab leaves with that plate’s charge sign and magnitude Q = σs² = (50 × 10⁻⁶)(0.05)² = 1.25 × 10⁻⁷ C; thus the initial charge q is irrelevant after many collisions. The field between the plates is E = σ/ε₀, directed downward, so after a lower-plate collision the negative slab accelerates upward and after an upper-plate collision the positive slab accelerates downward; therefore the acceleration always follows its post-collision vertical motion and has magnitude a = QE/m = σ²s²/(mε₀) = 7.0588 m/s². The horizontal speed remains vx = v cos θ, so traveling L horizontally takes T = L/(v cos θ) = 15/[3 cos(30°)] = 5.7735 s. Its initial vertical speed is u = v sin θ = 1.5 m/s, giving total vertical path length Y = uT + aT²/2 = 1.5(5.7735) + 7.0588(5.7735)²/2 = 126.307 m. Starting midway between the plates, the first collision occurs after d/2 and each subsequent collision after another d, so N is the largest integer satisfying (N − 1/2)d ≤ Y: N = floor(Y/d + 1/2) = floor(126.307/0.005 + 0.5) = 25,261. Final answer: 25,261 collisions.

The image depicts the coin edge tilted by θ above the horizontal, with the lower rim point acting as the pivot and the opposite point falling toward the surface. Treating the unspecified rim thickness as negligible for inertia, a uniform thin disk has moment of inertia about a tangent pivot axis Iₚ = mr²/4 + mr² = 5mr²/4. For the small angle shown, the gravitational torque is approximately mgr, so the angular acceleration is α ≈ mgr/Iₚ = 4g/(5r), and the time for a coin released from rest at angle θ to reach horizontal is τ₀ = √(2θ/α) = √(5rθ/(2g)). At each collision the retained energy is multiplied by k, while the small-angle potential energy is mgrθ, so the successive maximum angles are θₙ = kⁿθ and the corresponding half-swing times are τₙ = τ₀kⁿᐟ². The figure shows two equal-mass particles leaving A in opposite directions with speeds v and 2v. The image shows the upper solid hemisphere fixed to a support and the lower hemisphere beneath it, with their parallel circular faces of radius 4 cm separated by a thin water layer having a concave meniscus at the rim. The image shows the very long, nearly vertical thread attached to the bar’s lower end, with the bar initially extending vertically upward in unstable equilibrium. For thread length L ≫ l, the joint’s vertical displacement and the horizontal component of tension are negligible during the fall, so the rod’s center of mass has fixed horizontal position and vertical coordinate yCM = (l/2)cosθ, where θ is measured from the initial upward vertical. Therefore K = ml²(1 + 3sin²θ)θ̇²/24 and U = mgl cosθ/2; conservation of energy gives θ̇² = 12g(1 − c)/[l(4 − 3c²)], where c = cosθ. Differentiating this relation gives θ̈ = (6g/l)sinθ[D − 6c(1 − c)]/D², with D = 4 − 3c². Taking torque about the center of mass, T(l/2)sinθ = (ml²/12)θ̈, hence T/(mg) = (3c² − 6c + 4)/(4 − 3c²)². Writing x = 1 − c, this becomes (1 + 3x²)/(1 + 6x − 3x²)²; minimization gives x³ + x = 2/3, whose positive root is x = (2/√3)sinh[(1/3)asinh(√3)] ≈ 0.5233355. The image shows the slab midway between the upper +σ plate and lower −σ plate, moving upward and to the right at 30°, with plate separation d. The image shows the block on a plane inclined at angle α, with gravity having components mg sin α down the plane and mg cos α normal to it; the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane. The image shows the cylinder moving right at 10 m/s while spinning counterclockwise and maintaining a horizontal path over 200 m, with gravity downward. In the cylinder’s center-of-mass frame, the far-field fluid velocity is u = −v, so at r = R the given potential yields vθ = −2u sinθ + Γ/(2πR) = 2v sinθ + Rω, where Γ = 2πR²ω. Applying Bernoulli’s equation, p = C − ρvθ²/2 − ρgR sinθ, and integrating the pressure force over the cylindrical surface gives an upward buoyant force ρgπR²H and an upward circulation-induced lift ρvΓH = 2πρHvR²ω. A horizontal path requires vertical force balance: ρgπR²H + 2πρHvR²ω = Mg. Therefore, ω = [Mg − ρgπR²H]/(2πρHvR²) = [(10)(9.81) − (700)(9.81)π(0.08)²(0.20)]/[2π(700)(0.20)(10)(0.08)²] = 1.25 rad/s. Final answer: 1.25 rad/s counterclockwise.

The image shows a horizontal ray striking the first radial half-lens perpendicularly at r=λ/2 and leaving the last half-lens at r=2λ, with successive lens normals rotating clockwise. Let θ be the cumulative clockwise rotation, x=r/λ, and m=tan p, where p is the ray’s angle counterclockwise from the current forward normal. Adjacent lenses are separated by dθ=1/n, and f=nλ, so each thin lens changes the local slope by −r/f=−x dθ, while rotation of the normal contributes (1+m²)dθ; therefore dm/dθ=1+m²−x. Straight-line propagation between radial lenses gives dx/dθ=xm. Eliminating θ yields d(m²)/dx−2m²/x=2/x−2, whose solution is m²=−1+2x+Cx². Perpendicular incidence at x=1/2 gives m=0 and hence C=0, so m=√(2x−1) on the outward branch. Thus θ=∫ from 1/2 to 2 of dx/[x√(2x−1)]=2 arctan(√3)=2π/3, while the exit angle relative to the last normal is p=arctan(√3)=π/3. The global outgoing angle is p−θ=−π/3 relative to the incident ray, indicating clockwise deflection. Final answer: π/3 rad (approximately 1.047 rad, clockwise).

The image shows A at the bottom of the vertical circle, B at the top, and θ measured from the downward vertical through A. The image shows the loop wrapping once around the cylinder, with its two symmetric branches meeting at the lower knot and the free end pulled downward parallel to the cylinder axis. At impending downward sliding, friction acts upward; consider one half of the loop, spanning an azimuthal angle 0 ≤ φ ≤ π from the upper symmetry point to the knot. If α is the angle the thread makes with the circumferential direction and T is its tension, the circumferential component H = T cos α is constant because the contact force has only radial and axial components. The normal force per unit length is n = T cos²α/R = H cos α/R. At the critical condition the axial friction is μn, while vertical force balance gives d(H tan α)/ds = μH cos α/R. Since dφ/ds = cos α/R, this reduces to d(tan α)/dφ = μ. The thread is horizontal at the upper symmetry point, so tan α = μφ. Hence the critical loop length is L₀ = 2R∫₀^π sec α dφ = 2R∫₀^π√(1+μ²φ²)dφ. Using the supplied integral gives L₀ = πR√(1+π²μ²) + (R/μ)arcsinh(πμ). For a shorter loop the required local friction ratio is below μ and the loop can remain locked, whereas a longer loop would require a ratio greater than μ and must slide. Final answer: L₀ = πR√(1+π²μ²) + (R/μ)arcsinh(πμ), with L₀ = 2πR for μ = 0 by continuity.

The image places positive charges Q1 and Q2 at (-2a,0) and (-a,0), negative charges Q3 and Q4 at (a,0) and (2a,0), and the positive test charge q at (0,b). Pairing charges at equal distances d=a and d=2a from the y-axis, the vertical components cancel because the paired forces have equal magnitudes and opposite y-components, while their positive x-components add: F_x=2kqQ[a/(a²+b²)^(3/2)+2a/(4a²+b²)^(3/2)]>0 and F_y=0. Final answer: The net force is directed horizontally along the positive x-axis, toward Q3 and Q4.

The image shows q at (0,b), with positive Q1 and Q4 symmetrically located at x=−2a and +2a and negative Q2 and Q3 at x=−a and +a. By symmetry, the horizontal force components cancel. Since b²+4a²>b²+a², this expression is negative: the closer negative charges exert a stronger downward attraction than the upward repulsion from the farther positive charges. Final answer: Along the negative y-axis, toward the origin.

The image places the positive test charge q at (0,b), with positive Q1 at (−2a,0), negative Q2 at (−a,0), positive Q3 at (a,0), and negative Q4 at (2a,0). The image shows the loop’s two strands meeting at a low point on the cylinder, with the free end pulled downward parallel to the cylinder axis, so impending motion is axial and friction on the loop acts upward. Unroll the cylindrical surface and let x be circumferential distance from the point opposite the knot toward the knot, so one symmetric half-loop has 0 ≤ x ≤ πR; write p = dz/dx for its axial slope. If T is the tension, its constant circumferential component is H = T/√(1+p²), while the cylinder’s normal force per unit thread length is n = T/[R(1+p²)] = H/[R√(1+p²)]. With u=μx/R and the supplied integral, this becomes L₀ = (R/μ)[πμ√(1+π²μ²)+arcsinh(πμ)]. Final answer: L₀ = (R/μ)[πμ√(1+π²μ²)+arcsinh(πμ)], with the continuous μ→0 limit L₀=2πR.

The image shows superconducting ring B positioned horizontally above cylindrical magnet A, so moving B into A’s magnetic field changes the magnetic flux through the ring. By Faraday–Lenz law, ε = −dΦ/dt, this changing flux produces an induced current whose magnetic field opposes the flux change, creating the repulsive force needed for levitation. Once B is stationary, dΦ/dt = 0 and the induced emf becomes zero; however, because the superconducting ring has zero electrical resistance, the established current does not decay and remains as a persistent current that maintains the levitating force. Final answer: An induced current is generated while B is placed into the magnetic field, and it continues to exist after B becomes stable.

The image shows a vertical bar magnet with its S pole at the lower end falling downward along the axis of a fixed horizontal conducting ring. By Faraday–Lenz law, ε = −dΦB/dt: as the S pole approaches from above, the upward magnetic flux through the ring increases, so the induced field is downward, requiring a clockwise current when viewed from top to bottom; after the magnet passes through and moves away below the ring, the upward flux decreases, so the induced field is upward and the current reverses to counterclockwise, passing through zero at the flux maximum.
