The spring therefore changes from compression δ0 to extension δ1, so A travels s=δ0+δ1=2mg sinθ/k, independent of F provided F is sufficient to reach this displacement; for a suddenly applied constant force, actual separation requires F>mg sinθ. Final answer: 2mg sinθ/k

The graph shows car B at x = 20 m when t = 5 s, and its displacement-time curve is tangent to the t-axis at t = 10 s, so x(10) = 0 and its velocity v(10) = 0. Since B has constant acceleration, x(t) = x(10) + v(10)(t - 10) + (1/2)a(t - 10)^2. Substituting t = 5 s and x = 20 m gives 20 = (1/2)a(5 - 10)^2 = 12.5a, hence |a| = 1.6 m/s². Final answer: 1.6 m/s²

In both tapes, the particle is at position 0 at t0 and position 8 at t4; each undergoes the same displacement, ΔxA=ΔxB=8, during four identical counting intervals. Using the average-velocity formula v̄=Δx/Δt, and since ΔtA=ΔtB, their average velocities have the same magnitude and direction; if one counting interval is T, then both equal 8/(4T)=2/T. Final answer: The average velocities of particles A and B are equal, v̄A=v̄B.

The vertical axis is velocity and the horizontal axis is time; from 0 to t1, B’s shallower velocity line lies above A’s steeper line until they meet at t1. Since displacement is the area under a velocity–time graph, |Δx| = ∫0^t1 v dt, the area under B’s graph is larger than that under A’s graph. Final answer: The displacement magnitude of B is greater than that of A, |ΔxB| > |ΔxA|.

The image shows a vertical drop-tower ride, consistent with the cabin moving vertically. At 40 m above the ground, the cabin has not yet reached the 28 m braking height, so both the tourist and the bottle are in free fall with downward acceleration a=g. Taking downward as positive, the bottle satisfies mg−N=ma, where N is the force of the hand on the bottle; thus N=m(g−a)=1×(9.8−9.8)=0 N. By Newton’s third law, the bottle exerts an equal and opposite force of zero magnitude on the hand. Final answer: 0 N

The figure shows coil P immediately to the right of the magnet’s S pole, so swinging P to the right moves it away and decreases the magnetic flux directed from right to left toward S. By Faraday–Lenz law, ε = −dΦB/dt, the induced current produces a magnetic field from right to left to oppose this decrease. Viewed from right to left, this field points away from the observer, so the right-hand rule gives a clockwise current. Final answer: clockwise.

The copper disk rotates at constant angular velocity about its vertical axle in a uniform upward magnetic field, with P contacting the rim and Q contacting the axle so that resistor R connects the rim to the center. At distance r from the axis, the disk speed is v = ωr, giving a radial motional emf dε = Bv dr = Bωr dr; hence ε = ∫₀ᵃ Bωr dr = Bωa²/2, where a is the disk radius. Since B, ω, a, and the circuit resistance are constant, I = ε/Rtotal is time-independent. Final answer: The magnitude of the current remains constant.

The graph shows a period T = 2×10⁻² s: for the first half-cycle the voltage is +100 V, while for the second half-cycle it is a negative half-sine wave with peak magnitude 50 V. An ideal AC ammeter reads the rms current, and the ideal voltmeter draws no current, so I_rms = U_rms/R. Thus U_rms² = (1/T)[100²(T/2) + 50²(T/2)(1/2)] = 5000 + 625 = 5625 V², where the mean value of sin² over a half-cycle is 1/2. Therefore U_rms = 75 V and I_rms = 75/100 = 0.75 A. Final answer: 0.75 A

The image shows bulb A connected in parallel with coil L, while bulb B is connected in parallel with capacitor C; after the switch is opened, L and A form one discharge loop, and C and B form another. Let each bulb have resistance r and the coil have DC resistance rL. In the steady DC state before opening, C is an open circuit, and the currents through L and A combine through B, so IB=IL+IA; because L and A are parallel, ILrL=IAr, giving IL=IBr/(r+rL)<IB. Immediately after opening, the inductor current cannot change abruptly, so the initial current through A has magnitude IL and flows oppositely to its former direction; this is smaller than the steady current that the identical bulb B had already safely carried. The large inductance only makes A glow for a longer time as the current decays and does not create a larger initial current, while C discharges separately through B. Final answer: No, bulb A’s filament will not be burned out.

Figure A shows a uniform square wire frame with side ab forming one of its four equal sides; although only half the frame lies in the changing magnetic field shown in Figure B, the induced current has the same magnitude throughout the single closed loop. Since the total resistance is R and the wire is uniform, the resistance of side ab is R/4. Its heating power is therefore P=I²(R/4), so I=√(4P/R)=2√(P/R). Final answer: 2√(P/R).

The image shows C to the right of D with horizontal separation CD=L, while the rope remains inclined by β from the vertical and trails to the right as the helicopter moves left from C to D, so the tension component toward D opposes the horizontal air drag. Starting from hover, L=at²/2, hence the camera’s horizontal acceleration is a=2L/t² because its position relative to the helicopter is constant. If T is the rope tension, vertical equilibrium gives T cos β=mg, so T sin β=mg tan β. Taking the direction from C to D as positive, T sin β−F=ma, and therefore F=mg tan β−2mL/t², with g tan β≥2L/t² for the drag direction shown. Final answer: F=m(g tan β−2L/t²).

The figure shows a copper disk of radius L rotating in a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to the disk, with contacts a and b connecting the rim and central axis to a circuit of total resistance R. At radius r, the disk’s tangential speed is v=ωr, so the motional electric field has magnitude vB=Bωr along the radial direction; therefore the induced emf between the axis and rim is ε=∫₀ᴸBωr dr=BωL²/2. By Ohm’s law, the current magnitude is I=ε/R. Final answer: I=BωL²/(2R).

The graph shows that from t1 to t2 the positive magnetic field B increases with an increasing slope, while ring L is coplanar with and enclosed by the wire frame connected to the solenoid. Using Faraday’s law, ε = −NS(dB/dt), and I = ε/R when self-inductance is neglected, the increasing magnitude of dB/dt means that the induced current in the wire frame increases in magnitude, so the magnetic flux it produces through L also increases. By Lenz’s law, L develops an induced current opposite to the current around the surrounding frame; the facing current elements are therefore antiparallel and repel, producing forces directed toward the center of L. Final answer: The circular ring L tends to contract.

The figure shows coil A connected to the power supply through S1, while coil B forms a closed circuit through S2. When S1 is opened, the magnetic flux through B decreases, inducing an emf εB = −NB dΦ/dt; by Lenz’s law, the induced current in B produces a magnetic field that opposes this decrease and temporarily maintains the electromagnet’s attraction on D, delaying its release. Final answer: coil B.

The image shows “Luojia-1” moving on a circular orbit of radius R centered on Earth. Circular orbital motion has constant angular speed ω=θ/t when θ is measured in radians, and one complete revolution corresponds to 2π radians, so T=2π/ω=2πt/θ; the given gravitational constant G is not needed because the observed angular displacement and elapsed time already determine the period. Final answer: T=2πt/θ.

In the x–t graph, the trajectories of cars A and B intersect at the dashed time t1; an intersection means their position coordinates are equal at that instant, so xA(t1)=xB(t1). Final answer: The two cars are at the same position at time t1.

From Figure A, each period T = 2 × 10⁻² s consists of a constant +100 V during the first half-period and a negative half-sine wave of peak magnitude 50 V during the second half-period. An ideal AC ammeter reads the RMS current, so U_rms² = (1/T)[100²(T/2) + 50²(T/2)(1/2)], where the final factor 1/2 is the mean value of sin² over a half-cycle. Thus U_rms² = 5000 + 625 = 5625 V², giving U_rms = 75 V. Since R = 100 Ω, I_rms = U_rms/R = 75/100 = 0.75 A. Final answer: 0.75 A

The image shows coil P at the right-hand S-pole end of the horizontal bar magnet, so when P swings to the right it moves away from the S pole. At that side of an S pole, the magnetic field points from right to left; therefore the magnetic flux through P in that direction decreases. By Faraday–Lenz law, ε = −dΦ/dt, the induced current must produce a magnetic field from right to left to oppose this decrease. By the right-hand rule, viewed from right to left this requires a clockwise current. Final answer: clockwise.

The image shows M and N on opposite sides of the center O along the same diameter, with OM = ON = R/2. Inside a uniformly charged insulating sphere, the electric field is radial and is given by E⃗(r⃗) = Qr⃗/(4πε₀R³). Since the position vectors of M and N satisfy r⃗M = −r⃗N, their electric fields satisfy E⃗M = −E⃗N; thus they have equal magnitudes but point in opposite directions along MN. Final answer: The electric field intensities at M and N are in opposite directions.

The image shows workers directly handling high-voltage transmission lines while wearing conductive shielding suits. The woven metal clothing forms an approximately equipotential enclosure around each worker, so induced charges remain on its outer surface and the electric field inside is greatly reduced, preventing dangerous current from passing through the body; this is the Faraday-cage effect. Final answer: Electrostatic shielding using the Faraday-cage principle.

The image shows that the ball is launched horizontally at A, all accelerations are vertical because gravity and the electric field are vertical, and its velocity is again horizontal at C. Hence the horizontal velocity remains v0 throughout, while the vertical velocity is zero at both A and C, so v_A=v_C=v0. Therefore Δv_AB=v_B−v_A and Δv_BC=v_C−v_B=v_A−v_B=−Δv_AB, meaning the two velocity changes are opposite vectors with equal magnitudes; the condition AB=2BC is not needed for this comparison. Final answer: |Δv_AB|=|Δv_BC|, or 1:1.

The image shows A carrying +Q and B carrying −Q fixed equidistant from the vertical rod, so C carrying +q remains at equal distances r from A and B throughout its descent. Its electric potential energy due to A and B is U = k(+Q)(+q)/r + k(−Q)(+q)/r = kQq/r − kQq/r = 0 at every height; the interaction energy between A and B is also constant because they remain fixed. The loss of gravitational potential energy is dissipated by friction, consistent with C reaching the tabletop at zero speed, but this does not change the electric potential energy. Final answer: Yes, the electric potential energy remains unchanged.

The figure shows that A is at the fixed height h directly above C, while changing the incline from θ1 to the smaller θ2 shifts its junction with the horizontal track but leaves A and B fixed. Let L=BC and let the friction coefficient be μ. For an incline angle θ, its length is h/sinθ, so friction on it dissipates μmg cosθ·h/sinθ=μmgh cotθ; the junction is h cotθ horizontally from C, making the remaining horizontal distance to B equal to L−h cotθ, where friction dissipates μmg(L−h cotθ). Thus the total frictional loss is μmgh cotθ+μmg(L−h cotθ)=μmgL, independent of θ. Since the initial gravitational potential energy mgh and the contact-transition loss are also the same, 1/2 mv²=mgh−μmgL in both experiments. Final answer: v1=v2.

The image shows two horizontal plates with the upper plate positive and the lower plate negative, so the electric-field magnitude between them is E = U/d. For the oil drop to remain suspended, the electric force balances its weight: |q|E = mg. Therefore |q| = mg/E = mgd/U. Final answer: mgd/U

The image shows the ion velocities symmetrically distributed about the y-axis, with boundary directions making angles α/2 with it, while the deflected ions land between M and N on the positive x-axis with MN=L. In the magnetic field, each ion follows a circular path of radius R=mv/(|q|B). If the initial velocity makes an angle θ with the positive x-axis, its next intersection with the x-axis is at x=2R sinθ. The central ray has θ=π/2 and lands at N, so ON=2R; either boundary ray has θ=π/2±α/2 and lands at M, so OM=2R cos(α/2). Therefore L=MN=2R−2R cos(α/2), giving cos(α/2)=1−L/(2R)=1−|q|BL/(2mv). Final answer: \(\cos(\alpha/2)=1-\frac{|q|BL}{2mv}\).

The image places wires a and b symmetrically above and below O, while M and N lie symmetrically to the left and right of O on the perpendicular bisector. Let Oa=Ob=d and OM=ON=x; each wire is then at distance R=√(d²+x²) from either M or N, so each individual field has magnitude B=μ₀I/(2πR). By the right-hand rule, at each point the components along MN from the two wires cancel, while the components parallel to ab add, giving a resultant magnitude 2B(x/R)=μ₀Ix/[π(d²+x²)]. This value is the same at M and N, but reflection across the line ab reverses the resultant direction, so the two fields point oppositely along ab. Final answer: The magnetic induction intensities at M and N are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

The intersection of curve a and line b gives the operating point U=2.5 V and I=0.20 A, while the dashed tangent to curve a at this point intersects the voltage axis at 5.0 V. Because the photocell is nonlinear, its internal resistance at the operating point is the magnitude of the tangent slope, r=|dU/dI|=(5.0−2.5)/(0.20−0)=12.5 Ω. Final answer: 12.5 Ω

At t=0 the two trajectories are at x=16 m and x=12 m; since the cars move toward decreasing x and B is in front, B corresponds to the curved trajectory starting at x=12 m. On an x–t graph, velocity is the slope v=dx/dt; this curve has a negative slope whose magnitude continually increases, starting approximately from zero. Thus B moves in the negative x-direction and speeds up continuously; if the drawn curve is intended to be parabolic, its velocity decreases uniformly in algebraic value. Final answer: Car B’s velocity becomes increasingly negative, so its speed increases continuously in the negative x-direction.

The image shows small horizontal ring B falling coaxially toward, through, and then away from the larger fixed horizontal ring A, which carries a constant current I. By Faraday–Lenz law, ε = −dΦB/dt: while B approaches A, the magnetic flux from A through B increases, so B’s induced current produces an opposing field and is opposite to the current in A; when B is momentarily in the plane of A, the flux is maximal and its rate of change is zero, so the induced emf is instantaneously zero; after B passes through and moves away, the flux decreases, so B’s induced current reinforces the original flux and is in the same direction as the current in A. Final answer: Opposite before passing through A, instantaneously zero in A’s plane, and the same direction after passing through A.

The battery’s longer plate is on the right, so when S is closed the conventional current flows up the right lead and through the fixed coil toward the left; following the winding shown, this current is counterclockwise when viewed from the left, producing an increasing magnetic field directed leftward. By Faraday–Lenz law, ε = −dΦ/dt, the ring must produce a field opposing this increase, namely rightward; the right-hand rule then gives a clockwise induced current as viewed from the left. Final answer: clockwise.

The image shows a uniformly positively charged insulating sphere, with M and N on opposite sides of the center O along the same diameter and each at radial distance r=R/2. For a uniformly charged solid sphere, the enclosed charge at radius r is Q_enclosed=Q(r³/R³), so Gauss’s law gives E=kQ_enclosed/r²=kQr/R³. Substituting r=R/2 gives equal field magnitudes at the two points: E_M=E_N=k|Q|/(2R²). Final answer: E_M=E_N=k|Q|/(2R²).

The image shows charged oil droplets sprayed between two parallel plates connected to a voltage, with their motion observed through a microscope. By balancing the electric force qE against the droplet’s effective weight, Millikan determined the droplet charge and found that all measured charges were integer multiples of a smallest value, the elementary charge e ≈ 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Final answer: the electron’s electric charge

The graph shows that the particle is at the origin at t1, reaches its highest position Hm at t2, and returns to the origin at t3. Since displacement relative to O is y(t), it increases in the positive y direction from 0 to Hm during t1 to t2, then decreases from Hm to 0 during t2 to t3; therefore, the net displacement over the entire interval is y(t3)−y(t1)=0. Final answer: The displacement first increases from 0 to Hm and then decreases to 0, with zero net displacement from t1 to t3.

Figure B shows a sinusoidal voltage that is zero at t=0 and initially increases, with peak value Um=200 V and period T=2×10⁻² s. Thus ω=2π/T=100π rad/s, and since the initial phase is zero, u=Um sin(ωt). The transformer turn ratio and inductance do not affect the expression of the applied primary voltage. Final answer: u=200sin(100πt) V.

The image shows a high-speed maglev train, a car braking from 100 km/h over 31 m, a shell being fired, and Liu Xiang completing the 110 m hurdles in 13.07 s. A is correct because high speed does not imply acceleration; if the train moves in a straight line at constant velocity, its acceleration is zero. For B, \(v_0=100/3.6=27.78\ \mathrm{m/s}\), and \(0-v_0^2=2as\) gives \(a=-27.78^2/(2\times31)\approx-12.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\), so 12.5 m/s² is only the magnitude, not the acceleration under the direction of motion as positive. C is incorrect because the shell may momentarily have zero velocity when ignition begins, but the propellant force gives it nonzero acceleration. For D, the average speed is \(v=110/13.07\approx8.42\ \mathrm{m/s}\). Final answer: A and D

The image shows superconducting ring B horizontally levitating above the upper face of cylindrical magnet A. As B approaches A, the magnetic flux through the ring changes and induces a current opposing that change according to Lenz’s law. For the ring, the circuit equation is L(dI/dt) + RI = −dΦext/dt; after stable levitation, dΦext/dt = 0, and because the superconducting ring has R = 0, this gives dI/dt = 0 rather than I = 0. Thus the previously induced current remains constant as a persistent current, maintaining the magnetic interaction needed for levitation, provided B remains superconducting. Final answer: Yes, the induced current still exists as a persistent current.

The figure shows the closed metal ring N surrounding the right end of solenoid M and free to move left or right; closing S toward a energizes M, so the magnetic flux through N begins increasing from zero. By Lenz’s law, ε = −dΦ/dt, the induced current in N produces a magnetic field opposing this increase, making the adjacent faces of M and N like magnetic poles and therefore causing repulsion. Since N is on the right of M, it moves away from M. Final answer: To the right.

The image shows block A uphill of block B on a smooth incline, with B held at the downhill fixed stop C and the spring lying along the incline. Initially A is in equilibrium, so the spring is compressed by x₁ = mg sinθ/k and pushes A uphill; when B is just about to leave C, the stop’s reaction is zero, so the spring is stretched by x₂ = mg sinθ/k and pulls B uphill. Thus the initial and final spring deformations have equal magnitudes, so the spring’s elastic potential energy has no net change and its total work on A is zero. By the work-energy theorem, W_F + W_g + W_s = ΔK_A, where W_g = −ΔU_g and W_s = 0, hence W_F = ΔK_A + ΔU_g, which is the increase in A’s mechanical energy. Final answer: block A’s mechanical energy increase.

The image shows rod ab bridging two rails in a magnetic field directed out of the page, with the rail circuit passing through a solenoid next to the suspended copper coil c. The rod’s motional emf is ε=Bℓv, so with negligible rail resistance the solenoid current is I=Bℓv/R. For coil c to have an induced current, I must change; for c to be attracted, its induced current must flow in the same sense as the solenoid current, which by Lenz’s law occurs when the solenoid’s magnetic flux is decreasing. Thus v and I must decrease while the rod continues moving leftward. Final answer: The rod should move leftward with decreasing speed.

The fixed pulley is horizontally level with ring A at the stated instant, so A’s vertical velocity v1 is perpendicular to the rope segment joining A to the pulley. For the inextensible rope, L=l_AP+l_PB+constant, hence 0=dL/dt=dl_AP/dt+dl_PB/dt. Since dl_AP/dt is the component of A’s velocity along AP, dl_AP/dt=v1 cos 90°=0, so dl_PB/dt=0 and weight B is instantaneously at rest. Final answer: v2=0.

The figure shows that object A is farther from the vertical rotation axis than object B, so r_A>r_B; both objects have equal mass m and rotate with the same angular speed ω. The resultant force for uniform circular motion is the centripetal force F=mω²r, hence F_A=mω²r_A and F_B=mω²r_B. Therefore, because r_A>r_B, the resultant force on A is greater than that on B. Final answer: F_A>F_B

The figure shows a 10-turn coil of area 0.2 m² and internal resistance 2 Ω rotating about axis OO′ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B = 2/π T, with the external resistor R = 18 Ω connected in series with the coil. The peak induced emf is Eₘ = nBSω = 10 × 0.2 × (2/π) × 10π = 40 V; starting from the neutral-plane position determines only the phase and not the average power. Thus Eᵣₘₛ = Eₘ/√2 = 20√2 V, and the rms current is Iᵣₘₛ = Eᵣₘₛ/(R + r) = 20√2/(18 + 2) = √2 A. The average power consumed by R is P = Iᵣₘₛ²R = (√2)² × 18 = 36 W. Final answer: 36 W

The image shows the vertical pole translating horizontally a distance x while the monkey climbs vertically a height h. The horizontal displacement is x=v0t, and because the monkey starts from rest with uniform upward acceleration a, its vertical displacement is h=at²/2. These perpendicular components give a ground-relative displacement of √(x²+h²)=√[(v0t)²+(at²/2)²]. Final answer: √(v0²t²+a²t⁴/4)

The image shows equal forces F1 and F2 acting at the same angle θ to the horizontal, with each object moving the same horizontal distance s in the direction of the forces’ horizontal components; the opposite vertical components do no work because there is no vertical displacement. Using W=Fs cos θ, W1=F1s cos θ and W2=F2s cos θ, and since F1=F2, the masses do not affect the work done by these forces. Final answer: W1 = W2.

Coil A is connected through the switch and sliding rheostat to the AC source M–N, while nearby coil B forms a closed circuit with the small bulb and has no direct electrical connection to A. After the switch is closed, the alternating current in A produces a continuously changing magnetic field, so the magnetic flux through B changes and induces an emf according to εB = −NB dΦ/dt, equivalently εB = −M dIA/dt. If the coils are sufficiently coupled and the induced voltage is large enough, current flows through B and the bulb lights; the rheostat can adjust the current in A and hence the induced voltage. Final answer: Yes, the small bulb can light up due to mutual electromagnetic induction.

The image shows a vertical-drop amusement ride with tall guide towers and a passenger cabin moving vertically. The cabin free-falls from 76 m to 28 m, a distance of 48 m, so its speed when braking begins satisfies v² = 2g(48). It then stops uniformly over the remaining 28 m, so 0 = v² − 2a(28), giving the upward deceleration a = 2g(48)/(56) = 12g/7 = 16.8 m/s². At 15 m the cabin is still in this constant-deceleration stage. For the 1 kg bottle to accelerate upward with the cabin, the hand force F must satisfy F − mg = ma, hence F = m(g + a) = 1(9.8 + 16.8) = 26.6 N. Final answer: 26.6 N

The image shows Saturn on a larger orbit than Earth around the Sun, but it gives no numerical orbital distances or periods and is not necessarily drawn to scale. For two bodies orbiting the same central mass, Kepler’s third law gives T_S²/a_S³=T_E²/a_E³, so T_S/T_E=(a_S/a_E)^(3/2); because a_S>a_E, Saturn’s period is longer, but no numerical ratio can be obtained from the image alone. Final answer: T_S/T_E=(a_S/a_E)^(3/2)>1.

In the figure, coil M is located on the left side of metal ring N. After S is closed toward a, power supply E1 makes the current in M increase from zero, and the magnetic flux passing through N increases accordingly. According to Faraday's law ε=-dΦ/dt and Lenz's law, the magnetic field formed by the induced current generated in N must oppose the increase of the magnetic flux in M, so the adjacent parts of N and M have the same magnetic pole and repel each other; N is on the right side of M, so the direction away from M is to the right. Final answer: move to the right.

The image shows an elevator of mass M pulled upward by a cable, with an object of mass m resting on its floor; because the question asks for the resultant work on the elevator itself, its kinetic energy is based on M, not M+m. By the work–energy theorem, W_resultant=ΔK=1/2 Mv_2^2−1/2 Mv_1^2; equivalently, if the acceleration is constant, v_2^2−v_1^2=2aH gives W_resultant=MaH. Final answer: \(\frac{1}{2}M(v_2^2-v_1^2)\).

The image shows R0 in series with the load R across the transformer secondary, with the voltmeter connected across R; for an ideal transformer, I1/I2=N2/N1, so an unchanged primary input current means the secondary current is also unchanged. When R=5R0, the voltmeter reads 5.0 V, giving I2=5.0/(5R0)=1/R0. Originally R=11R0, so the total secondary voltage was U2=I2(R0+11R0)=(1/R0)(12R0)=12 V. Since N1:N2=4:1, U1/U2=4, and the original primary-coil RMS voltage was U1=4×12=48 V. Final answer: 48 V

The image shows Q sliding without friction on a horizontal rod, with the rope pulling it toward the vertical line through the fixed smooth ring O, while P hangs from the other end. While Q is to the left of O, its horizontal equation is m_Q a_Q = T cos θ; since the rope tension T is positive and 0 < θ < 90°, Q accelerates in its direction of motion and its speed increases. When Q is directly below O, θ = 90° and the horizontal component T cos θ becomes zero; after Q passes this position, the horizontal tension opposes its motion, so its speed decreases. Final answer: θ = 90° (π/2).

The figure shows a 10-turn coil rotating about axis OO′ perpendicular to the uniform magnetic field B and connected through slip rings to the external resistor R; the coil resistance r and resistor R are therefore in series. Starting from the neutral plane only fixes the phase, so the generated emf is sinusoidal with peak value Eₘ = nBSω = 10 × (2/π) × 0.2 × 10π = 40 V and rms value E = Eₘ/√2 = 20√2 V. The rms current is I = E/(R + r) = 20√2/(18 + 2) = √2 A, hence the average electric power consumed by R is P = I²R = (√2)² × 18 = 36 W. Final answer: 36 W.

The figure shows bulb L1 in series with the self-inductance coil L across the power supply, while L2 is in the separate resistor branch. Immediately after S is closed, the inductor prevents its current from changing suddenly, so the current through L1 starts at zero. For the L1 branch, E=I(R_{\text{branch}})+L\,dI/dt, giving I=E/R_{\text{branch}}[1-e^{-R_{\text{branch}}t/L}]; hence the current and the bulb power P=I²R_{\text{L1}} increase gradually. Because L is very large, this increase is slow. Final answer: L1 is initially off and gradually becomes brighter until reaching a steady brightness.

The figure shows that side ab is the rotation axis, the magnetic field B points upward along ab, and side bc of length l extends radially from the axis; for the depicted counterclockwise rotation, the angular-velocity vector is parallel to B. At a point on bc a distance r from b, the speed is v=ωr, so v×B is radially outward with magnitude Bωr. In electrostatic equilibrium inside the moving metal, E+v×B=0 and E=−∇U, hence dU/dr=Bωr. Therefore Uc−Ub=∫₀ˡBωr dr=Bωl²/2, so with Ubc=Ub−Uc, Final answer: Ubc=−Bωl²/2

The image shows that the triangular frame rotates rigidly about side ab, while the uniform magnetic field B is parallel to ab; because ab remains in the plane of the frame during rotation, B remains parallel to the frame’s plane at every instant. Thus the magnetic flux is Φ = B·A = BA cos 90° = 0, so the motional emf is ℰ = −dΦ/dt = 0 and therefore I = ℰ/R = 0. Final answer: No, there is no current in the metal frame.

Figure A shows the primary voltage has a peak value of 22√2 V, and Figure B shows capacitor C connected directly across the active 135-turn section of the secondary coil. For an ideal transformer, U2m/U1m=n2/n1, so U2m=22√2×135/270=11√2 V. Since C is just not broken down, its breakdown voltage equals the maximum instantaneous voltage across it; the lamp and rheostat do not change this voltage because they are in a parallel branch. Final answer: 11√2 V

The graph shows one particle’s velocity increasing uniformly from 0 to 6 m/s during the first 5 s, while the other moves at a constant 4 m/s. Displacement equals the area under a v–t graph, so by t=5 s their displacements are (1/2)(5)(6)=15 m and (5)(4)=20 m. Since they started from the same point, their separation is |20−15|=5 m. Final answer: 5 m

The image shows “Luojia-1” in a circular orbit of radius R measured from Earth’s center, with R greater than Earth’s radius rₑ. The first cosmic velocity v₁ = √(GM/rₑ) ≈ 7.9 km/s is the minimum launch speed for a near-Earth circular orbit; reaching a higher orbit requires a launch speed above this threshold, although the satellite’s circular orbital speed √(GM/R) at that higher altitude is less than 7.9 km/s. Final answer: greater than 7.9 km/s.

The image shows “Luojia-1” moving in a circular orbit of radius R measured from Earth’s center. For circular motion, Earth’s gravitational force supplies the centripetal force: GMm/R²=mω²R. Since the satellite turns through angle θ in time t, its angular velocity is ω=θ/t, with θ measured in radians. Substitution gives M=ω²R³/G=θ²R³/(Gt²). Final answer: M=θ²R³/(Gt²)

The image shows Tianzhou-1 and Tiangong-2 docked in Earth orbit; treating the combination as a body in uniform circular motion, Earth’s gravitational force provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = m(4π²r/T²), so Earth’s mass is M = 4π²r³/(GT²). Since Earth’s average density is ρ = M/[(4/3)πR³], substitution gives ρ = 3πr³/(GT²R³). Final answer: ρ = 3πr³/(GT²R³)

The athlete is leaning into a curved path around the track marker, consistent with motion along a circular arc. Because his speed v is constant, his tangential acceleration is zero, but his velocity continually changes direction; therefore he has centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = ω²r directed toward the center of curvature, requiring a net inward force F = mv²/r. Final answer: He undergoes uniform circular motion with centripetal acceleration toward the center of the bend.

The image shows an electron gun producing an electron beam perpendicular to the magnetic field generated by the excitation coil, so the beam follows a circular orbit in the glass bulb. The magnetic Lorentz force provides the centripetal force: |q|vB = mv²/r, hence r = mv/(|q|B). With the electron speed and other conditions unchanged, increasing the excitation-coil current increases the magnetic field strength B, so the orbit radius decreases inversely with B. Final answer: The radius decreases.

In the figure, end A is connected to the central metal wire, while end B is connected to the metal pipe wall. Dust adsorbs electrons and therefore becomes negatively charged; by F=qE and the attraction between opposite charges, the negatively charged dust must be attracted to a positively charged pipe wall. Thus B is connected to the positive pole, and A to the negative pole. Final answer: A is connected to the negative pole, and B is connected to the positive pole.

The image shows live-line workers wearing conductive shielding suits while positioned on high-voltage power lines. The suit forms an approximately equipotential Faraday shield, so the potential difference across the body is zero; using E = −∇V, a constant potential gives E = 0 inside the shield and thus inside the body, ideally. Final answer: The electric field strength inside the human body is zero.

The image shows the ball deflected from the vertical between two vertical capacitor plates, with both plates still connected to the power supply; moving the left plate left while fixing the right plate increases the plate separation d, while the voltage U remains constant. Neglecting edge effects, the electric field is E=U/d, so the horizontal electric force on the ball is |q|E=|q|U/d and decreases as d increases. At equilibrium, the tension components satisfy T cos θ=mg and T sin θ=|q|E, hence T=√[(mg)²+(|q|U/d)²]. Therefore, as the left plate is moved left, T decreases and approaches mg. Final answer: decreases.

The image shows a right-triangular magnetic-field region ABC, with AB vertical, BC horizontal, and crosses indicating a field B into the page. Under the stated condition that the ion enters at B along BC, its magnetic force points toward AB, so the center of its circular path lies on AB; an ion that exits through AB therefore completes a semicircle. Since the cyclotron angular speed is ω = |q|B/m and the angular displacement is π, the time is t = π/ω = πm/(|q|B), independent of its speed. Final answer: πm/(|q|B)

The image shows a right-isosceles triangular magnetic-field region with the ion entering from B along BC and curving toward the diagonal side AC; the crosses indicate a uniform magnetic field into the page. In a uniform magnetic field, the ion’s angular speed is \(\omega=qB/m\), so its turning angle after time \(t\) is \(\theta=\omega t=qBt/m\). The limiting trajectory that just reaches AC is tangent to AC, which requires a turn of \(135^\circ=3\pi/4\); therefore an ion that exits through AC must do so within \(t_{\max}=(3\pi/4)/\omega=3\pi m/(4qB)\). If its motion time is greater than this, it has missed AC and will encounter another boundary instead. Final answer: No, it will not exit from side AC.

The uniformly charged rectangular plate is centered at O, while a and b lie on the symmetry axis MN at equal distances d on opposite sides of O; the point charge −q is distance d from a. At a, the field produced by −q points toward −q and has magnitude E=kq/d², where k=1/(4πε₀). Since the total electric field at a is zero, the plate produces a field of equal magnitude kq/d² in the opposite direction. By the central symmetry of the uniformly charged plate, its fields at the symmetric points a and b have equal magnitudes and opposite directions. Final answer: kq/d²

The image shows A and B on the same straight line, with A to the left of B; let AB=d, Q1=+Q at A, and Q2=-4Q at B. The field due to these charges can cancel only outside segment AB on the side of the smaller charge Q1, so let Q3 be placed a distance x to the left of A. For Q3 to have zero net force, kQ/x²=k(4Q)/(d+x)², hence d+x=2x and x=d. At this point, choosing Q3=-4Q also makes the forces on Q1 and Q2 balance, confirming equilibrium of the entire system. Final answer: On the extension of AB beyond A, at a distance from A equal to AB.

The image shows the ball launched horizontally to the right with speed v0 above the ground, in a vertical electric field E and a magnetic field directed into the page, represented by crosses. For the positively charged ball under the stated conditions, qv×B points upward and opposes the net downward acceleration a that acts after the magnetic field is removed. Let h be the launch height and ω=qB/m. Without the magnetic field, h=at2²/2. With the magnetic field, taking downward as positive, the equations of motion give the downward displacement h=(a−ωv0)[1−cos(ωt1)]/ω². Since 1−cos x<x²/2, h<(a−ωv0)t1²/2<at1²/2; comparing this with h=at2²/2 gives t1>t2. Final answer: t1 > t2.

The image shows a 220 V water heater with a broken grounding path and a person exposed through the outlet water; in the leakage-current path, the electricity-isolating resistance lies between the heater and the person, so it is connected in series with the human body resistance. The current is I = 220/(R_isolating + R_body), and the body voltage is U_body = 220R_body/(R_isolating + R_body). To keep the body current and voltage small, the electricity-isolating resistance must be much greater than the human body resistance. Final answer: The electricity-isolating resistance is much greater than the human body resistance, and they are connected in series in the leakage-current circuit.

The image shows the ball moving along a straight path obliquely downward at an angle θ to the downward vertical. Since gravity and the electric force are constant, the resultant force and acceleration must point along the trajectory; if the acceleration magnitude is a and the ball moves a distance s, then W_e=W_total−W_g=mas−mgs cosθ=ms(a−g cosθ). Thus the electric field does positive work if a>g cosθ, zero work if a=g cosθ, and negative work if 0<a<g cosθ; equivalently, its negative work must satisfy W_e>−mgs cosθ while the ball is moving. Final answer: The electric field force may do positive work, negative work, or zero work.

The image shows the ball moving along a straight path obliquely downward at angle θ to the vertical. Let a be its constant acceleration along the path and s the distance traveled; projecting qE + mg = ma along the path gives qE·t = ma − mg cosθ. Thus the electric work is We = (ma − mg cosθ)s, so the change in electric potential energy is ΔUe = −We = ms(g cosθ − a). Therefore it increases if a < g cosθ, remains constant if a = g cosθ, and decreases if a > g cosθ; since a or the electric-field direction and magnitude are not specified, all three are possible. Final answer: The electric potential energy may increase, decrease, or remain unchanged.

The image shows four equal-radius arcs carrying current clockwise around O, while the straight portions lie along the coordinate axes and produce no magnetic field at O. Since the first-quadrant arc produces field magnitude B and all four arcs have the same current and radius, each produces B into the page by the right-hand rule, so the total field is 4B into the page. For wire P, F = IL × Btotal; with L directed along +x and Btotal along −z, +x × (−z) = +y. Thus the force magnitude is 4BIL and its direction is along the positive y-axis. Final answer: 4BIL, along the positive y-axis.

The figure shows an upward magnetic field in coil A increasing with time, parallel wires a and b attracting, plasma moving rightward between upper plate P1 and lower plate P2, and the winding direction shown. By Lenz’s law, the induced current in coil A must produce a downward magnetic field; applying the right-hand rule to the shown winding gives a downward current in wire a. Parallel wires attract when their currents have the same direction, so the current in b is also downward, meaning conventional current flows from P1 through the external circuit toward P2; thus P1 is positive and positive ions are deflected upward. Since the magnetic force is F = qv × B, with v directed rightward and F on positive ions directed upward, B must point perpendicular to and into the page. Final answer: Perpendicular to the plane of the page and directed into the page.

The image shows disk A fixed at the end of the pendulum and moving along a circular arc about the upper pivot; ignoring the disk’s own rotation, at the lowest point the tourists’ centripetal acceleration is directed vertically upward toward the pivot. If N is the seat’s supporting force, then N − mg = ma = mv²/L > 0, so N > mg and the tourists feel heavier than normal; if the stated 4.3g is the upward acceleration at that point, N = m(g + 4.3g) = 5.3mg. Final answer: The tourists must be in an overweight state.

The image shows the athlete falling vertically below an airborne craft while the wind force is specified as horizontal. Horizontal and vertical motions are independent: vertically, h = ½gt² for a jump from rest, so t = √(2h/g), while the horizontal force only produces acceleration ax = Fwind/m and horizontal displacement x = Fwindt²/(2m). Therefore, for a fixed falling height and a purely horizontal wind force, changing the wind force does not change the falling time. Final answer: The athlete’s falling time is independent of the horizontal wind force.

The image shows a water-filled cup resting on the platform scale, with a wooden ball fully submerged and tied to the cup bottom. Let the total mass be M, the ball’s volume be V, and its mass be m; initially the reading is R0=Mg. When the ball rises by a distance z, an equal volume of denser water effectively moves downward, so while the ball is submerged, MzCM=constant+(m−ρwaterV)z and R−Mg=MaCM=(m−ρwaterV)z̈. Since a wooden ball has m<ρwaterV, its initial upward acceleration z̈>0 makes aCM<0 and hence R<R0. As the ball reaches the surface and is decelerated to rest, the system’s downward center-of-mass motion must be arrested, so aCM becomes upward and R temporarily exceeds R0; after all motion ceases, aCM=0 and R=R0. Final answer: The reading first falls below its original value, then rises above it as the ball settles at the surface, and finally returns to the original value.

The figure shows the ideal transformer’s secondary supplying a fixed series resistor and then a parallel load, with voltmeter V connected across that load; the rheostat’s slider P is connected to the upper rail, so the effective resistance is the portion from P to the lower end. Sliding P upward lengthens this portion and increases the rheostat resistance, thereby increasing the equivalent parallel-load resistance R_L. Since the ideal transformer provides a constant secondary voltage U_2, the voltmeter reads U_V=U_2R_L/(R_s+R_L), where R_s is the fixed series resistance; because this expression increases with R_L, the voltmeter reading increases. Final answer: increases.

In figure A, the length of the bright line of the car lights is about 3 times the marked length L, and L=3 m; the exposure time given in figure B is 1/2 s. The distance traveled by the car during the exposure is about s=3L=9 m, so the average speed is v=s/t=9÷0.5=18 m/s, which converts to about 65 km/h. Final answer: about 18 m/s (about 65 km/h)

The figure shows the liquid entering from the right-hand pipe and being driven left through the pump; the current crosses the upper and lower faces through distance L2 and area L1L2, while B points out of the page. Thus the liquid resistance is R=ρL2/(L1L2)=ρ/L1, and the magnetic thrust is F=BIL2; to produce a leftward force, the conventional current must flow downward, so the upper face is connected to the positive terminal. The source supplies power UI, the Joule heat generated in time t is Q=I²Rt=I²ρt/L1, and the useful lifting work is mgh, giving efficiency η=mgh/(UIt). In the stated ideal model with no flow resistance or other mechanical loss, UIt=mgh+I²ρt/L1, equivalently m=It(U−Iρ/L1)/(gh) and η=1−Iρ/(UL1). Final answer: upper face connected to the positive terminal; R=ρ/L1, F=BIL2, Q=I²ρt/L1, η=mgh/(UIt)=1−Iρ/(UL1), and m=It(U−Iρ/L1)/(gh).

The image shows two horizontal plates separated by d, with the upper plate positive and the lower plate negative, so the uniform electric field has magnitude E = U/d and points downward; droplet A is above droplet B. Before the voltage is applied, each mass-m₀ droplet falls at terminal speed v₁ = h₁/t, so force balance gives m₀g = k m₀^(1/3)v₁ and hence k = m₀^(2/3)gt/h₁. Since A continues falling at the same terminal speed after the field is applied, its electric force must be zero, so q_A = 0 and A is neutral. Droplet B rises at terminal speed v₂ = h₂/t; gravity and drag act downward, so its electric force is upward, which means B is negatively charged. Its terminal-force balance is |q_B|U/d = m₀g + k m₀^(1/3)h₂/t = m₀g(1 + h₂/h₁), giving q_B = −m₀gd(h₁ + h₂)/(Uh₁). During its upward displacement h₂, the electric potential increases by Uh₂/d, so B’s electric potential-energy change is ΔE_e = q_BUh₂/d = −m₀gh₂(1 + h₂/h₁), meaning it decreases by m₀gh₂(1 + h₂/h₁); its gravitational potential energy increases by m₀gh₂, and therefore its total gravitational-plus-electric potential energy changes by −m₀gh₂²/h₁. After merging, the new droplet has mass 2m₀ and charge q_B; its upward electric force minus its weight is m₀g(h₂/h₁ − 1), so at terminal speed k(2m₀)^(1/3)v = m₀g|h₂/h₁ − 1|, yielding v = |h₂ − h₁|/(2^(1/3)t), upward if h₂ > h₁ and downward if h₂ < h₁. Final answer: k = m₀^(2/3)gt/h₁; A is neutral with q_A = 0; B is negative with q_B = −m₀gd(h₁ + h₂)/(Uh₁); ΔE_e = −m₀gh₂(1 + h₂/h₁), or ΔE_total = −m₀gh₂²/h₁ if gravitational and electric potential energies are combined; the merged droplet’s terminal speed is |h₂ − h₁|/(2^(1/3)t), upward for h₂ > h₁ and downward for h₂ < h₁.

The image shows the positively charged sphere at A to the right of the vertical OC, with OA making 30° with the vertical; B is horizontally to the right of O and C is the lowest point. At equilibrium at A, resolving the tension T gives T cos 30° = mg vertically and T sin 30° = qE horizontally, so qE = mg tan 30° and E = mg/(√3q); since the tension’s horizontal component is toward the left, the electric force and hence the field must point horizontally to the right, toward B. From B to C, gravity does work mgL while the rightward electric force does work qE(0 − L) = −qEL, so ½mv² = mgL − qEL = mgL(1 − 1/√3), giving v = √[2gL(1 − 1/√3)]. At C the electric force is horizontal and has no radial component, so T_C − mg = mv²/L; therefore T_C = mg + 2mg(1 − 1/√3) = mg(3 − 2/√3). Final answer: E = mg/(√3q), directed horizontally toward B; v_C = √[2gL(1 − 1/√3)]; T_C = mg(3 − 2/√3).

The image shows that capacitor plate M is connected to the upper rail and ring rim, plate N is connected through switch position 1 to the shaft, the upward B₁ field and indicated rotation make v×B₁ point radially outward, and on the return motion side ab leads side cd by l₃ through a B₂ region of length l₂<l₃. At any instant one rotating radial rod is in B₁ and has motional emf ε=B₁ωr²/2=1×600×0.2²/2=12 V, while the other is outside the field; since the two equal resistances R₀ form the internal circuit, the ring-to-shaft terminal voltage is ε/2=6 V. Thus Q=CU=0.09×6=0.54 C, and the outward magnetic force on positive charges makes the ring rim and plate M positive. Taking g=10 m/s², if u is the speed of the combined frame just after the perfectly inelastic collision, its rise by h=0.2 m gives (1/2)(2m)u²=2mgh, so u=2 m/s; momentum conservation in the collision gives mv=2mu, hence the rod’s speed before collision was v=4 m/s. The magnetic impulse while the capacitor discharges is B₂l₁ΔQ=mv, giving ΔQ=0.01×4/(1×0.25)=0.16 C. When the frame returns, its mass is 2m and its loop resistance is 2R; while one transverse side is in the field, I=B₂l₁v/(2R), so dv/ds=−B₂²l₁²/(4mR)=−15.625. As ab crosses the field length l₂, its speed falls to v₁=2−15.625×0.068=0.9375 m/s. Since l₂<l₃, the frame then coasts until cd reaches the left boundary at x=l₃; cd penetrates a further distance s=v₁/15.625=0.060 m before the frame stops, so x=l₃+s=0.08+0.06=0.14 m. Final answer: Q=0.54 C with plate M positively charged; ΔQ=0.16 C; x=0.14 m.

The image shows parallel plates of length L separated by d, with airflow and particles moving horizontally at v₀; the lower plate is positive, so negatively charged particles drift downward, and a particle initially near the upper plate must cross the full distance d during the residence time t=L/v₀ for collection to be exactly 100%. Since E=U/d, neglecting resistance gives transverse acceleration a=αU₁/(md), so d=at²/2=[αU₁/(2md)](L/v₀)² and therefore U₁=2md²v₀²/(αL²). With resistance, the terminal-speed assumption requires the intended drag law to be f=krv, because the stated f=kr alone would not determine a maximum speed; force balance gives qU₂/d=kRv, while exact collection requires v=d/t=dv₀/L, hence U₂=kRd²v₀/(qL). For uniformly distributed particles, the collected fraction equals their transverse displacement divided by d; because q is proportional to r², the terminal drift speed qU/(krd) is proportional to r, and the radius ratio of the 2.5 μm and 10 μm particles is 1/4, so the smaller particles move through d/4 and 25% are collected. Final answer: U₁=2md²v₀²/(αL²), U₂=kRd²v₀/(qL), 25%.

No usable image is available, so the relevant data are the furnace’s remaining volume 0.13 m³, 10 argon bottles of volume 3.2×10⁻² m³ each, the bottle pressure decrease from 1.5×10⁷ Pa to 2.0×10⁶ Pa, and temperatures of 27°C and 1227°C. At room temperature, the amount of gas transferred is determined by ΔPV = 10(1.5×10⁷−2.0×10⁶)(3.2×10⁻²), so for the initially evacuated chamber, P₁(0.13) = 10(1.3×10⁷)(3.2×10⁻²), giving P₁ = 3.2×10⁷ Pa. During heating, the chamber volume and gas amount remain constant, so P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂; with T₁ = 27+273 = 300 K and T₂ = 1227+273 = 1500 K, P₂ = (3.2×10⁷)(1500/300) = 1.6×10⁸ Pa. Final answer: (1) 3.2×10⁷ Pa; (2) 1.6×10⁸ Pa.

The image shows P approaching the stationary block Q at point A with uphill speed v0, while an elastic bumper lies a distance s downhill from A along the fixed incline of angle θ. For a one-dimensional elastic collision of masses m and 4m with Q initially at rest, vP1=(m−4m)v0/(m+4m)=−3v0/5 and vQ1=2mv0/(m+4m)=2v0/5, so their speed magnitudes are 3v0/5 and 2v0/5, with P moving downhill and Q uphill. Let wn be P’s uphill speed immediately before the n-th collision, so w1=v0. While Q moves uphill, gravity and kinetic friction both act downhill; since μ=tanθ, its deceleration is g sinθ+μg cosθ=2g sinθ. After the n-th collision Q has speed 2wn/5, so its vertical rise is hn=[(2wn/5)²/(4g sinθ)]sinθ=wn²/(25g). P leaves that collision downhill at 3wn/5, reflects elastically from the bumper, and climbs to Q’s new resting position; conservation of mechanical energy for P gives w(n+1)²=(3wn/5)²−2ghn=(7/25)wn². Hence wn²=v0²(7/25)^(n−1), giving hn=v0²(7/25)^(n−1)/(25g), and the total vertical rise is H=Σhn=[v0²/(25g)]/[1−7/25]=v0²/(18g). For the no-early-collision condition, let Ln be the along-plane distance from the n-th collision point to the bumper and set a=g sinθ. P reaches the bumper with speed bn=√(9wn²/25+2aLn), and its time to travel down to the bumper and then up to Q’s stopping point is Tn=[2bn−(3+√7)wn/5]/a; Q stops after tn=wn/(5a). The limiting case Tn=tn gives bn=(4+√7)wn/10 and therefore Ln=(8√7−13)wn²/(200a). Since Ln increases after each rise whereas wn² decreases by the factor 7/25, the first collision is the restrictive case, for which L1=s and w1=v0. Final answer: vP1=3v0/5, vQ1=2v0/5; hn=[v0²/(25g)](7/25)^(n−1); H=v0²/(18g); smin=(8√7−13)v0²/(200g sinθ).

The figure shows the cardboard being pulled to the right, with the point-like object initially d = 0.15 m from the table’s right edge. While the cardboard and object move together over the tabletop, the tabletop supports their combined weight, so N = (m₁ + m₂)g = 0.5 × 10 = 5 N and the tabletop friction on the cardboard is f = μN = 0.2 × 5 = 1.0 N, directed left. Their common acceleration would be a = [F − 1.0]/(m₁ + m₂) = (F − 1.0)/0.5; the object can share this acceleration only if m₂a ≤ μm₂g, or a ≤ μg = 2 m/s², giving F ≤ 2.0 N, so relative sliding occurs when F > 2.0 N. During relative sliding, the object accelerates rightward at μg = 2 m/s²; in 0.3 s it moves s₁ = ½μgt² = 0.09 m and reaches speed v = μgt = 0.60 m/s. After the thin cardboard is removed, tabletop friction stops it over s₂ = v²/(2μg) = 0.09 m, so its total displacement is 0.18 m, greater than d = 0.15 m; therefore, it reaches the edge before stopping. Final answer: the tabletop friction is 1.0 N leftward; relative sliding occurs for F > 2.0 N; the object will not remain on the table and will slide off.

The image shows the particle leaving O at 53° above the positive x-axis, crossing from region I to region II at the vertical line x=12 cm, and leaving region II through the line x=26 cm; the crosses indicate that B points into the paper. Straight motion in region I requires the electric and magnetic forces to cancel, q(E+v×B)=0, so E=vB and v=E/B=(1.0×10^3)/1.0=1.0×10^3 m/s. The entry point into region II is P=(12 cm,12tan53° cm)=(12 cm,16 cm). In region II the radius is r=mv/(|q|B)=(1×10^-14×10^3)/(1×10^-10×1)=0.10 m=10 cm; because the charge is negative, the magnetic force initially points down and right, so the circle’s center is 10(0.8,-0.6) cm from P, namely (20 cm,10 cm). Thus the orbit satisfies (x-20)^2+(y-10)^2=100 in cm, and at x=26 cm it gives y=18 cm or 2 cm; the clockwise motion reaches Q=(26 cm,18 cm) first. The radius vectors to P and Q are (-8,6) cm and (6,8) cm, whose dot product is zero, so the arc angle is π/2, and the exit velocity is directed as (0.8,-0.6). From Q to the x-axis the required path length is 18/0.6=30 cm, giving a horizontal displacement 30×0.8=24 cm and hence D=(50 cm,0). The travel times are t_OP=0.20/1000=2.0×10^-4 s, t_PQ=(πr/2)/v=π/20000 s, and t_QD=0.30/1000=3.0×10^-4 s, so t_OD=5.0×10^-4+π/20000=6.57×10^-4 s. Final answer: v=1.0×10^3 m/s, D=(50 cm,0), t=6.57×10^-4 s.

The image shows one rope segment hanging vertically to m1 and the other running down to m2 at α = 60° from the vertical, while the pulley is supported from the ceiling by string OA. Since m2 is at rest and the rope is inextensible, m1 is also at rest, so the ideal-rope tension is T = m1g = 2(10) = 20 N. On m2, the rope has an upward component T cos 60° = 10 N and a horizontal component T sin 60° = 10√3 N; therefore vertical equilibrium gives the ground’s normal force N = m2g − T cos 60° = 50 − 10 = 40 N, and horizontal equilibrium requires a friction force of 10√3 N ≈ 17.3 N opposite the rope’s horizontal pull. The two forces exerted by the rope on the pulley are 20 N vertically downward and 20 N downward along the inclined segment, with 60° between them, so their resultant is √(20² + 20² + 2·20² cos 60°) = 20√3 N; consequently, OA exerts an equal opposite force directed upward toward O along the angle bisector, 30° from the upward vertical toward the m1 side. Final answer: pressure on the ground = 40 N; friction magnitude = 10√3 N ≈ 17.3 N; tension exerted by OA on the pulley = 20√3 N ≈ 34.6 N, directed upward toward m1 at 30° to the vertical.

The image shows an object sliding from rest down a fixed incline at θ = 30°. On a smooth plane, the component of gravity along the plane gives a = g sin θ = 10 sin 30° = 5 m/s² downward. With kinetic friction, N = mg cos θ and friction is μN, so a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) = 10[1/2 − (√3/6)(√3/2)] = 10(1/2 − 1/4) = 2.5 m/s² downward. For a plane of length s = 5 m, the original smooth-plane condition gives s = at²/2, so t = √(2s/a) = √2 s, and v = √(2as) = 5√2 m/s; if the length question is instead intended to continue the rough-plane case, t = 2 s and v = 5 m/s. Final answer: smooth acceleration = 5 m/s²; rough-plane acceleration = 2.5 m/s²; for the original smooth plane, time = √2 s and final speed = 5√2 m/s (or, if friction applies, time = 2 s and final speed = 5 m/s).

The image shows rod a spanning the rails in the upward magnetic field of region I, rod b spanning the rails at the midpoint EF of the downward magnetic field of region II and tied to the right support, with both rods having resistance R, rail separation L, and each dashed-line interval having width d. Denote the supply emf by ε. Before rod a crosses the insulating section, the capacitor initially has charge Cε; with q/C=IR+BLv, m dv/dt=BLI, and dq/dt=−I, integration gives mv=BL(Cε−q). At steady motion I=0 and q=CBLv, so the speed at the insulating section is v=CBLε/(m+CB²L²). After rod a enters the right-hand circuit while b is fixed, the two rods are in series, giving I=BLv/(2R) and a magnetic force BLI=B²L²v/(2R) on b. Thus b remains fixed provided this force does not exceed F₀, which gives ε≤E₀, where E₀=2RF₀(m+CB²L²)/(CB³L³). For ε<E₀ and entry speed v₁, rod a obeys m dv/dt=−B²L²v/(2R), so dv/dx=−B²L²/(2mR) and its speed at M₂N₂ is v₁−B²L²d/(2mR). Since the equal rod resistances receive equal Joule heat while only a loses kinetic energy, the heat in rod a is Qₐ=m[v₁²−(v₁−B²L²d/(2mR))²]/4=B²L²dv₁/(4R)−B⁴L⁴d²/(16mR²), assuming v₁>B²L²d/(2mR) so that a reaches M₂N₂. For ε>E₀ the thread breaks; because the magnetic fields are opposite while the loop currents in the two rods are also opposite, both magnetic forces point left and have the same magnitude, so m dvₐ/dt=3m dv_b/dt. With vₐ(0)=v₂ and v_b(0)=0, vₐ−v₂=3v_b; therefore, when vₐ=v₂/2, v_b=−v₂/6, meaning rod b moves left with speed v₂/6. Final answer: E₀=2RF₀(m+CB²L²)/(CB³L³); Qₐ=B²L²dv₁/(4R)−B⁴L⁴d²/(16mR²); rod b’s speed at t₀ is v₂/6.

No usable image is available; the relevant quantities stated are the release height h, impact speed v, Mars’s radius R, and the gravitational constant G. Conservation of mechanical energy between radii R + h and R gives v²/2 = GM(1/R − 1/(R + h)) = GMh/[R(R + h)], so GM = v²R(R + h)/(2h). Therefore the surface gravitational acceleration is g = GM/R² = v²(R + h)/(2hR), the mass is M = v²R(R + h)/(2Gh), and, using the spherical volume 4πR³/3, the uniform density is ρ = M/(4πR³/3) = 3v²(R + h)/(8πGhR²). If h is negligible compared with R, these reduce to g ≈ v²/(2h), M ≈ v²R²/(2Gh), and ρ ≈ 3v²/(8πGhR). Final answer: g = v²(R + h)/(2hR), M = v²R(R + h)/(2Gh), ρ = 3v²(R + h)/(8πGhR²).

From the image, when S₂ is at a, R₁ and R₂ are parallel and then in series with R₃, so Rₐ=(2×2)/(2+2)+2=3 Ω; at b, R₁ is disconnected and R₂ and R₃ are in series, so R_b=4 Ω; at c, R₃ is short-circuited and R₁ is disconnected, so R_c=R₂=2 Ω. Using I=E/(R+r), the readings give E=3(3+r) and E=2.5(4+r), hence 9+3r=10+2.5r, so r=2 Ω and E=15 V. At c, the current through R₂ is I₂=15/(2+2)=3.75 A. The power supplied to the external circuit is P=I²R: Pₐ=3²×3=27 W, P_b=2.5²×4=25 W, and P_c=3.75²×2=28.125 W, so it is greatest at c. Final answer: E=15 V, r=2 Ω; current through R₂ at c is 3.75 A; maximum output power occurs at c and is 28.125 W.

The image shows rod a moving right from AC through a field-free distance R to the boundary EF, while rod b is initially at rest near MP, where the horizontal rails join the bottoms of the vertical circular rails; the magnetic field occupies EMPF. Before a reaches EF, the magnetic flux through the circuit does not change, so no induced current acts on the rods. Work-energy for rod a gives 32mgR = (1/2)(2m)v₀², hence v₀ = 4√(2gR). After b leaves the magnetic field at MP, mechanical energy is conserved on the frictionless circular rails. At the highest point, gravity and the total normal force both point toward the center, so mg + 3mg = mv_t²/R, giving v_t² = 4gR. Since the highest point is 2R above MP, (1/2)mv_b² = (1/2)mv_t² + 2mgR, so v_b = 2√(2gR) as b exits the field. From the instant a enters the field until b exits, the magnetic forces on the two rods are equal and opposite, so their total horizontal momentum is conserved: 2m[4√(2gR)] = 2mv_a + m[2√(2gR)], which gives v_a = 3√(2gR). Final answer: 1. 4√(2gR), to the right; 2. 3√(2gR), to the right.

Final answer: A-to-B time 2.25 s and scratch length 0.50 m; minimum plank length for μ₂=0.2 is 2/3 m; minimum plank length for μ₂=0.1 is 0.40 m, and the plank displacement is 0.20 m to the right.

The image shows a motor-driven reciprocating piston connected to the chamber of volume V through an inlet check valve and to the atmosphere through an outlet check valve, so each suction stroke sweeps a volume ΔV of chamber gas and each compression stroke exhausts it at pressure Pa. With V0=0 and ΔV≪V, a stroke at chamber pressure P removes approximately Δn=PΔV/(RTa), while the chamber contains n=PV/(RTa); if f is the number of pumping cycles per unit time, then V(dP/dt)/(RTa)=−fPΔV/(RTa), giving dP/dt=−(fΔV/V)P and P(t)=Pa exp(−fΔVt/V). The frequency f is required because the question does not otherwise specify the piston rate; equivalently, if N(t) is the number of completed strokes, replace ft by N(t). For a monatomic gas γ=5/3, and adiabatic compression from chamber conditions (P(t),Ta) to the outlet pressure Pa gives Temit/Ta=(Pa/P(t))^((γ−1)/γ)=(Pa/P(t))^(2/5), so Temit(t)=Ta exp(2fΔVt/(5V)); ideal adiabatic discharge at the constant outlet pressure leaves the emitted gas at this temperature. When V0>0, the gas left at Pa in the clearance volume V0 expands adiabatically to V0+ΔV, reaching Pc,min=Pa[V0/(V0+ΔV)]^γ; below this pressure the cylinder pressure never falls below the chamber pressure, so the inlet cannot open. Final answer: P(t)=Pa exp(−fΔVt/V), Temit(t)=Ta[Pa/P(t)]^(2/5)=Ta exp(2fΔVt/(5V)), and Pmin=Pa[V0/(V0+ΔV)]^(5/3), where f is the pumping-cycle frequency.

The figure shows O on the vertical interface AB, OC horizontal with OC=R, and AC inclined so that ∠OAC=60°; hence △AOC is right-angled at O and AO=OC/tan60°=R/√3. At i=60°, the reflected ray from AB is normal to AC and exits toward the right side of the screen, so having only one spot requires total internal reflection at AB; thus n sin60°≥1, giving n≥1/sin60°=2/√3=2√3/3. For n=√3 and a decreasing i, the reflected ray makes angle i with the horizontal, while the outward normal to AC makes 60° with the horizontal, so its incidence angle at AC is 60°−i. If its refraction angle at AC is r, Snell’s law gives sin r=√3 sin(60°−i). The right-hand spot just disappears when this emerging ray becomes parallel to the horizontal screen, for which r=60°; therefore √3 sin(60°−i₀)=sin60°=√3/2, yielding i₀=30°. At AB, the left-going refracted ray then satisfies sin r₁=√3 sin30°=√3/2, so r₁=60°; rising through AO=R/√3 to the screen, it moves horizontally by AO/tan60°=R/3. Final answer: n≥2√3/3; i₀=30°, and the remaining spot is R/3 to the left of A.

No usable image is available, so the stated speeds and distances are used directly. Taking forward as positive and assuming constant braking acceleration, v² = v₀² + 2aΔx gives 0 = 30² + 2a(1800), so aB = −0.25 m/s². With B initially at xB = 0 and A at xA = 750 m, while A maintains 10 m/s their separation is d(t) = xA − xB = (750 + 10t) − (30t − 0.125t²) = 750 − 20t + 0.125t². Setting d = 0 gives t² − 160t + 6000 = 0, whose first root is t = 60 s, so the trains collide before B stops; A travels 10(60) = 600 m before the collision. In the third case, after 8 s of braking B has traveled 30(8) − 0.125(8²) = 232 m, while A has traveled 80 m, leaving a separation of 750 + 80 − 232 = 598 m. Let τ be the time after A begins accelerating; then the separation is d(τ) = 598 + 10τ + 0.25τ² − (28τ − 0.125τ²) = 598 − 18τ + 0.375τ². This is minimized when d′(τ) = −18 + 0.75τ = 0, giving τ = 24 s and dmin = 598 − 18(24) + 0.375(24²) = 382 m, so no collision occurs. Final answer: B’s acceleration is −0.25 m/s²; without A accelerating, the trains collide after A travels 600 m; if A accelerates after 8 s, the accident is avoided and the minimum separation is 382 m.

The image shows the square’s vertical faces AB and CD separated by a horizontal distance a, with the parallel rays directed downward and to the right at 45° to AB; hence the angle of incidence relative to the horizontal normal is also 45°. The ray entering at A travels a distance L = a/cos 30° = 2a/√3 before reaching CD, and its speed in the glass is c/√2, so t = L/(c/√2) = 2√6a/(3c). Rays with y₀ < a/√3 first strike BC at 60° to its normal; since the critical angle is arcsin(1/√2) = 45°, they undergo total internal reflection and then reach CD at heights from 0 to a/√3. These intervals overlap, and a/√3 > a − a/√3, so the total illuminated width is a/√3. Final answer: t = 2√6a/(3c), d = a/√3.

The image shows the piston initially at the left opening, the gas occupying the full length 2l to the closed end, and the opposing stops A and B at the midpoint, a distance l from either end. Initially the horizontal piston has no weight component along the cylinder, so the gas pressure is p0 and p0(2lS)=nRT0. After the opening is turned vertically upward, the gas remains at T0 because the rotation is slow and the cylinder is thermally conductive; force balance on the piston gives p1S=p0S+Mg, so p1=p0+Mg/S. If the piston descends by h, the gas volume is (2l−h)S, and isothermal compression gives p0(2lS)=(p0+Mg/S)(2l−h)S, hence h=2lMg/(p0S+Mg). Since p0S>Mg, h<l, so the piston does not reach the midpoint stops during rotation. During subsequent cooling, it reaches the stops when the gas volume becomes lS, at temperature Tc=T0(p0S+Mg)/(2p0S)>T0/2; it therefore remains at the stops while cooling to T0/2. At that temperature, p2(lS)/(T0/2)=p0(2lS)/T0, giving p2=p0. Final answer: the piston descends by 2lMg/(p0S+Mg), and the final gas pressure is p0.

The image shows a small block of mass m at the left end of a horizontal board of mass M and length L, with the board resting on rough ground. Taking the usual textbook convention that the given friction coefficients also determine the limiting static friction, the block-board friction limit is μ2mg=0.4×1×10=4 N, while the sliding friction between the board and ground is μ1(M+m)g=0.1×2×10=2 N. For F=1 N, the system remains at rest and the friction on the block balances the pull, so its magnitude is 1 N. For F=5 N, the block and board can move together with acceleration a=[F−2]/(M+m)=(5−2)/2=1.5 m/s²; hence F−f=ma gives f=5−1×1.5=3.5 N, which is below the 4 N limiting value. For F=8 N, moving together would require f=8−1×[(8−2)/2]=5 N>4 N, so the block slides; its acceleration is am=(8−4)/1=4 m/s², while the board’s acceleration is aM=(4−2)/1=2 m/s². Their relative acceleration is 2 m/s², so L=(1/2)(am−aM)t² gives 1=(1/2)(2)t² and t=1 s. Final answer: (1) 1 N; (2) 3.5 N; (3) 1.0 s.

The image shows O directly above A’s initial position O′, with the smooth part of plate B and its baffle to the left and the rough part to the right; the ball therefore strikes A at the pendulum’s lowest point and sends A leftward at v₀=4 m/s. Taking rightward as positive, just before the elastic A–baffle collision, u_A=−4 m/s and u_B=0; conservation of momentum and kinetic energy gives v_A=(m_A−m_B)u_A/(m_A+m_B)=2 m/s and v_B=2m_Au_A/(m_A+m_B)=−2 m/s. The friction magnitudes are f₂=μ₂(m_A+m_B)g=0.9 N at the ground and f₁=μ₁m_Ag=0.4 N between A and B. While A returns rightward over the smooth part, its speed remains 2 m/s, while B has acceleration 0.9/0.3=3 m/s² to the right. Once A enters the rough part, its acceleration is −f₁/m_A=−4 m/s²; because it stops exactly at the fixed point below O, its rough-entry coordinate x satisfies 0=2²+2(−4)(0−x), giving x=−0.50 m. The rough-boundary point moves with B, so −2t+(1/2)(3)t²=−0.50 gives the applicable time t=1/3 s after the baffle collision and B’s velocity then is −2+3t=−1 m/s. If d is the initial distance from O′ to the baffle, −d+2(1/3)=−0.50 gives d=7/6 m, so A takes d/v₀=7/24 s to reach the baffle and another 2/4=1/2 s to stop on the rough part; the total time after the ball–A collision is therefore 7/24+1/3+1/2=9/8 s. After A enters the rough part, B’s rightward acceleration is (0.9+0.4)/0.3=13/3 m/s², so it slides a further distance 1²/[2(13/3)]=3/26 m before stopping; hence the ground-friction heat is Q=0.9(1/2+3/26)=0.55 J. The ball starts its simple harmonic motion at the equilibrium position, so its first highest point occurs after one-quarter period: (π/2)√(L/g)=9/8, giving L=g[9/(4π)]²=81/16 m≈5.1 m using π²=10. Final answer: v_A=2.0 m/s, Q=0.55 J, L=81/16 m≈5.1 m.

The image shows that the smooth quarter-circle lowers the slider by the radius R = 5 m from A to B, after which it moves on the rough horizontal segment BC of length s = 9.5 m. Conservation of mechanical energy on the smooth arc gives ½mv_B² = mgR, so v_B = √(2gR) = √(2·10·5) = 10 m/s. On BC the frictional deceleration is μg = 1 m/s², hence at the first collision v_C² = v_B² − 2μgs = 100 − 2·0.1·10·9.5 = 81, giving v_C = 9 m/s. Each rebound preserves speed, and each complete trip from C to B and back to C reduces the squared speed by 4μgs = 38 m²/s²; therefore the squared speeds at successive collisions are 81, 43, and 5, while a fourth collision is impossible because 5 < 38, so n = 3. After the third collision the slider rebounds toward B with speed squared equal to 5 and stops after traveling 5/(2μg) = 2.5 m from C, placing it 9.5 − 2.5 = 7.0 m from B. Final answer: v_B = 10 m/s; v_C = 9 m/s; n = 3; the slider stops 7.0 m from B.

The image shows a car yielding at a zebra crossing while pedestrians cross. Convert the initial speed: v1 = 36 km/h = 10 m/s. With constant deceleration over s = 20 m, 0 = v1² + 2as gives a = -10²/(2×20) = -2.5 m/s²; hence the stopping time is t = (0 - 10)/(-2.5) = 4.0 s, and the resistance force magnitude is F = m|a| = 1.0×10³×2.5 = 2.5×10³ N. The last child must cover the 6 m line length plus the 6 m road width, so all children clear the road after (l + L)/v0 = (6 + 6)/0.5 = 24 s from the start of braking; since the car takes 4 s to reach the crosswalk, its waiting time there is 24 - 4 = 20 s. For v2 = 54 km/h = 15 m/s, the same resistance produces a = -2.5 m/s², so at the crosswalk v² = 15² + 2(-2.5)(20) = 125, giving v = 5√5 ≈ 11.2 m/s, or about 40.2 km/h. Final answer: 1. 4.0 s and 2.5×10³ N; 2. 20 s; 3. 5√5 m/s ≈ 11.2 m/s (40.2 km/h).

The image shows the cylinder initially suspended by pulling the piston rod upward, with the gas below the piston, and then inverted so that the rod rests on the ground and the gas is above the piston; piston mass and friction are taken as negligible. Initially, the upward atmospheric force on the cylinder bottom is p0S, while the downward forces are the internal-gas force p1S and the cylinder weight Mg, so p0S=p1S+Mg and p1=p0−Mg/S, requiring p0S>Mg. After inversion, when the cylinder is supported by the gas, the internal pressure must satisfy p2S=p0S+Mg, giving p2=p0+Mg/S. When the piston returns to its initial position relative to the cylinder, the gas volume equals its initial volume, so the ideal-gas relation gives p1/T1=p2/T2; hence T2=T1(p0+Mg/S)/(p0−Mg/S)=T1(p0S+Mg)/(p0S−Mg), corresponding to a temperature increase ΔT=T2−T1=2MgT1/(p0S−Mg). Final answer: p1=p0−Mg/S; the gas must be heated to T2=T1(p0S+Mg)/(p0S−Mg), i.e. by ΔT=2MgT1/(p0S−Mg).

The speed at the bottom is v=v0+at=16√3−2≈25.7 m/s; on the horizontal track, uniform deceleration from v to zero gives 22=(v+0)t/2, so t=44/(16√3−2)≈1.71 s. The figure shows that the gas and spring occupy the length between the piston and the fixed right end, initially l0; since the spring is initially unstretched and the massless piston is exposed to atmospheric pressure p0, the initial gas pressure is p0 and its volume is Sl0 at temperature T0, so nR = p0Sl0/T0. After the piston moves 0.2l0 to the right, the gas length is 0.8l0 and p1 = 1.1p0, giving T1/T0 = p1(0.8Sl0)/(p0Sl0) = 1.1 × 0.8 = 0.88. At this position the spring is compressed by 0.2l0, so piston equilibrium gives F + p0S = 1.1p0S + k(0.2l0); using k = p0S/l0 gives F = 0.3p0S. During subsequent heating F remains constant, and when the piston is 1.2l0 from the right end the spring is stretched by 0.2l0 and pulls the piston rightward, so p2S = F + p0S + k(0.2l0) = (0.3 + 1 + 0.2)p0S, hence p2 = 1.5p0. The gas volume is then 1.2Sl0, and therefore T2/T0 = p2(1.2Sl0)/(p0Sl0) = 1.5 × 1.2 = 1.8. Final answer: T1 = 0.88T0; T2 = 1.8T0.

The figure shows the mass initially above the shore edge with the 2 m rope at 53° to the vertical, while the suspension point is 3 m above the water. The vertical drop to the lowest point is Δh=l(1−cos α)=2(1−0.6)=0.8 m, so conservation of energy gives mv²/2=mgΔh and v=√(2gΔh)=4 m/s; at the lowest point, F−mg=mv²/l, hence F=60×10+60×4²/2=1080 N. The release point is H−l=1 m above the water, so the flight time is t=√[2(H−l)/g]=√0.2 s, and the additional horizontal travel is vt=4√0.2≈1.79 m; because the lowest point is l sin α=2×0.8=1.6 m horizontally from the shore edge shown beneath the initial position, the landing point is 1.6+1.79≈3.39 m, or 3.4 m, from shore. At the highest point the speed is zero and the height above the water is h=H−l cos α=3−2×0.6=1.8 m; applying work-energy from release until the contestant momentarily stops underwater gives mg(h+d)−(f1+f2)d=0, so d=mgh/(f1+f2−mg)=60×10×1.8/(800+700−600)=1.2 m. Final answer: the rope tension is 1080 N, the landing point is approximately 3.4 m from the shore, and the maximum depth is 1.2 m.

The image shows the primary connected to u=U sinωt and the secondary connected in series with an AC ammeter and a motor lifting mass m at constant speed; therefore U is the peak primary voltage, while I is an RMS current. Taking the turns ratio as n=Np/Ns, the RMS primary voltage is U/√2, so the ideal-transformer relations give U2=U/(√2n) and I0/I=Ns/Np=1/n, hence I0=I/n. In the intended idealized motor model with unity power factor, its electrical input power is P=U2I=UI/(√2n). The winding dissipates I²R, while constant-speed lifting requires mechanical power mgv; thus mgv=P−I²R, giving v=[UI/(√2n)−I²R]/(mg). Final answer: I0=I/n, P=UI/(√2n), v=[UI/(√2n)−I²R]/(mg).

No usable image is available, so the stated coordinate directions are used directly. The acceleration during each of the first two stages is a=qE/m=(1.0×10^−10)(2.0×10^6)/(1.0×10^−3)=0.20 m/s².
