Figure 2 shows a sinusoidal magnetic field with maximum value Bm = 1.0 × 10^-2 T, starting from zero and increasing; the interval from t = 0 to the next zero crossing at t = (π/2) × 10^-2 s is T/2, so T = π × 10^-2 s and 2π/T = 200 rad·s^-1. Thus the maximum induced emf is Em = nBmS(2π/T) = 100 × 1.0 × 10^-2 × 0.040 × 200 = 8.0 V. The coil and bulb are in series, so their total resistance is r + R = 10.0 Ω; the rms current is Irms = Em/[√2(r + R)], giving the bulb’s average power P = Irms²R = [8.0/(10√2)]² × 9.0 = 2.88 W. From 0 to T/4, the charge is q = ∫e dt/(r + R) = Em/[(r + R)(2π/T)] = nBmS/(r + R) = 4.0 × 10^-3 C. Final answer: maximum induced emf = 8.0 V; bulb power = 2.88 W; charge = 4.0 × 10^-3 C.

The image shows a positively charged ball constrained to the inner side of a vertical circular track while the uniform electric field points horizontally right. Taking x rightward and y upward from the circle’s center, the lowest point is (0,−R), so Ug=mg(y+R) and Ue=−qEx; here mg=4 N and qE=3 N, giving a combined force magnitude F=√[(mg)²+(qE)²]=5 N. If c=(qE,−mg)·er, then the combined potential is U=mgR−Rc and the inward normal force is N=mv²/R+c; using conserved total energy H=K+U gives N=2(H−mgR)/R+3c, whose minimum occurs at c=−F, the point opposite the combined-force direction. For a ball just maintaining contact, N=0 there, so mv²/R=F and Kmin=FR/2=5 J. At that point U is maximal: Umax=mgR+FR=8+10=18 J, hence H=Kmin+Umax=23 J. Mechanical energy in the usual sense M=K+Ug satisfies M=H−Ue=H+qEx, so its minimum occurs at x=−R and equals 23−qER=23−6=17 J. Finally, Ug+Ue has minimum value Umin=mgR−FR=8−10=−2 J. Final answer: (1) 5 J; (2) 17 J; (3) −2 J.

The image shows rod ab bridging two smooth rails on a plane inclined at θ = 30°, with the rod horizontal and the magnetic field B directed vertically upward; therefore the Ampere force is horizontal, and its component along the rails is F_A cos θ. For equilibrium along the incline, F_A cos θ = mg sin θ, so F_A = mg tan θ = 0.012 × 10 × tan 30° = 0.04√3 N ≈ 6.9 × 10⁻² N. Since the horizontal rod is perpendicular to the vertical field, F_A = BId, where d = 10√3 cm = 0.10√3 m, giving I = F_A/(Bd) = (0.04√3)/(0.2 × 0.10√3) = 2 A. The total circuit resistance is R + r = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 Ω, so E = I(R + r) = 2 × 2.0 = 4 V. Final answer: 1. 0.04√3 N (approximately 6.9 × 10⁻² N); 2. 4 V.

No usable image is available, so the calculation uses the stated motion and assumes uniform braking. The speed decreases from 20 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s, giving acceleration a=(10−20)/4=−2.5 m/s², whose magnitude is 2.5 m/s². At this rate, the stopping time is t=20/2.5=8 s, so the car has already stopped after 10 s and its speed is 0 m/s. Its displacement before stopping is s=v₀t+(1/2)at²=20(8)+(1/2)(−2.5)(8²)=80 m; once stopped, it travels no farther. Final answer: 1. 2.5 m/s²; 2. 0 m/s and 80 m.

The image shows an endless conveyor rising from the lower-left entry to the upper-right pulley at θ = 30°, with the block initially moving upslope at 6 m/s and the clockwise upper run moving upslope at 2 m/s. The downslope gravitational acceleration is g sin θ = 5 m/s², while kinetic friction produces acceleration μg cos θ = (√3/5)(10)(√3/2) = 3 m/s². Initially the block is faster than the belt, so friction acts downslope and its acceleration is −(5 + 3) = −8 m/s²; it slows from 6 to 2 m/s after (6 − 2)/8 = 0.5 s and travels (6² − 2²)/(2·8) = 2 m. It then lags behind the belt, so friction acts upslope, giving a net downslope acceleration of 5 − 3 = 2 m/s²; its additional upslope distance before stopping is 2²/(2·2) = 1 m. Thus its maximum distance from the bottom, and hence the limiting minimum conveyor span, is l0 = 2 + 1 = 3 m. During the first 0.5 s the relative displacement over the belt is 2 − 2(0.5) = 1 m; during the next 1 s the block travels 1 m while the belt travels 2 m, so this 1 m is retraced and the block is again over its initial belt material point at the turning point. On sliding back through 3 m with acceleration 2 m/s², the time is determined by 3 = (1/2)(2)t², so t = √3 s; the belt moves 2√3 m upslope, making the relative sweep 3 + 2√3 m. With negligible pulley sizes, the endless belt has two straight runs and total material length 2l0 = 6 m; since 3 + 2√3 > 6, the returning block sweeps over the entire belt, so the scratch length is 6 m. Final answer: l0 = 3 m; s = 6 m.

No usable image is available, so the relevant data are m = 8 kg, maximum rope tension 120 N, maximum motor power 1200 W, and height 90 m; taking g = 10 m/s², the initial maximum acceleration is a = (120 − mg)/m = (120 − 80)/8 = 5 m/s². Maximum tension can be maintained until P = Tv reaches 1200 W, which occurs at v1 = 1200/120 = 10 m/s, after t1 = v1/a = 2 s and a rise s1 = v1²/(2a) = 10 m; the motor’s work in this stage is W1 = Ts1 = 1200 J. At constant maximum speed the tension equals mg, so vmax = Pmax/(mg) = 1200/80 = 15 m/s. Since the object has reached this speed near 90 m, its final kinetic energy is mvmax²/2 = 900 J, and the total required work is mgh + mvmax²/2 = 7200 + 900 = 8100 J. After the initial stage, the remaining 6900 J is supplied at 1200 W, requiring 6900/1200 = 5.75 s, so the total time is 2 + 5.75 = 7.75 s. Final answer: 7.75 s

The image shows a symmetric smooth circular arc of radius 2 m and central angle 120°, tangent to the two 60° rough inclines; therefore each endpoint is 60° from the downward vertical radius and lies y=R(1−cos60°)=2(1−0.5)=1 m above the lowest point. Friction acts only on the inclines with constant magnitude f_k=μMg cos60°=0.2Mg(0.5). As the block repeatedly crosses the smooth arc, its excursions onto the rough inclines shrink toward zero, leaving limiting mechanical energy Mgy at the junction height; hence the total energy dissipated by friction is Mg(h−y). If S is the total distance traveled on the inclines, μMg cos60°S=Mg(3−1), so S=(3−1)/(0.2 cos60°)=2/0.1=20 m. Final answer: 20 m

The image shows that both vehicles begin decelerating at line AB and that vehicle 2 stops at the toll-station centerline, so the distance from AB to the centerline is found from 0²=15²−2(2.5)s, giving s=45 m. Vehicle 1 decelerates from 15 m/s to 5 m/s over s₁=(15²−5²)/(2×2.5)=40 m, leaving 45−40=5 m traveled at the constant speed of 5 m/s. Its total time is (15−5)/2.5+5/5+(15−5)/2.5=4+1+4=9 s, while vehicle 2 takes 15/2.5+10+15/2.5=6+10+6=22 s, so vehicle 1 uses 22−9=13 s less. Final answer: 5 m; 13 s

The figure shows the rotating coil connected by slip rings directly across the ideal transformer’s primary winding, with the voltmeter across the primary and the ammeter in series with it. Starting from the neutral plane, the magnetic flux is maximum and the induced emf is zero, so e(t)=Em sin(ωt), where Em=nBSω=200×√2×0.01×100=200√2 V; hence e(t)=200√2 sin(100t) V. Its effective value is E=Em/√2=200 V, and because the coil resistance is negligible, the voltmeter reads 200 V. For an ideal transformer with N1:N2=2:1, U2=U1(N2/N1)=200×1/2=100 V and I2=I1(N1/N2)=2×2=4 A, so R=U2/I2=100/4=25 Ω. Final answer: 1. e(t)=200√2 sin(100t) V; 2. 200 V; 3. 25 Ω.

The image shows a heavy central ram being lifted by four bamboo poles, consistent with four people each applying an upward force of 450 N through a lifting distance h₁ = 0.20 m. From the initial position to the instant the ram returns to ground level, gravity does zero net work because the initial and final heights are equal, so the total work done by the four people becomes impact kinetic energy: 4Fh₁ = ½mv². Thus v = √(8Fh₁/m) = √[8(450)(0.20)/80] = 3.0 m/s. During penetration through h₂ = 0.03 m, the ram stops while gravity does positive work mgh₂ and the average ground resistance R does negative work Rh₂; hence ½mv² + mgh₂ − Rh₂ = 0, giving R = mg + mv²/(2h₂). Taking g = 9.8 m/s², R = 80(9.8) + 80(3.0)²/[2(0.03)] = 1.2784 × 10⁴ N ≈ 1.28 × 10⁴ N; by Newton’s third law, this is also the magnitude of the average impact force exerted by the ram on the ground. Final answer: 3.0 m/s; 1.28 × 10⁴ N.

The image shows a fixed vertical spring supporting ball A, while ball B hangs below A by a string, so before the string is cut the spring supports both masses. At rest, kx = (mA + mB)g, hence k = [(0.100 + 0.500)(10)]/0.15 = 40 N/m. After B is removed, A’s new equilibrium extension is xA = mAg/k = (0.100 × 10)/40 = 0.025 m; at the instant of cutting, A is still at the original extension of 0.15 m with zero velocity, so its amplitude about the new equilibrium is 0.15 − 0.025 = 0.125 m. For SHM, the maximum acceleration is amax = ω²A = (k/mA)A = (40/0.100)(0.125) = 50 m/s². Final answer: spring constant = 40 N/m; amplitude of A = 0.125 m (12.5 cm); maximum acceleration of A = 50 m/s².

The image shows the generator feeding a 1:4 step-up transformer, a transmission line with total series resistance R=4 Ω, and a 4:1 step-down transformer supplying the lamps in parallel; assuming ideal transformers, voltage follows the turns ratio, current follows the inverse ratio, and only the line and generator internal resistance dissipate power. There are 22×6=132 lamps, so their rated total power is Pload=132×40=5280 W and their total current at 220 V is 5280/220=24 A. The step-down transformer requires a primary voltage of 4×220=880 V and has primary, hence line, current 24/4=6 A. The line loss is 6²×4=144 W and its voltage drop is 6×4=24 V, so the step-up secondary voltage is 880+24=904 V. Its primary voltage is 904/4=226 V and its primary current is 4×6=24 A; therefore the generator’s terminal output power is 226×24=5424 W, equivalently 5280+144 W. With internal resistance 1 Ω, the generator emf is E=226+24×1=250 V. The transmission efficiency is 5280/5424=110/113≈97.3%. If the number of lamps is halved, their rated power is 2640 W, the line current is halved to 3 A, and the line loss becomes 3²×4=36 W, so the required generator output is 2640+36=2676 W, not 5424/2=2712 W, because line loss varies as the square of current. Final answer: 5424 W; 250 V; 97.3%; no—the new output power is 2676 W, about 49.3% of the original.

The image shows that the pedestrian has one lane width M–B = L₂ = 3.6 m left to walk, each vehicle’s front is initially L₃ = 40 m from the stop line, the crosswalk is L₁ = 4 m wide in the vehicles’ direction, and complete passage requires the vehicle’s front to travel L₃ + L₁ + D; Figure B identifies d₂ as the rear cargo clearance and d₁ as the front clearance. The available time is t = L₂/v = 3.6/1.2 = 3 s. For the sedan, the required displacement is 40 + 4 + 4 = 48 m, so 48 = 12(3) + ½a(3²), giving a = 8/3 m/s². For the truck, the minimum passing acceleration satisfies 40 + 4 + 6 = 10(3) + ½aₜ(3²), hence aₜ = 40/9 m/s². During these 3 s the cargo accelerates at 4 m/s², so it shifts rearward relative to the truck by ½(40/9 − 4)(3²) = 2 m and has a rearward relative speed (40/9 − 4)3 = 4/3 m/s when the truck becomes uniform. Friction then accelerates the cargo until it matches the truck’s speed, producing a further rearward shift (4/3)²/(2·4) = 2/9 m; therefore d₂,min = 2 + 2/9 = 20/9 m. For braking, let b be the positive deceleration magnitude. The truck’s stopping distance is 10²/(2b) = 50/b, so stopping at or before the line requires 50/b ≤ 40, or b ≥ 5/4 m/s²; for a larger b, braking can begin closer to the line. If b ≤ 4 m/s², the cargo remains fixed relative to the truck. If b > 4 m/s², the cargo’s total stopping distance is 10²/(2·4) = 12.5 m while the truck’s is 50/b, so the cargo advances relative to the truck by 12.5 − 50/b; requiring this not to exceed d₁ = 2.5 m gives 12.5 − 50/b ≤ 2.5, hence b ≤ 5 m/s². Within this range the required braking delay is (40 − 50/b)/10 = 4 − 5/b, which lies from 0 to 3 s, so braking can begin no later than the pedestrian’s arrival at B and end at the stop line. Final answer: the sedan’s minimum acceleration is 8/3 m/s², the minimum d₂ is 20/9 m, and the truck’s braking deceleration magnitude must satisfy 5/4 m/s² ≤ b ≤ 5 m/s².

The image shows the coil rotating about the in-plane axis OO′ while the crossed symbols indicate a magnetic field directed into the page, so at the shown neutral-plane position the coil’s flux is maximum and the induced emf is zero. The coil area is S = πr² = π(0.10)² = 0.01π m², and n = 600 r/min = 10 Hz gives angular speed ω = 2πn = 20π rad/s. Taking the initial linked flux as Φ = NBS cos(ωt), the induced emf is e = −dΦ/dt = NBSω sin(ωt), whose maximum value is NBSω = 100(5/π²)(0.01π)(20π) = 100 V; hence e(t) = 100 sin(20πt) V. At t = 1/60 s, e = 100 sin(π/3) = 50√3 V ≈ 86.6 V. Over 0 ≤ t ≤ 1/60 s, the average emf is e_avg = (1/(1/60))∫₀^(1/60)100 sin(20πt)dt = 150/π V ≈ 47.7 V. Final answer: e(t) = 100 sin(20πt) V; e(1/60 s) = 50√3 V; e_avg = 150/π V.

The image shows the rotation axis at height h = 5.5 m and the ball at the lowest point, L = 0.5 m below the axis, where its tangential velocity is horizontal; thus its release height is h − L = 5.0 m. At the highest point, the inward radial equation is Ttop + mg = mvtop²/L, so the speed is not uniquely fixed unless the intended value is the minimum for completing a vertical circle; setting Ttop = 0 gives vtop,min = √(gL) = √5 ≈ 2.24 m/s. At the lowest point when the rope just breaks, Tmax − mg = mv²/L, hence v = √[(Tmax − mg)L/m] = √[(42 − 10)(0.5)] = 4.0 m/s. The fall time is t = √[2(h − L)/g] = √(10/10) = 1.0 s, so the horizontal range is x = vt = 4.0 m. Strictly, a complete circle is impossible with this rope because the critical motion would require a lowest-point tension of 60 N, exceeding 42 N. Final answer: (1) minimum/critical speed √5 m/s ≈ 2.24 m/s, though the literal speed is otherwise undetermined; (2) 4.0 m/s and 4.0 m.

The image shows P moving left from A across the rough plank toward B, where the plank touches the horizontal entry D of the quarter-circular slider; because the plank and slider are initially in contact on the smooth floor, they move together while P is on AB. Taking left as positive, the kinetic friction is f=μmg, so aP=−μg and the common acceleration of the plank and slider, whose total mass is 2m, is a=μg/2. Since P slows from v0 to v0/2, the elapsed time is t=(v0−v0/2)/(μg)=v0/(2μg), giving vAB=at=v0/4 to the left. Relative to the plank, P has acceleration −μg−μg/2=−3μg/2 and its speed changes from v0 to v0/2−v0/4=v0/4, so (v0/4)²=v0²−3μgL, yielding L=5v0²/(16μg). At D, P and the slider have velocities v0/2 and v0/4 to the left; on the arc the slider separates from the plank, and, interpreting “reaches C” as just reaching it with zero relative speed, horizontal momentum gives 2mV=m(v0/2+v0/4), hence V=3v0/8. Mechanical-energy conservation for P and the smooth slider then gives (m/2)[(v0/2)²+(v0/4)²]=m(3v0/8)²+mgR, so R=v0²/(64g). Final answer: vAB=v0/4 to the left; L=5v0²/(16μg); R=v0²/(64g).

The image shows the negatively charged droplet moving from P to O at 45° upward and rightward through a leftward electric field and an outward magnetic field, while in the first quadrant the electric field is downward and the magnetic field is into the paper only for y>h. Since v0=2√2 m/s and θ=45°, vx=vy=2 m/s; straight uniform motion in the third quadrant requires qE−qBvy=0 and qBvx−mg=0, so B=E/vy=1/2=0.50 T and q/m=g/(Bvx)=10 C/kg, with the signed charge-to-mass ratio equal to −10 C/kg. In the first quadrant, the upward electric force qE equals the downward weight mg because qE/m=10 m/s²=g, so below y=h the droplet moves uniformly. It first reaches (h,h)=(0.4,0.4) m after t1=h/vy=0.20 s. Above y=h, only the magnetic force remains unbalanced, giving angular speed ω=qB/m=5 rad/s and radius r=v0/ω=0.4√2 m; the circular path has center (0.8,0), and it crosses y=h again at (1.2,0.4) after turning through π/2, requiring t2=(π/2)/ω=π/10 s. It then has velocity components (2,−2) m/s and takes t3=0.4/2=0.20 s to reach y=0, moving another 0.4 m in x, so the exit coordinate is x=1.2+0.4=1.6 m and the total first-quadrant time is t1+t2+t3=0.4+π/10 s≈0.714 s. Final answer: B=0.50 T; q/m=10 C/kg in magnitude (signed value −10 C/kg); time in the first quadrant=0.4+π/10 s≈0.714 s; exit x-coordinate=1.6 m.

The image shows rods ab and cd connecting the same two parallel rails on opposite sides of MN, with equal but oppositely directed perpendicular magnetic fields; since each rod has resistance R and the rails have negligible resistance, the loop resistance is 2R. While ab is fixed, cd moving downhill at speed v produces emf BLv and current I = BLv/(2R); the magnetic forces on both rods are uphill. When ab just leaves the posts, its magnetic force equals its downhill weight component, so BLI_t = mg sin 30° = mg/2. Hence I_t = mg/(2BL) and v_t = 2RI_t/(BL) = mgR/(B²L²). For cd, 2m dv/dτ = mg − kv, where k = B²L²/(2R); solving with v(0) = 0 and using v(t) = v_t gives t = 4mR ln 2/(B²L²), so equivalently v_t = gt/(4 ln 2). If cd travels distance x before time t, integrating its equation gives 2mv_t = mgt − kx; since kv_t = mg/2, x = 2v_t t − 4v_t²/g. The electrical energy supplied by cd equals its gravitational-energy loss minus its kinetic-energy gain, E_cd = mgx − mv_t² = 2mgv_t t − 5mv_t² = m v_t²(8 ln 2 − 5). After ab leaves the posts, let v_a and v_c be signed downhill velocities and u = v_a + v_c; because the fields are opposite, the net emf is BLu and I = BLu/(2R), while both magnetic forces remain uphill. Adding the acceleration equations m dv_a/dτ = mg/2 − BLI and 2m dv_c/dτ = mg − BLI gives du/dτ = g − 3BLI/(2m). The initial current mg/(2BL) is below the stable limiting value obtained by setting du/dτ = 0, so the current increases toward its maximum 2mg/(3BL). Final answer: v_t = mgR/(B²L²) = gt/(4 ln 2); E_cd = 2mgv_t t − 5mv_t² = m³g²R²(8 ln 2 − 5)/(B⁴L⁴) = mg²t²(8 ln 2 − 5)/(16(ln 2)²); I_max = 2mg/(3BL).

The image shows that the magnetic field exists only inside the circular region of radius 1 cm centered at O, so coils A and B enclose the same field-filled area π(0.01 m)² even though B is larger; the 10 turns of A affect flux linkage and induced emf, not the magnetic flux through each turn. Thus, when B decreases from 0.8 T to 0.4 T, the magnitude of the flux change in each of A and B is |ΔΦ|=|ΔB|S=(0.8−0.4)π(0.01)²=4π×10⁻⁵ Wb≈1.26×10⁻⁴ Wb. Coil C is entirely within the field and has area π(0.005 m)²; when the 0.8 T field rotates 30° away from the normal to the coil, its flux decreases from BS to BS cos30°, so |ΔΦC|=BS(1−cos30°)=0.8π(0.005)²(1−√3/2)=π(2−√3)×10⁻⁵ Wb≈8.42×10⁻⁶ Wb. Final answer: ΔΦA=ΔΦB=1.26×10⁻⁴ Wb, and ΔΦC=8.42×10⁻⁶ Wb, all decreases in magnitude.

The image shows piston A above piston B, with a spring between them, atmospheric air communicating through the small hole in A, and sealed gas below B; initially the three vertical distances are each 0.10 m. Since atmospheric pressure acts equally on both sides of A, its equilibrium requires the compressed spring to exert F₁=mg=10 N upward, so its natural length is l₀=0.10+F₁/k=0.1167 m. For piston B, initial equilibrium gives P₁S=p₀S+mg+F₁, hence P₁=10⁵+(10+10)/(5×10⁻⁴)=1.4×10⁵ Pa. During slow heating, while A is free, its equilibrium keeps the spring force and A–B distance unchanged, so both pistons rise until A reaches the retaining ring; thereafter A remains at the 0.30 m height. When the A–B distance is 0.05 m, B is therefore 0.25 m above the bottom, and the spring force is F₂=k(l₀−0.05)=600(0.1167−0.05)=40 N. Equilibrium of B then gives P₂=10⁵+(10+40)/(5×10⁻⁴)=2.0×10⁵ Pa. The sealed gas initially has height 0.10 m and finally 0.25 m, and its temperature equals the slowly varying ambient temperature, so P₁V₁/T₁=P₂V₂/T₂ gives T₂=300(2.0×10⁵/1.4×10⁵)(0.25/0.10)=1.07×10³ K. Final answer: initial gas pressure = 1.4×10⁵ Pa; ambient temperature = 1.07×10³ K.

No usable image is available, so the final expansion volume is not specified; denote it by V_f, with V_f=2V if the intended setup is expansion into an equal-sized vacuum chamber. For number density n=N/V, an interior atom has average potential energy ū_int=n∫_d^∞[−ε(d/r)^6]4πr²dr=−4πεd³n/3=−2a′N/V, neglecting container-size corrections because d≪V^(1/3). At a locally planar boundary, away from edges and corners, only half the surrounding solid angle contains gas, so ū_boundary=ū_int/2=−a′N/V. In equilibrium v=0, and the corresponding difference in attraction-energy density is n(ū_int−ū_boundary)=−a′N²/V²; Bernoulli’s law with P_int=Nk_BT/V therefore gives P_boundary=Nk_BT/V−a′N²/V². Counting each interacting pair only once, the total potential energy is Nū_int/2=−a′N²/V, so the total energy is E=(3/2)Nk_BT−a′N²/V. During isolated free expansion, energy conservation gives (3/2)Nk_BT−a′N²/V=(3/2)Nk_BT_f−a′N²/V_f, hence T_f=T−(2a′N/3k_B)(1/V−1/V_f). From dS=(dE+P dV)/T, the attraction terms cancel and dS=(3/2)Nk_BdT/T+Nk_BdV/V, so ΔS_univ=Nk_Bln(V_f/V)+(3/2)Nk_Bln(T_f/T)=Nk_B[ln(V_f/V)−a′N(1−V/V_f)/(Vk_BT)]+O((a′N/(Vk_BT))²). Final answer: ū_int=−2a′N/V; ū_boundary=−a′N/V; P_boundary=Nk_BT/V−a′N²/V²; E=(3/2)Nk_BT−a′N²/V; T_f=T−(2a′N/3k_B)(1/V−1/V_f); ΔS_univ=Nk_B[ln(V_f/V)−a′N(1−V/V_f)/(Vk_BT)] to first order, and for V_f=2V these become T_f=T−a′N/(3Vk_B) and ΔS_univ=Nk_B[ln2−a′N/(2Vk_BT)].

The image shows AB inclined at 30° to the horizontal and BC at 60°, making the groove right-angled, while the cube moves inward perpendicular to the paper. Let the normal reactions from AB and BC be N_AB and N_BC. Since there is no acceleration in the cross-sectional plane, horizontal equilibrium gives N_AB cos 60° = N_BC cos 30°, so N_AB = √3N_BC; vertical equilibrium gives N_AB sin 60° + N_BC sin 30° = mg, yielding N_AB = √3mg/2 and N_BC = mg/2. The kinetic friction forces are collinear along the groove, so their total magnitude is μN_AB + μN_BC = μmg(√3 + 1)/2. Friction opposes the inward motion, so it is perpendicular to the paper and directed outward. Final answer: The frictional force is μmg(1 + √3)/2, directed outward from the plane of the paper.

The image shows P at (0,h) with initial velocity v0 along +x, an electric field directed along +y in the first quadrant, and an inward magnetic field inside the equilateral triangle abc in the fourth quadrant, with a=(2h,0) and ab vertical. Because the particle moves downward while the electric field points upward, its charge must be negative. Its horizontal motion gives t=2h/v0, while its vertical motion gives 0=h−(|q|E/2m)t², so E=mv0²/(2|q|h). At a, vx=v0 and vy=−(|q|E/m)t=−v0, hence va=v0 i−v0 j, with magnitude √2v0 and direction 45° below the +x-axis. In the inward magnetic field, the negative charge curves clockwise; to leave toward the third quadrant at 45° to the −y-axis, its direction must rotate from −45° to −135°, a 90° turn. If the circular radius is R, taking a as the local origin gives the circle center at (−R/√2,−R/√2), and after this quarter-circle turn the exit point on ab is (0,−√2R). Since ab has length L, √2R≤L, so the largest allowable radius, which gives the minimum field, is Rmax=L/√2; using R=m(√2v0)/(|q|B) gives Bmin=2mv0/(|q|L). Final answer: E=mv0²/(2|q|h); at a the velocity is v0 i−v0 j, of magnitude √2v0 and directed 45° below the +x-axis; Bmin=2mv0/(|q|L), directed into the plane.

The solid waveform has consecutive crests at x = 0 m and x = 8 m, so the wavelength is λ = 8 m; at t₂ the dashed crest is at x = 3 m, meaning the profile is displaced 3 m toward +x modulo one wavelength, equivalently 5 m toward −x. Using v = λ/T and 3T < Δt < 4T with Δt = 0.5 s gives 24 m < vΔt < 32 m. For propagation toward +x, the distance must be 3 + nλ, so the only value in this interval is 27 m, giving v = 27/0.5 = 54 m/s. For propagation toward −x, the distance must be 5 + nλ, so it is 29 m and v = 29/0.5 = 58 m/s; thus the first part has two possible speeds unless the direction is specified. If v = 74 m/s, the wave travels 74 × 0.5 = 37 m = 4λ + 5 m; a 5 m displacement toward −x is equivalent to the observed 3 m shift toward +x, so the wave propagates toward negative x. Final answer: 54 m/s toward +x or 58 m/s toward −x; if the speed is 74 m/s, the propagation direction is toward −x.

The image shows O between the two equal masses, with OA = 2l and OB = l; on release, A moves downward while B moves upward, so in the vertical position A is 2l below O and B is l above O. Conservation of mechanical energy gives mgl = ½Iω², where the net decrease in gravitational potential energy is 2mgl − mgl = mgl and I = m(2l)² + m(l)² = 5ml²; hence ω² = 2g/(5l). Ball A then has kinetic energy ½m(2lω)² = 4mgl/5. Since gravity does 2mgl of work on A, the work done by the rod is Wrod,A = 4mgl/5 − 2mgl = −6mgl/5. At the top, ball B has downward centripetal acceleration ω²l = 2g/5; taking downward as positive, mg + Frod = mω²l gives Frod = −3mg/5, so the rod exerts an upward force of magnitude 3mg/5 on B, which is a pushing force. Final answer: 1. −6mgl/5; 2. 3mg/5, pushing force.

The image shows the block m on a smooth incline of angle α belonging to a wedge of mass M, with the spring parallel to the incline and fixed to its upper end, while the wedge rests on rough horizontal ground. Let x=l−L be the spring’s extension, positive when the block moves down the incline; then mẍ=mg sinα−kx, so equilibrium requires xeq=mg sinα/k and leq=L+mg sinα/k. Initially x0=−L/4, and release from rest makes this a turning point, giving amplitude A=xeq−x0=mg sinα/k+L/4; hence the opposite turning point is xmax=xeq+A=L/4+2mg sinα/k, corresponding to maximum spring length lmax=5L/4+2mg sinα/k. For the wedge-block system, if a=ẍ is positive down the incline, the required ground-friction magnitude is m|a|cosα and the ground normal reaction is R=(M+m)g−ma sinα. During the oscillation, ma=mg sinα−kx ranges from −F0 to F0, where F0=mg sinα+kL/4; the largest friction-to-normal ratio occurs at the initially compressed turning point, where ma=F0 and R is smallest. Thus μF must satisfy μR≥F0cosα, with R>0. Final answer: equilibrium length = L+mg sinα/k; maximum elongation beyond natural length = L/4+2mg sinα/k, so maximum spring length = 5L/4+2mg sinα/k; μ≥[(mg sinα+kL/4)cosα]/[(M+m)g−(mg sinα+kL/4)sinα], provided (M+m)g>(mg sinα+kL/4)sinα.

The image shows MN inclined upward to the right at 45°, with O level with M and the dashed trajectory just tangent to MN near N. Taking M as the origin, MN has equation y=x, while O=(d,0). Since qE=√2mg, the electric-force components are qE cos45°=mg horizontally right and qE sin45°=mg upward; the upward component cancels gravity, leaving acceleration a=(g,0). Thus x=d+gt²/2, y=v₀t, and the velocity is (gt,v₀). At the closest point the trajectory is parallel to the 45° barrier, so v₀/(gt)=1, giving t=v₀/g and speed √[(gt)²+v₀²]=√2v₀. Tangency also requires x=y, so d+v₀²/(2g)=v₀²/g; hence at N, x=y=v₀²/g. Therefore MN=√(x²+y²)=√2v₀²/g. Final answer: (1) √2v₀; (2) √2v₀²/g.

The image shows that the lower mercury surface on the right is initially 6 cm above the left surface, while gas B is beneath an 18 cm mercury column open to atmospheric pressure. Thus initially pB=76+18=94 cmHg and, because the left interface is 6 cm lower, pA=94+6=100 cmHg. Since the tube is uniform, making the lower surfaces level raises the left surface and lowers the right surface by 3 cm each, reducing the length of A from 13 cm to 10 cm. The injection is isothermal, so Boyle’s law gives pA′=100×13/10=130 cmHg. At equal mercury levels pB′=pA′=130 cmHg, requiring an upper mercury-column height of 130−76=54 cm; therefore the injected mercury has equivalent height Δh=54−18=36 cm. During the subsequent heating, the upper mercury column remains 54 cm high, so pB stays 130 cmHg. Restoring A from 10 cm to 13 cm lowers its interface by 3 cm and raises the right interface by 3 cm, restoring the 6 cm difference; hence the final pressure of A is 130+6=136 cmHg. Since A has the same final and initial volume, Tfinal/Tinitial=pfinal/pinitial=136/100, giving Tfinal=300×136/100=408 K=135°C. Final answer: Δh=36 cm; TA=408 K (135°C).

The image shows that the incident beam travels radially through the curved surface to O without refraction, then meets the flat glass–air boundary MN at angle θ to its normal OO′; the screen is a horizontal distance ON = R from O. For a component of refractive index n, Snell’s law at O gives n sin θ = sin β, and its intersection with the screen is R cot β below N. At θ = 30°, β₁ = arcsin(√2 sin 30°) = 45° and β₂ = arcsin(√3 sin 30°) = 60°, so the two band edges are R cot 45° = R and R cot 60° = R/√3 below N; hence the band width is R − R/√3 = R(1 − 1/√3). As θ increases, components undergo total internal reflection when n sin θ ≥ 1; for all colors to be reflected into the same ray and thus form one light spot, this condition must hold for the smallest index n₁ = √2, giving θmin = arcsin(1/√2) = 45°. Final answer: width = R(1 − 1/√3); minimum angle = 45°.

No usable image is available, so the calculation uses the stated distances, speeds, and times. For the truck, 0² = 20² + 2a(80), giving a = −2.5 m/s² and an acceleration magnitude of 2.5 m/s². The taxi begins braking 3.5 + 0.5 = 4.0 s after the malfunction; by then the truck has traveled 20(4) − ½(2.5)(4²) = 60 m, while the taxi has traveled 15(4) = 60 m, so their initial 15 m separation remains 15 m. The figure shows A resting on the ground at the left end of the rope, B suspended 1.2 m above the ground at the right end, and the frictionless ring C initially 0.8 m above B; after C sticks to B, the inextensible rope requires A to move upward with the same speed v that B and C move downward. The ring falls freely from rest, so its speed just before collision is u = √(2gd) = √(2 × 10 × 0.8) = 4 m/s downward. During the very short collision, gravity has negligible impulse; letting J be the rope-tension impulse and I the collision impulse, the impulse equations are mv = J for A, mv = I − J for B, and 2m(v − u) = −I for C. Adding them eliminates I and J, giving 4mv = 2mu, so v = u/2 = 2 m/s, with A moving upward. Afterward, the right-hand mass is 3m while the left-hand mass is m, so B accelerates downward at a = [(3m − m)/(3m + m)]g = 5 m/s². For B to descend 1.2 m, 1.2 = 2t + (1/2)(5)t², whose positive solution is t = 0.40 s. Final answer: the speed of A is 2.0 m/s upward, and B reaches the ground 0.40 s after the collision.

The image shows the piston connected to the negligible-mass basket by one rope passing over two fixed pulleys, so the pulleys provide no mechanical advantage and the rope tension is T = Mweight g. Initially T = 0, and piston equilibrium gives p1S = p0S + mg, hence p1 = p0 + mg/S and V1 = Sh. When the cylinder’s ground reaction becomes zero, the rope supports the combined mass of the piston and cylinder, so T = (M_i + m)g and therefore Mweight = M_i + m. Final piston equilibrium gives p2S + T = p0S + mg, so p2 = p0 − M_i g/S. Since the cylinder is thermally conductive and the weights are added gradually, the ideal-gas expansion is isothermal: p1Sh = p2SH, where H is the final piston height. Thus H = h(p0S + mg)/(p0S − M_i g), and the rise is H − h = (M_i + m)gh/(p0S − M_i g), requiring p0S > M_i g. Final answer: Mweight = M_i + m; piston rise = (M_i + m)gh/(p0S − M_i g).

The image shows that the stone falls vertically by 200 brick thicknesses before reaching A, and its trajectory at A is perpendicular to the slope inclined at 37° to the horizontal. The vertical displacement is h = 200 × 0.10 = 20 m, so for a horizontal throw h = ½gt², giving 20 = ½ × 10 × t² and t = 2.0 s. At impact the downward velocity is vy = gt = 10 × 2 = 20 m/s. Because the impact velocity is perpendicular to the 37° slope, it makes an angle 53° with the horizontal, so tan53° = vy/v0 = cot37° = 0.8/0.6 = 4/3; therefore v0 = 20 × 3/4 = 15 m/s. Final answer: t = 2.0 s; v0 = 15 m/s.

The image shows a square room of width and height L, with the mirror on y=0 and the source at (L/2,d); hence the right wall is x=L and the top wall is y=L. For a point (L,y) on the right wall, the direct and image-source path lengths are rD=√[(L/2)²+(y−d)²] and rR=√[(L/2)²+(y+d)²], so their difference is Δ=rR−rD=4yd/(rR+rD)≈4yd/L because d,y≪L. The mirror adds a phase π, so constructive interference requires 2πΔ/λ+π=2πm; the smallest positive path difference is therefore λ/2, giving y=λL/(8d). The shell adds optical path a=(n−1)s only to the direct ray, changing the condition to 2π(Δ−a)/λ+π=2πm; the least nonnegative allowed geometric path difference is ρ=a+λ/2−λ⌊a/λ+1/2⌋, and therefore y=Lρ/(4d), with y=0 if the corner itself is bright. On the top wall, at horizontal displacement u from its midpoint, Δtop=√[u²+(L+d)²]−√[u²+(L−d)²]≈2Ld/√(L²+u²), which decreases from 2d at u=0 to 4d/√5 at either corner; since successive bright fringes differ by λ in path difference and the wall has two symmetric halves, the estimated total is (4d/λ)(1−2/√5), rounded to the nearest integer. Final answer: without the shell, y=λL/(8d); with the shell, y=(L/(4d))[(n−1)s+λ/2−λ⌊(n−1)s/λ+1/2⌋]; the top-wall fringe count is ⌊(4d/λ)(1−2/√5)+1/2⌋.

The image shows the ball at the lowest point of a vertical circle of radius R, with the rope directed upward toward the center. At this point the radial equation is T − mg = mv₁²/R; using T = 7mg gives v₁² = 6gR and initial kinetic energy K₁ = 3mgR. To just maintain the circular path at the highest point, the rope tension there is zero, so mg = mv₂²/R, giving v₂² = gR and K₂ = mgR/2. The ball rises through a height 2R, increasing its gravitational potential energy by 2mgR, while rope tension does no work. Therefore the energy expended against air resistance is K₁ − K₂ − 2mgR = 3mgR − mgR/2 − 2mgR = mgR/2. Final answer: mgR/2

No usable image is available, so the relevant data are the stated maximum power 60 kW, mass 2000 kg, maximum speed 108 km/h, and acceleration 5 m/s². Convert the maximum speed: 108 km/h = 30 m/s. At maximum speed the car moves uniformly, so the traction balances the constant resistance; using P = fv gives f = 60,000/30 = 2000 N. During uniform acceleration, F − f = ma, so F = 2000 × 5 + 2000 = 12,000 N. This stage ends when the traction power reaches 60 kW, hence its final speed is v = P/F = 60,000/12,000 = 5 m/s; from v² = 2as, the distance is s = 5²/(2 × 5) = 2.5 m. Therefore, the work done by resistance is W = −fs = −2000 × 2.5 = −5000 J. Final answer: 2000 N; 12,000 N; −5000 J.

The image shows the square frame MNPQ with its lower side PQ initially at the upper boundary of the into-the-page magnetic field, whose vertical width is h, so the frame first enters the field, then falls wholly inside it, and finally begins leaving when PQ reaches the lower boundary. At that instant the frame moves at constant velocity, so the upward magnetic force equals its weight: mg=BIL, where I=BLv/R; hence mg=B²L²v/R and v=mgR/(B²L²)=10 m/s. Before PQ reaches the lower boundary, the frame descends h, so energy conservation gives the heat produced during entry as Q₁=mgh−mv²/2=1×10×5.2−1×10²/2=2 J; while the frame subsequently exits at constant speed through an additional distance L, its loss of gravitational potential energy becomes heat, Q₂=mgL=10 J, giving Q=Q₁+Q₂=12 J. Until PQ reaches the lower boundary, magnetic force acts only while the frame enters; its impulse is J=∫(B²L²v/R)dt=(B²L²/R)∫vdt=B²L³/R=1 N·s. Applying impulse-momentum over the total falling time t gives mgt−J=mv, so t=(mv+J)/(mg)=(10+1)/10=1.1 s. Final answer: v=10 m/s, Q=12 J, t=1.1 s.

The image shows a semicircular single-turn coil of area S = πa²/2 initially entirely in the magnetic field, with its plane perpendicular to B, while its diameter ab lies on the field boundary and serves as the rotation axis; the slip rings connect the coil and load in series, so the total resistance is R + r. Taking n as revolutions per second gives angular speed ω = 2πn. During the first quarter-turn the flux changes from BS to zero according to Φ = BS cosθ, so the maximum emf is εmax = BSω = π²Ba²n and the maximum current is εmax/(R + r). The quarter-turn time is 1/(4n), hence the magnitude of the average emf is BS/[1/(4n)] = 2πBa²n, and the charge is q = |ΔΦ|/(R + r) = πBa²/[2(R + r)]. The coil is in the field only during the first and last quarter-turns; therefore, for one full turn, the external work equals the total Joule heat W = ∫ε²dt/(R + r) = (BSω)²[π/(2ω)]/(R + r) = π⁴B²a⁴n/[4(R + r)]. Final answer: Imax = π²Ba²n/(R + r); Eavg = 2πBa²n; q = πBa²/[2(R + r)]; Wext = π⁴B²a⁴n/[4(R + r)].

The figure shows the disk initially at the center of a square table of side L, with the trailing edge of the cloth initially at AB and moving perpendicular to AB with acceleration a. While the cloth slides beneath the disk, kinetic friction accelerates the disk at μ₁g, so the cloth edge reaches the disk at time t₁ given by at₁²/2 = L/2 + μ₁gt₁²/2, hence t₁² = L/(a − μ₁g). By then the disk has moved s₁ = μ₁gt₁²/2 and has speed v₁ = μ₁gt₁. After contacting the bare table, it is decelerated at μ₂g and travels an additional distance s₂ = v₁²/(2μ₂g). Requiring s₁ + s₂ ≤ L/2 gives μ₁gL/[2(a − μ₁g)] + μ₁²gL/[2μ₂(a − μ₁g)] ≤ L/2, which simplifies to a ≥ μ₁g(2 + μ₁/μ₂). Final answer: a ≥ μ₁g(2 + μ₁/μ₂).

The figure shows the spring pulling C upward-left at 60° to the vertical, while the rope pulls C upward-right at 30° to the vertical and pulls A horizontally left after passing over the smooth pulley. Let the spring force be F_s and the rope tension be T; equilibrium of C gives T sin30°=F_s sin60° and T cos30°+F_s cos60°=m_Cg=10 N, so T=√3F_s and (3/2+1/2)F_s=10, yielding F_s=5 N and T=5√3 N. By Hooke’s law, k=F_s/Δx=5/0.02=250 N/m. For A to remain at rest, the static friction exerted by B must balance the leftward rope tension, so it is 5√3 N to the right. Considering A, B, and C together, all rope forces are internal, and the spring’s leftward horizontal component F_s sin60° must be balanced by ground friction on B; hence this friction is 5sin60°=5√3/2 N to the right. Final answer: 1. k=250 N/m; 2. 5√3 N to the right; 3. 5√3/2 N to the right.

No usable image is available, so the solution relies on the stated quantities m, P, and v. At the maximum speed v, the net force is zero, so the traction force equals the constant resistance force f; using the power relation P = fv gives f = P/v. At speed v/4 while the engine operates at rated power, the traction force is P/(v/4) = 4P/v, so the net force is 4P/v − P/v = 3P/v and the instantaneous acceleration is 3P/(mv). For the uniformly accelerated stage, the traction force is 2f = 2P/v, giving a constant net force f = P/v and acceleration a = P/(mv); this stage ends when the traction power reaches P, which occurs at P = (2P/v)u, so u = v/2. Starting from rest, the duration is t = u/a = (v/2)/(P/(mv)) = mv²/(2P). Final answer: 1. P/v; 2. 3P/(mv); 3. mv²/(2P).

The image shows n1 connected to the 400 V generator, n2 connected to the 2 kV transmission line, a line resistance R between n2 and n3, and n4 supplying the user at 220 V. For an ideal transformer, the turns ratio equals the voltage ratio, so n1/n2 = U1/U2 = 400/2000 = 1/5. The transmission current is I = P/U2 = 10,000/2,000 = 5 A; because the line and the n3 coil carry the same current, and the ideal step-down transformer receives the user’s 9.5 kW, its primary voltage is U3 = 9,500/5 = 1,900 V. Therefore, n3/n4 = U3/U4 = 1,900/220 = 95/11 ≈ 8.64. Final answer: n1/n2 = 1/5; n3/n4 = 95/11 ≈ 8.64.

The image shows rod MN spanning rails separated by L = 0.15 m on a plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal, with the vertical magnetic field perpendicular to the horizontal rod; therefore the Ampere force F_A = BIL is horizontal and its component up the rails is F_A cos30°. For smooth rails, equilibrium requires F_A cos30° = mg sin30°, so F_A = mg tan30° = 0.017×10/1.7 = 0.10 N. Thus I = F_A/(BL) = 0.10/(0.6×0.15) = 10/9 A, and since the stationary rod produces no motional emf, R₂ = E/I − R₁ − r = 10/(10/9) − 4 − 1 = 4 Ω. When R₂ = 10 Ω, I = 10/(4+10+1) = 2/3 A, giving F_A = 0.6×(2/3)×0.15 = 0.060 N and an upward component F_A cos30° = 0.060×1.7/2 = 0.051 N; the downward gravitational component is mg sin30° = 0.017×10/2 = 0.085 N, so friction must be 0.085−0.051 = 0.034 N directed upward along the rails. Final answer: For smooth rails, the Ampere force is 0.1 N and R₂ = 4 Ω; when R₂ = 10 Ω, the frictional force is 3.4×10⁻² N upward along the rails.

The image shows the horizontal rod PQ suspended symmetrically by two vertical identical springs, with current flowing from P to Q and the dotted magnetic field directed out of the page. Each spring exerts an upward force kx = 100 × 0.02 = 2 N, so the total upward spring force is 4 N. The rod’s weight is mg = 0.1 × 10 = 1 N downward; therefore, vertical equilibrium requires the Ampere force to be downward with magnitude F = 4 − 1 = 3 N. This direction also follows from F = IL × B: current to the right crossed with a field out of the page gives a downward force. Since the rod is perpendicular to the field, F = BIL, so B = F/(IL) = 3/(3 × 2) = 0.5 T. Final answer: The Ampere force is 3 N downward, and the magnetic induction is 0.5 T.

The image shows that the capacitor plates A and B are connected in parallel with R2, while R1, R2, and the internal resistance r form a series conducting path with the source; the upper source terminal is positive, so A is at a higher potential than B. The steady current is I=E/(r+R1+R2)=60/(2+8+15)=2.4 A, giving the capacitor voltage UAB=IR2=2.4×15=36 V. Thus the capacitance is C=Q/UAB=(6×10^-8)/36=1.67×10^-9 F. For plate separation d=4 cm=0.04 m, the uniform electric-field strength is Efield=UAB/d=36/0.04=900 V/m, directed from A to B. Since VA=0, VB=-36 V; point C is 1 cm from B toward A, so VC=VB+(VA-VB)(1/4)=-36+9=-27 V. Final answer: 1.67×10^-9 F; 900 V/m from A to B; -27 V.

The image shows plate 0 connected with the even-numbered cylinders, the odd-numbered cylinders connected to the opposite terminal, and the voltage Vodd−Veven alternating between +U and −U with period T, reversing every T/2. At t=0 cylinder 1 is at the higher potential, so the electric field points toward plate 0 and the force on the electron points toward cylinder 1. The electric field does work eU, so ½mv₁²=eU and v₁=√(2eU/m). The electron accelerates uniformly across the gap from plate 0 to cylinder 1, moves uniformly through cylinder 1 at v₁ because its internal field is zero, and reaches the next gap after the voltage has reversed; it is then accelerated toward cylinder 2, gaining another eU, so v₂=√(4eU/m)=√2v₁, after which it moves uniformly through cylinder 2 and exits it at v₂. Neglecting gap-crossing times and choosing the shortest synchronous transit, the electron must spend T/2 in every cylinder. Since its kinetic energy after n gaps is ½mvₙ²=neU, vₙ=√(2neU/m), and hence Lₙ=vₙT/2=T√(neU/(2m)). If each gap has width d, its field magnitude is U/d and the electron’s acceleration magnitude is a=eU/(md). The time spent in the jth successfully crossed gap is τⱼ=(vⱼ−vⱼ₋₁)/a, so the accumulated gap time after n gaps is Στⱼ=vₙ/a. Because each unchanged cylinder already requires T/2, this accumulated time is the phase lag relative to the voltage; acceleration remains correctly directed only until the lag reaches T/2. Thus vₘₐₓ/a=T/2, giving vₘₐₓ=eUT/(2md). Final answer: v₁=√(2eU/m), the electron accelerates uniformly in each gap and moves uniformly in cylinders 1 and 2, leaving cylinder 2 at v₂=√(4eU/m); Lₙ=T√(neU/(2m)); vₘₐₓ=eUT/(2md).

The image shows S at (0,d)=(0,1.2 m), the collection device along y=0 for x≥0, and a magnetic field directed into the paper; therefore a negative particle entering the first quadrant follows a clockwise circular path with angular speed ω=|q|B/m=(2×10^6)(5×10^-3)=1.0×10^4 rad/s and radius r=v/ω. To reach y=0, the maximum possible vertical displacement 2r must satisfy 2r≥d, so the minimum speed is v1=ωd/2=6.0×10^3 m/s. For v2=8.0×10^3 m/s, r=v2/ω=0.80 m; if θ is the initial velocity angle from +x and φ=ωt is the angle through which the velocity turns, reaching y=0 requires d=2r sin(φ/2)sin(φ/2−θ)≤2r sin(φ/2), so the minimum time occurs when sin(φ/2)=d/(2r)=0.75; using sin48.5°=0.75 gives φ=97°=1.693 rad and tmin=φ/ω=1.69×10^-4 s. For two different initial directions to reach the same collection position, the largest possible x follows from the source-to-impact chord not exceeding the diameter: sqrt(xmax^2+d^2)=2r, giving xmax=sqrt(4r^2−d^2)=sqrt(1.12)=1.058 m; the second trajectory first becomes possible when its circle is tangent to the x-axis, for which the center height d−r cosθ equals r, hence cosθ=(d−r)/r=0.5, θ=60°, and x0=r sin60°=0.4sqrt(3)=0.693 m. Thus the required length is xmax−x0=1.058−0.693=0.365 m. Final answer: v1=6.0×10^3 m/s; minimum time=1.69×10^-4 s; length=0.365 m (approximately 0.37 m).

The image shows length c along x, width b along z, and thickness a along y, so the cross-sectional area normal to x is ab and the top-face area normal to z is ac; the current is along +x, B is along +y, and the Hall field is along −z. A free electron contributing to the conventional current along +x drifts along −x, so F_B=qv×B=(−e)[(−x)×(+y)] points along +z. If its x-direction drift-speed magnitude is v_nx, then I_n=neabv_nx, giving v_nx=I_n/(neab); its magnetic-force magnitude is ev_nxB=BI_n/(nab), while the Hall electric force is qE=(−e)(−Ez)=+eEz, so the forces add and F_nz=eE+BI_n/(nab). During Δt, the volume swept toward the top surface by each carrier type is acv_zΔt, so N_n=nacv_nzΔt electrons and N_p=pacv_pzΔt holes reach it. Electron motion along +z produces current along −z, I_nz=−enacv_nz, whereas hole motion produces current along +z, I_pz=epacv_pz; a stable open-circuit Hall field requires zero net z-current, so I_nz+I_pz=0, equivalently nv_nz=pv_pz and N_n=N_p. Final answer: the electron’s Lorentz force is along +z; F_nz=eE+BI_n/(nab); N_n=nacv_nzΔt and N_p=pacv_pzΔt, with I_nz+I_pz=0, or nv_nz=pv_pz.

The dashed line is the lower boundary of the into-the-page magnetic field at height h = 0.8 m, and the square frame of side l = 0.2 m enters upward through this boundary with side ab first at v0 = 2 m/s. During entry, the induced current is I = Blv0/R, so the downward magnetic force is FB = BIl = B²l²v0/R; constant velocity requires F − mg − FB = 0, giving B²(0.2)²(2)/0.08 = 2 − 0.1(10) = 1 and hence B = 1 T. The frame takes l/v0 = 0.2/2 = 0.10 s to enter completely; once fully inside, its flux is constant, so there is no induced current, and after F is removed it rises under gravity for v0/g = 2/10 = 0.20 s, making the total time 0.30 s. On falling back to the boundary it again has speed 2 m/s; while exiting, the upward magnetic force B²l²v/R equals mg at v = 2 m/s, so it exits at constant speed. When fully outside, its lower side is at h − l = 0.6 m, and free fall from there gives the landing speed v = √[2² + 2(10)(0.6)] = 4 m/s. Joule heat is produced only while entering and exiting; for each passage, Q = FB l = (1)(0.2) = 0.20 J, so the total is 0.40 J. Final answer: B = 1 T; time to the highest point = 0.30 s; landing speed = 4.0 m/s; total Joule heat = 0.40 J.

The image shows a square field region of side L, with the positive ions entering at a horizontally toward b at speed v₀, while the electric field points vertically from a toward d. Acceleration from rest through voltage U₀ gives qU₀=½mv₀², so U₀=mv₀²/(2q). To reach c, the horizontal travel time is t=L/v₀, while the vertical displacement satisfies L=½(qE/m)t², giving E=2mv₀²/(qL); since potential decreases along the field, U_ac=V_a−V_c=EL=2mv₀²/q. For an exit kinetic energy mv₀², ½m(v₀²+v_y²)=mv₀² gives v_y=v₀; an exit through the top would require t=2L/v₀ and hence horizontal displacement 2L, which is impossible, so the ion exits side bc after t=L/v₀, and v_y=qEt/m yields E=mv₀²/(qL), with exit height L/2. Final answer: U₀=mv₀²/(2q); U_ac=2mv₀²/q; E=mv₀²/(qL).

The graph shows car A moving constantly at 4 m/s, while car B’s velocity decreases uniformly from 10 m/s at t = 0 to 0 at t = 5 s, so for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5 s, vB = 10 − 2t. The separation is greatest when both cars have the same velocity: 10 − 2t = 4, giving t = 3 s. The increase in separation by then is the relative displacement ∫₀³[(10 − 2t) − 4]dt = [6t − t²]₀³ = 9 m, so the maximum separation is 35 + 9 = 44 m. By t = 5 s, car B has traveled ½ × 5 × 10 = 25 m and car A has traveled 4 × 5 = 20 m, so their separation is 35 + 25 − 20 = 40 m. Car B is then stationary, and car A takes 40/4 = 10 s more to reach it, giving a total collision time of 5 + 10 = 15 s. Final answer: maximum separation = 44 m; rear-end collision occurs after 15 s.

The image shows a rectangular coil ABCD rotating about its vertical symmetry axis OO′ in a horizontal uniform magnetic field; when timing starts, the coil passes through the neutral plane, so its magnetic flux is maximum and the induced electromotive force is zero. The coil area is S=lABlBC=0.2×0.5=0.10 m², so the flux linkage is nBS cos(ωt), and the induced electromotive force magnitude is |e|=nBSω|sin(ωt)|=100×0.1×0.10×100π|sin(100πt)|=100π|sin(100πt)| V, with maximum value 100π V. The period is T=2π/ω=0.020 s; from t=0 to T/4, the flux linkage changes in magnitude from nBS to 0, so the average electromotive force magnitude is |ē|=|Δ(nΦ)|/(T/4)=nBS/(T/4)=1/0.005=200 V. Final answer: 1. |e|=100π|sin(100πt)| V, with maximum value 100π V; 2. 200 V.

The image shows P on the horizontal screen MN, PC vertical, the magnetic field B directed into the page, and launch directions ranging from −θ to +θ relative to PC, where θ=60°. Let α be the signed launch angle from PC and R=mv/(qB) the circular-orbit radius. For charge −q, the orbit center relative to P is (R cos α, −R sin α), so the greatest height of that orbit is ymax=R(1−sin α); the greatest height among all launch directions occurs at α=−θ and equals R(1+sin θ). Since the descending plate first collects particles at height d, d=R(1+sin60°), giving R=2d/(2+√3)=2(2−√3)d and v=qBR/m=2(2−√3)qBd/m. After EF is removed, setting y=0 in the orbit equation gives the second intersection with MN at x=2R cos α; therefore the impact region extends from 2R cos60°=R to 2R, so L=2R(1−cos60°)=R=2(2−√3)d. Final answer: v=2(2−√3)qBd/m; L=2(2−√3)d.

Figure 2 shows pipe A resting symmetrically between pipe B and the adjacent bottom pipe; since all pipes have equal diameters, each contact force is directed along the line joining the centers, at 30° to the vertical. At uniform velocity, vertical equilibrium of A gives 2N cos 30° = mg, so N = mg/√3 = 1500×10/√3 = 5000√3 N. During emergency braking, each top pipe slides longitudinally over two bottom pipes and experiences total kinetic friction f = 2μN = 2×(√3/3)×5000√3 = 10000 N, giving the top layer a deceleration a = f/m = 20/3 m/s². The initial speed is 43.2/3.6 = 12 m/s; therefore, the truck stops in sₜ = v²/(2×8) = 9 m, while the top pipes stop in sₚ = v²/[2×(20/3)] = 10.8 m. Their maximum forward displacement relative to the truck is 10.8−9 = 1.8 m, which is the required minimum clearance. Final answer: the elastic force between A and B is 5000√3 N, and the minimum initial distance is 1.8 m.

The figure shows a vertical wooden rod of length 5 m released from rest with its upper end initially at the suspension point; the cylinder’s upper end A is 20 m below that point, and its lower end B is another 5 m lower. Thus the rod’s lower end initially travels 20−5=15 m to reach A. For free fall, s=gt²/2, so the lower end reaches A at √(2×15/10)=√3 s, while the upper end reaches A after falling 20 m at √(2×20/10)=2 s; hence the time for the whole rod to pass A is t1=2−√3≈0.268 s. For the whole rod to pass through the cylinder, timing begins when its lower end reaches A and ends when its upper end reaches B, after the upper end has fallen 20+5=25 m; therefore t2=√(2×25/10)−√3=√5−√3≈0.504 s. Final answer: t1=2−√3 s≈0.268 s; t2=√5−√3 s≈0.504 s.

The image shows the coil plane inclined at 60° to the horizontal, with cd as the horizontal rotation axis and the uniform magnetic field directed vertically downward. Choosing the initial surface normal to have a component along the field, its angle with B is 60°, so Φ1 = BS cos 60° = (0.6)(0.4)(0.5) = 0.12 Wb. A clockwise rotation of 120° brings the coil into the horizontal plane on the opposite side of cd, so its continuously tracked normal is then opposite to B; hence Φ2 = BS cos 180° = −(0.6)(0.4) = −0.24 Wb. Therefore ΔΦ = Φ2 − Φ1 = −0.24 − 0.12 = −0.36 Wb, corresponding to a flux-change magnitude of 0.36 Wb. Final answer: Φ = 0.12 Wb; ΔΦ = −0.36 Wb (magnitude 0.36 Wb).

Figure B shows the ball striking the vertical backboard at the crest of its incoming trajectory, at a point h=0.2 m above the basket center and L=0.6 m horizontally from it. The work needed to accelerate the ball from rest to v1=5 m/s is W=ΔK=mv1²/2=(0.6)(5²)/2=7.5 J. Since θ=53° is measured from the vertical, the initial horizontal and vertical components are v1x=v1sinθ=5(0.8)=4 m/s and v1y=v1cosθ=5(0.6)=3 m/s; at the crest v1y has fallen to zero, so the speed immediately before impact is v2=4 m/s. The backboard’s impulse is horizontal, so the ball begins its rebound with zero vertical velocity; its fall through h therefore takes t=sqrt(2h/g)=sqrt[2(0.2)/10]=0.20 s, giving the rebound speed v3=L/t=0.6/0.20=3 m/s horizontally away from the board. Taking motion toward the board as positive, the horizontal velocity changes from +4 m/s to −3 m/s, so FΔt=m|Δvx| and F=0.6|−3−4|/0.01=420 N. Final answer: W=7.5 J, v2=4.0 m/s, v3=3.0 m/s, F=420 N.

The image shows upper plate A negatively charged, lower plate B positively charged and grounded, point C 0.5 cm below A, and point D 0.5 cm above B; therefore the electric field points upward from B to A and VB = 0. Taking upward distance x from B, V(x) = VB − Ex. For D, xD = 0.005 m, so VD = 0 − (1.2 × 10²)(0.005) = −0.60 V. For C, xC = 0.050 − 0.005 = 0.045 m, so VC = −(1.2 × 10²)(0.045) = −5.4 V; hence VC − VD = −5.4 − (−0.6) = −4.8 V, so the magnitude of the potential difference is 4.8 V. The plate voltage magnitude is Ed = (1.2 × 10²)(0.050) = 6.0 V, giving capacitance C = Q/ΔV = (6 × 10⁻⁸)/6.0 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ F. Final answer: VD = −0.60 V; VC − VD = −4.8 V (magnitude 4.8 V); capacitance = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ F.

The image shows two circular arcs of radii r = 40 m and R = 90 m whose centers are L = 100 m apart, joined by two equal common external tangents. On a curve, static friction supplies the centripetal force, so mv²/ρ ≤ 2.25mg and v_max = √(2.25gρ); hence the maximum speed on the small arc is √(2.25 × 10 × 40) = 30 m/s, while that on the large arc is √(2.25 × 10 × 90) = 45 m/s. Each straight has length s = √[L² − (R − r)²] = √[100² − 50²] = 50√3 m. Tangent geometry gives sin 30° = (R − r)/L, so the small and large curved sections subtend 2π/3 and 4π/3 radians, respectively; their lengths are 40(2π/3) = 80π/3 m and 90(4π/3) = 120π m. Uniform acceleration from 30 m/s to 45 m/s over one straight therefore has magnitude a = (45² − 30²)/(2 × 50√3) = 15√3/4 m/s², which is below the available straight-line frictional acceleration 2.25g = 22.5 m/s². Each straight takes 2s/(30 + 45) = 4√3/3 s, while the small and large arcs take (80π/3)/30 = 8π/9 s and 120π/45 = 8π/3 s. Thus the minimum lap time is 2(4√3/3) + 8π/9 + 8π/3 = 32π/9 + 8√3/3 s. Final answer: maximum small-arc speed = 30 m/s; straight-line acceleration magnitude = 15√3/4 m/s²; minimum lap time = 32π/9 + 8√3/3 s.

The image shows O at the perpendicular coordinate axes, A on the positive x-axis, B on the positive y-axis, and AB inclined at about 30° to the x-axis; thus the stated ∠AOB = 30° is inconsistent with Cartesian axes, and the evidently intended angle is ∠BAO = 30°. At B, the positive particle moving upward in an outward magnetic field experiences a force toward +x, so its circular path has center C directly to the right of B. Since CB = CA and ∠CBA = 30°, the minor central angle ∠BCA is 120°, while the trajectory in the magnetic-field region is the major arc with angular displacement φ = 240° = 4π/3. Therefore R = v₀t₀/φ = 3v₀t₀/(4π). The chord geometry gives OB = AB sin 30° = (2R sin 60°)sin 30° = √3R/2. During electric acceleration from rest, OB = v₀t₁/2, so t₁ = √3R/v₀ = 3√3t₀/(4π). Also qE/m = v₀/t₁ and qB/m = φ/t₀, hence B = Eφt₁/(v₀t₀) = √3E/v₀. Final answer: t₁ = 3√3t₀/(4π), B = √3E/v₀.

The image shows the horizontal 2L rod centered on MN, with A initially at x=L, B at x=−L, PQ at x=3L, and the electric field E directed right between MN and PQ; since all electric forces act along the rod, it remains horizontal and the balls have the same speed. With B uncharged, A is acted on by the field only while moving from x=L to x=3L, so 2qEL=2(½mv²)=m(8gL), giving E=4mg/q; therefore MN is at the higher potential and V_MN−V_PQ=3EL=12mgL/q. Interpreting “can move to PQ” as “just reaches PQ with zero speed,” let B’s charge be Q: A receives work 2qEL and B receives work 3QEL, so 2qEL+3QEL=0, hence Q=−2q/3, meaning B is negatively charged with magnitude 2q/3. Let X be the rod’s midpoint displacement from MN: for 0<X<L only A is in the field, so a₁=qE/(2m)=2g, t₁=√(L/g), and v₁=2√(gL); for L<X<2L both balls are in the field, so a₂=(q+Q)E/(2m)=2g/3, v₂²=v₁²+2a₂L=16gL/3, and t₂=(v₂−v₁)/a₂=(2√3−3)√(L/g); for 2L<X<4L only B is in the field, so its acceleration is −4g/3 and the time to stop at PQ is t₃=v₂/(4g/3)=√3√(L/g). The return from PQ to X=2L takes t₃ and from X=2L to B’s second crossing of MN at X=L takes t₂, so t=t₁+2t₂+2t₃=(6√3−5)√(L/g). Final answer: V_MN−V_PQ=12mgL/q; B has charge −2q/3; t=(6√3−5)√(L/g).

The image shows the rod spanning the two parallel rails, with conventional current flowing from a to b and the magnetic field tilted 37° above the rail plane; by the right-hand rule, the initial magnetic force has a component BIl sin 37° along the rails and an upward component BIl cos 37°. Interpreting “exactly stationary” as limiting equilibrium, these components at B = 2 T are F∥ = 2×1×0.5×0.6 = 0.6 N and Fup = 2×1×0.5×0.8 = 0.8 N, so the total normal force is N = mg − Fup = 0.2×10 − 0.8 = 1.2 N; therefore μ = F∥/N = 0.6/1.2 = 0.50. After the field is reversed, the magnetic force normal to the rails is downward, so for a variable field B the normal force is N = mg + BIl cos 37° = 2 + 0.4B, while the force along the rails is BIl sin 37° = 0.3B. At impending motion, using the stated equality of maximum static and kinetic friction, 0.3B = 0.50(2 + 0.4B), giving 0.1B = 1 and hence B = 10 T. Final answer: μ = 0.50; B = 10 T.

The figure shows the person standing upright directly in front of the vertical wall, with the horizontal cylindrical hole centered at half the person’s height; therefore, the limiting rays from the head and feet each have a vertical offset of 0.8 m from the hole axis. Their incidence angle i satisfies tan i=0.8/0.6=4/3, so sin i=4/5. A ray can just traverse the 1.4 cm-deep bore by going from one edge of the 1.0 cm-diameter opening to the opposite edge, giving tan rmax=1.0/1.4=5/7 and sin rmax=5/√74. From Snell’s law, sin i=n sin r, so complete imaging requires nmin=(4/5)/(5/√74)=4√74/25≈1.38. For grazing incidence, sin i=1, and the same traversal condition gives nmin=1/(5/√74)=√74/5≈1.72; at the exit this is the limiting critical-angle case. Final answer: 1.38; 1.72.

No usable image is available; the relevant data are m = 0.1 kg, v₀ = 10 m/s, and a constant air-resistance magnitude f = 0.1mg opposite the motion. During ascent, gravity and drag both act downward, so a↑ = 1.1g and 0 = v₀² − 2(1.1g)h gives h = v₀²/(2.2g) = 4.64 m for g = 9.8 m/s². Gravity does −mgh on the way up and +mgh on the way down, so its total work is zero; drag opposes both parts of the motion, so Wair = −f(2h) = −0.2mgh = −0.909 J. The ascent time follows from 0 = v₀ − 1.1gt, giving t↑ = v₀/(1.1g) = 0.928 s. During descent, drag acts upward, making the downward acceleration 0.9g, so h = ½(0.9g)t↓² and t↓ = √[2h/(0.9g)] = 1.026 s. Final answer: maximum height = 4.64 m; gravity work = 0 J; air-resistance work = −0.909 J; ascent time = 0.928 s; descent time = 1.026 s.

The image shows the wooden block of mass M moving right on a smooth horizontal surface while the iron block of mass m, initially at rest, is placed on top; kinetic friction therefore acts rightward on m and leftward on M, with magnitude f=μmg. As M moves a ground distance l and m slides left relative to M by L, the ground displacement of m is l−L. Thus the heat generated is friction times relative sliding distance, Q=fL=μmgL; the increase in the iron block’s kinetic energy equals the work done on it, ΔK_m=f(l−L)=μmg(l−L); the kinetic energy lost by the wooden block equals the magnitude of the friction work on it, −ΔK_M=fl=μmgl; and the reduction in total mechanical energy is μmgl−μmg(l−L)=μmgL, equal to the generated heat. Final answer: Q=μmgL; ΔK_m=μmg(l−L); kinetic energy lost by M=μmgl; reduction in mechanical energy=μmgL.

In figure (a), the closed end is above the ground-supported piston; in figure (b), it is below the ceiling-supported piston; and in figure (c), the cylinder axis is horizontal, so gravity has no axial component. Force balance on the cylinder in (a) gives p₁S − p₀S − mg = 0, so p₁ = p₀ + mg/S. In (b), force balance gives p₀S − p₂S − mg = 0, so p₂ = p₀ − mg/S; because both states have temperature T₁, the ideal-gas law gives p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, hence V₂ = V₁(p₀S + mg)/(p₀S − mg), with equilibrium requiring p₀S > mg. In (c), the smooth piston is horizontal and the equilibrium gas pressure is p₃ = p₀; conservation of the gas amount gives p₁V₁/T₁ = p₃V₃/T₃, so T₃ = T₁p₀SV₃/[(p₀S + mg)V₁]. Final answer: V₂ = V₁(p₀S + mg)/(p₀S − mg); T₃ = T₁p₀SV₃/[(p₀S + mg)V₁].

No usable image is available, so only the stated speed and 60 s round-trip time are used. In the spacecraft frame, the spacecraft is stationary; if reflection occurs after time t′, the signal has traveled a distance ct′, and the reflected signal takes another t′ to return, so 2t′=60 s, giving t′=30 s and a reflection-time distance of 30 light-seconds. For the Earth frame, γ=1/√(1−v²/c²)=1/√(1−16/25)=5/3, so the interval from transmission to reception is γ(60 s)=100 s. If the outbound signal reaches Earth after t seconds, the initial separation is ct, while at reception the spacecraft is ct+v(100 s)=ct+80 light-seconds from Earth; the reflected signal travels c(100−t), so 100−t=t+80, yielding t=10 s and a reception distance of c(90 s)=90 light-seconds. Final answer: at reflection the spacecraft-frame distance is 30 light-seconds (9.0×10^9 m), and at reception the Earth-frame distance is 90 light-seconds (2.7×10^10 m).

The figure shows a fixed 100-turn coil connected to an external circuit while the N–S magnet rotates at angular velocity ω, producing a sinusoidally varying magnetic flux through the coil. Thus e(t)=NBSω sin(ωt), so the peak emf is Em=NBSω=100×0.2×0.5×90=900 V and the effective emf is E=Em/√2=450√2≈636.4 V. With effective current I=50 A and coil resistance r=0.6 Ω, the terminal voltage is U=E−Ir=636.4−50×0.6=606.4 V, so the power delivered to the external circuit is P=UI=EI−I²r≈606.4×50=3.03×10^4 W. Final answer: E≈636 V; P≈3.03×10^4 W.

No usable image is available; the stated geometry is a thin glass concavo-convex lens with refractive index 1.5, radii 20 cm and 60 cm, and the convex surface silvered as a concave mirror. The glass lens power is P_g = (1.5 − 1)(1/20 − 1/60) = 1/60 cm⁻¹, while the mirror has focal length 20/2 = 10 cm and power 1/10 cm⁻¹. Since light passes through the lens twice, the effective reflecting power is P = 2P_g + 1/10 = 2/15 cm⁻¹, giving F = 7.5 cm; coincidence of object and image occurs at 2F, so the pin is 15 cm in front of the concave side. When the concavity is filled, the water forms a thin plano-convex addition of power P_w = (4/3 − 1)/60 = 1/180 cm⁻¹, so the combined lens power becomes 1/60 + 1/180 = 1/45 cm⁻¹. The new effective reflecting power is 2/45 + 1/10 = 13/90 cm⁻¹, hence the new pin distance is 2F′ = 2(90/13) = 180/13 cm. The required movement is 15 − 180/13 = 15/13 cm toward the lens. Final answer: (a) 15 cm in front of the concave side; (b) move the pin 15/13 cm, approximately 1.15 cm, toward the lens.

The image shows a slider moving upward from A to the top B of a vertical rod resting on a horizontal table, with AB=l=1.2 m; at B the slider sticks to the rod and they rise together. Initially the stationary slider is supported by static friction from the rod, so the slider exerts its weight mg on the rod and N1=(M+m)g=(0.6+0.2)×10=8 N. While the slider moves upward, the rod experiences an upward friction force f=1 N from the slider, and since the rod remains on the table, N2+f=Mg, giving N2=0.6×10−1=5 N. During the slider’s ascent, gravity and friction both do negative work, so (1/2)mv1²=(1/2)mv0²−(mg+f)l; hence v1²=10²−2[(0.2×10+1)/0.2]×1.2=64 and v1=8 m/s. In the perfectly inelastic collision, vertical momentum is conserved over the short collision interval, so mv1=(m+M)v, giving v=0.2×8/0.8=2 m/s. After leaving the table, the combined system rises under gravity until its velocity is zero, so h=v²/(2g)=2²/(2×10)=0.20 m. Final answer: N1=8 N, N2=5 N, v1=8 m/s, h=0.20 m.

The image shows piston-controlled region A on the left and region B on the right, separated by a movable partition. Since each region contains a fixed amount of ideal gas and the temperature is constant, p_AV_A=p_0V and p_BV_B=p_0V. During slow compression the partition slides to the right with the limiting pressure difference p_A-p_B=0.5p_0. When V_B=V/2, p_B=p_0V/(V/2)=2p_0, so p_A=2.5p_0 and V_A=p_0V/p_A=2V/5. On reversing the piston, the partition initially remains fixed; after the pressure difference reverses, it slides left with p_B-p_A=0.5p_0. When the piston returns to its initial position, V_A+V_B=2V. Writing a=V_A/V and b=V_B/V gives a+b=2 and 1/b-1/a=1/2, whose physical solution is b=3-\sqrt5 and a=\sqrt5-1. Thus V_A=(\sqrt5-1)V and p_B=p_0/(3-\sqrt5)=(3+\sqrt5)p_0/4. Final answer: At maximum compression, p_B=2p_0 and V_A=2V/5; after the piston returns, V_A=(\sqrt5-1)V and p_B=(3+\sqrt5)p_0/4.

The image shows C on the lower-left side of the circle and D diametrically opposite it, with COD inclined 37° to the vertical; the electric-field arrows point horizontally right, and the rightmost point of the circle is marked E. At C the wall’s normal force points toward O, so gravity and the electric force must have a resultant directed from O toward C; hence the ball is negatively charged and |q|E/(mg) = tan 37°. Thus E = (0.4 × 10 × 0.6/0.8)/(3 × 10⁻⁵) = 1.0 × 10⁵ N/C. The resultant of gravity and the electric force is F = √[(mg)² + (|q|E)²] = √(4² + 3²) = 5 N, directed toward C. For the ball to just maintain contact at the opposite point D, the normal force there is zero, so mv_D²/r = F and K_D = Fr/2 = 1.25 J. The combined gravitational and electric potential-energy increase from C to D is F(2r) = 5 J, giving conserved kinetic-plus-gravitational-plus-electric energy 6.25 J. Mechanical energy means kinetic plus gravitational potential energy, so it equals 6.25 J minus the electric potential energy. Since the electric force is 3 N leftward, the electric potential energy is greatest at the rightmost point E; with x_C = −r sin 37° = −0.3 m and x_E = 0.5 m, its maximum is 3[0.5 − (−0.3)] = 2.4 J. Therefore the minimum mechanical energy is 6.25 − 2.4 = 3.85 J. Final answer: electric field magnitude = 1.0 × 10⁵ N/C; minimum mechanical energy = 3.85 J.

No usable image is available; the stated data give A an initial speed of 16 m/s and acceleration −2 m/s², while B starts 18 m behind A with speed 4 m/s and acceleration 6 m/s² until t = 3 s. The image shows the board lying along a 37° incline with its downslope front end facing the baffle, while the block is thrown horizontally to the right and falls onto that front end. Using sin 37° = 0.6 and cos 37° = 0.8, the falling time is t₁ = √(2h/g) = √(1.6/10) = 0.4 s, so just before impact the block has horizontal velocity 3 m/s and downward velocity gt₁ = 4 m/s; hence its speed is √(3² + 4²) = 5 m/s at arctan(4/3) = 53° below the horizontal, which is perpendicular to the incline. Because the board’s upper surface is smooth, the collision supplies no impulse parallel to the incline; the block’s pre-impact tangential velocity is zero, so immediately afterward its tangential velocity is zero while the board continues downslope at 0.8 m/s. With the block on the board, the plane’s normal force is (M + m)g cos α = 32 N, so friction is 16 N and the board’s downslope acceleration is aB = [Mg sin α − 16]/M = (18 − 16)/3 = 2/3 m/s²; the block accelerates downslope at am = g sin α = 6 m/s². Taking relative displacement from the front end as positive downslope gives vrel,0 = −0.8 m/s and arel = 6 − 2/3 = 16/3 m/s², so the greatest rearward displacement is 0.8²/[2(16/3)] = 0.060 m, which is the minimum board length. The block returns to the front end when −0.8t + (1/2)(16/3)t² = 0, giving t = 0.30 s; during this time the board moves 0.8(0.30) + (1/2)(2/3)(0.30)² = 0.27 m, so its initial distance from the baffle must be 0.16 + 0.27 = 0.43 m. Final answer: 5 m/s directed 53° below the horizontal toward the board; minimum board length 0.060 m; initial front-end-to-baffle distance 0.430 m.

The image shows the positive plate on the left and the negative plate on the right, separated by l along +x, so the conventional current density in the liquid is J = U/(ρl) in the +x direction. The required Ampere force is upward along +y, and since f = J × B, the field must point along −z because (+x) × (−z) = +y. Let the unchanged outside liquid height be H and the inside height be h. The upward electromagnetic force density is f = JB = UB/(ρl), so hydrostatic balance at the bottom gives ρ₀gH = (ρ₀g − f)h. For h = 2H, this yields f = ρ₀g/2 and hence U₀ = ρρ₀gl/(2B). In general, h = ρ₀gH/[ρ₀g − UB/(ρl)], so a finite equilibrium exists only when UB/(ρl) < ρ₀g; therefore, the liquid rises continuously when UB/(ρl) ≥ ρ₀g. Final answer: B is directed along −z; U₀ = ρρ₀gl/(2B); continuous rise requires U ≥ ρρ₀gl/B.

The diagram shows the magnetic field B directed horizontally in the plane of the rectangular coil, while the rotation axis O′O lies in the coil’s plane and is perpendicular to B, so initially the magnetic flux is zero and the induced emf has maximum magnitude. The coil area is S=ab·ad=0.30×0.20=0.060 m², hence the maximum flux through each turn is Φm=BS=0.8×0.060=0.048 Wb. The maximum induced emf is Em=NBSω=100×0.8×0.060×100π=480π V≈1.51×10³ V. The image shows rod ab perpendicular to the rails, the magnetic field directed normally upward from the inclined rail plane, and the source polarity producing an Ampere force up the incline. The image shows method 1 connecting the wires to a and d, so current flows through ad=3L, while method 2 connects them to b and c, so current flows through bc=L; the two symmetric suspensions have the same wire inclination magnitude, although they lean in opposite horizontal directions. The image shows the box entering the horizontal upper section of the conveyor at the left platform with rightward speed v₀, while the belt moves rightward at speed v over the distance L to the right platform. The image shows the block m₂ moving right on top of the initially stationary board m₁, while the board rests on a smooth floor and is initially separated from the uncompressed wall-mounted spring on its right. Before contact with the spring, the kinetic-friction force is f=μm₂g=0.1×4×10=4 N, so the board and block accelerations are respectively 4 m/s² and −1 m/s²; hence 4t=5/4−t gives t=1/4 s, the common velocity is v=4t=1 m/s, and the board travels x₁=(1/2)×4×(1/4)²=1/8 m before touching the spring. While the two objects subsequently move together, their acceleration is a=−kx/(m₁+m₂)=−4x, requiring static friction of magnitude m₂|a|=16x; equating this to the maximum value 4 N gives x₂=1/4 m. Static friction dissipates no energy, so (1/2)(m₁+m₂)v₂²+(1/2)kx₂²=(1/2)(m₁+m₂)v², yielding v₂²=3/4 and v₂=√3/2 m/s. After sliding begins, friction remains leftward on the block and rightward on the board, giving a₂=−1 m/s² and a₁=4−20x; their accelerations are equal when x=1/4 m. For x>1/4 m, a₂−a₁=20x−5>0, so the block continues sliding right relative to the board, and the board obeys x″=4−20x both before and after its turning point. Therefore, if it takes t₀ to go from x=1/4 m with velocity v₂ to zero velocity, it takes another t₀ to return to x=1/4 m, when the accelerations first become equal again. Over the total time 2t₀, the board has zero net displacement, whereas the block moves (√3/2)(2t₀)−(1/2)(2t₀)²=√3t₀−2t₀², so the frictional conversion is ΔU=4(√3t₀−2t₀²) J. Final answer: v=1 m/s; x₁=1/8 m; x₂=1/4 m; v₂=√3/2 m/s; ΔU=(4√3t₀−8t₀²) J, with t₀ in seconds.

The image shows the trolley connected by parallel cables to the motor and, over a fixed pulley, to the hanging counterweight, so the trolley and counterweight have equal speeds and displacements; when the trolley moves uphill, the counterweight moves downward. The motor’s mechanical output power is P=UI-I²R=380×40−40²×0.25=14800 W, so its uphill pulling force at v=2 m/s is F=P/v=7400 N. With the loaded mass M=m₁+m₂=1300 kg moving uniformly uphill, force balance along the incline gives F+m₀g=Mg(sinθ+k), hence sinθ+k=(7400+40×10)/(1300×10)=0.60. After unloading, the 100 kg trolley moves uniformly downhill while the counterweight rises, so m₁g sinθ=m₀g+km₁g, giving sinθ−k=m₀/m₁=0.40. Solving the two equations gives sinθ=0.50 and k=0.10. After the motor is turned off, the initial kinetic energy of the loaded trolley and counterweight is 1/2(M+m₀)v², while the net resisting force is Mg(sinθ+k)−m₀g; therefore 1/2(M+m₀)v²=[Mg(sinθ+k)−m₀g]L, so L=[0.5×(1300+40)×2²]/[1300×10×0.60−40×10]=2680/7400≈0.362 m. Final answer: k=0.10; L≈0.36 m.

The image shows charged ball A initially a distance L to the left of uncharged ball B, with B at the edge of a table of height h, while the uniform electric field points horizontally to the right. Ball A has acceleration a=qE/m=(0.1×10)/0.2=5 m/s², so from L=at²/2 its collision time is t=√(2L/a)=√(2×0.1/5)=0.20 s, and its speed just before collision is v=at=1.0 m/s. Since the collision is perfectly elastic and the masses are equal, A and B exchange velocities, so B leaves the edge at 1.0 m/s while A is momentarily at rest. Both fall for t_f=√(2h/g)=√(2×0.05/10)=0.10 s; thus B travels x_B=vt_f=0.10 m, while A continues to accelerate horizontally in the electric field and travels x_A=at_f²/2=5×0.10²/2=0.025 m. Their landing points are therefore separated by x_B−x_A=0.075 m. Final answer: collision time 0.20 s; landing-point separation 0.075 m.

The figure shows that OA is directed upward at 45° to the vertical, OB is horizontal to the left, and OC pulls vertically downward on junction O with tension equal to the weight W. Equilibrium at O gives T_OA cos45° = W vertically and T_OB = T_OA sin45° horizontally, so T_OA = W/cos45° = √2W and T_OB = W tan45° = W. For W = 3 N, T_OA = 3√2 N ≈ 4.24 N and T_OB = 3 N. The strength limits require √2W ≤ 10 N and W ≤ 6 N, giving W ≤ 5√2 N ≈ 7.07 N from OA and W ≤ 6 N from OB; therefore OB reaches its limit first. Final answer: 1. T_OA = 3√2 N ≈ 4.24 N and T_OB = 3 N; 2. the maximum gravitational force is 6 N.

The image shows that A is 5 m above the dashed reference level while B is 1 m above it, so the vertical drop from A to B is 4 m; the question states that C is 10 m vertically below B. The image shows S1 and S2 separated by 4 m with B at their midpoint, so BS1 = BS2 = 2 m. The wavelength is λ = v/f = 8/4 = 2 m. The graph shows h_A = 4 km and h_B ≈ 1.5 km, a positive-temperature melting area A = 5.0 km·°C, a negative-temperature freezing area A′ = 4.0 km·°C, and a dashed no-inversion profile rising from 0°C at 4 km to 8°C at the ground. With constant fall speed, size, density, and heat-transfer coefficient, the heat transferred while the droplet is at the 0°C phase-change temperature is proportional to the corresponding graph area; taking A to represent the heat required to melt the droplet, the refrozen mass fraction is A′/A = 4.0/5.0 = 0.800. For the dashed profile, let x = 4 − h be downward distance in kilometres, so T_air = 2x; the heat-transfer constant per unit mass is K = L/A = 334/5 = 66.8 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ km⁻¹, and melting finishes where K∫₀ˣ 2s ds = Kx² = L, giving x_m = √5 = 2.236 km. After that, λ = K/c_water = 66.8/4.2 = 15.9048 km⁻¹ and the liquid temperature obeys dT_d/dx = λ(2x − T_d), with T_d(x_m) = 0; therefore T_d(4) = 8 − 2/λ + (2/λ − 2x_m)e^(−λ(4−x_m)) = 7.874°C. No usable image is available, so the solution relies on the stated charges and work values. For the positive charge q = 2×10⁻⁸ C moved from infinity to A, the work against the electric field equals the increase in potential energy: W = q(VA − V∞), so VA = 2×10⁻⁶/(2×10⁻⁸) = 100 V. For motion from B to infinity, the electric-field work is Wfield = q(VB − V∞), giving VB = 8×10⁻⁶/(2×10⁻⁸) = 400 V; hence the potential difference UAB = VA − VB = 100 − 400 = −300 V. The electric-field work on q′ = −2×10⁻⁵ C moving from A to B is WAB = q′(VA − VB) = (−2×10⁻⁵)(−300) = 6×10⁻³ J. Final answer: VA = 100 V; UAB = −300 V; WAB = 6×10⁻³ J.

The image shows the source at O, an upward electric field in 0≤y≤d, a magnetic field directed into the page in d≤y≤2d, and the plate ab at y=2d. From work–energy, 1/2 mv²=1/2 mv₀²+qEd=1/2 mv₀²+3/2 mv₀², so every particle enters the magnetic field with v=2v₀. The electric field does not change the horizontal velocity, so at magnetic-field entry vₓ=v₀cosθ and −v₀≤vₓ≤v₀. In the magnetic field the orbit radius is R=mv/(qB)=2mv₀/(qB), and for the into-page field the circle center has ordinate y_c=d+mvₓ/(qB); hence the greatest possible height is obtained for vₓ=v₀ and equals y_max=y_c+R=d+3mv₀/(qB). Requiring y_max<2d gives B>3mv₀/(qd); the critical field for which the limiting trajectory is tangent to the plate is B_c=3mv₀/(qd), so the observation alone determines a lower bound rather than a unique larger value. Final answer: v=2v₀; B>3mv₀/(qd), with critical magnitude B_c=3mv₀/(qd).

The figure shows positive ions leaving the ionization chamber and accelerating from electrode A toward B through the uniform electric field associated with the voltage magnitude U; their initial speed is negligible. For one ion, the electric work becomes kinetic energy, ZeU=mv²/2, so v=√(2ZeU/m). Since N ions enter per unit time, their momentum gain per unit time is Nmv, equal in magnitude to the engine thrust; hence F₁=Nmv and N=F₁/√(2mZeU). The accelerating power is the energy supplied per unit time, P=NZeU, while F=Nmv=N√(2mZeU), giving F/P=√(2m/(ZeU))=√(2Nm/P)=2/v. Therefore the thrust-to-power ratio can be increased by using heavier ions, using ions with a smaller charge number Z, ideally Z=1, and reducing the accelerating voltage U, although reducing U also reduces the absolute thrust when N is fixed. Final answer: N=F₁/√(2mZeU); F/P=√(2m/(ZeU))=√(2Nm/P); use heavier ions, lower Z, and lower U.

The image shows the dipole initially on the X-axis with −q at x=−d/2, +q at x=d/2, its center at the origin, and B perpendicular to the plane and directed outward; let n=(cosθ,sinθ) point from −q to +q, so θ(0)=0. If R is the center-of-mass position, V=Ṙ, and I=md²/2, summing the Lorentz forces and torques gives 2mV̇=qBdθ̇n and Iθ̈=−qBd(V·n). The bright-side balance is P = CT₁⁴ + Q₁ = CT₁⁴(1 + x³), while the wind power is P_w = Q₁ − Q₂ = CT₁⁴x³(1 − x); hence P_w = P x³(1 − x)/(1 + x³).
