The image shows the ring acting as a capacitance C connected through R₀ to a two-position switch between the source V₀ and ground, so its electrical time constant is τ = R₀C; because the drawing alone does not specify the switching instant, the dynamic result below assumes the ring is initially at V₀ and is switched to ground when the electron enters the active region. Let k = 1/(4πε₀) and take Φ(∞) = 0. Every element of a thin ring is a distance √(R² + z²) from an axial point, hence Φ(z) = kq/√(R² + z²). For z ≪ R, Φ(z) = (kq/R)(1 + z²/R²)^(−1/2) ≈ kq/R − kqz²/(2R³). Therefore E_z = −dΦ/dz ≈ kqz/R³, and an electron experiences F_z = −eE_z = −keqz/R³; this is restoring only for q > 0, and comparison with F_z = −mω²z gives ω = √[eq/(4πε₀mR³)]. At a point in the ring plane with ρ = r/R ≪ 1, Φ(r,0) = [kq/(2πR)]∫₀²π(1 + ρ² − 2ρ cosφ)^(−1/2)dφ. Expanding and using ⟨cosφ⟩ = 0 and ⟨cos²φ⟩ = 1/2 gives Φ(r,0) ≈ (kq/R)[1 + r²/(4R²)] = Φ(0) + qr²/(16πε₀R³). Thus, under the convention Φ = Φ(0) + βqr², β = 1/(16πε₀R³); if β instead denotes the entire coefficient of r², it is q/(16πε₀R³), while the equivalent dimensionless coefficient in Φ = Φ(0)[1 + β(r/R)²] is 1/4. The radial field and electron force are E_r = −2βqr = −qr/(8πε₀R³) and F_r = 2eβqr = eqr/(8πε₀R³), so a focusing electron lens requires q < 0. In an active region of axial length d, f ≫ d allows r to be treated as constant during the transit time d/v; thus Δv_r = 2eβqrd/(mv), and −r/f = Δv_r/v gives f = −mv²/(2eβqd) = −8πε₀mv²R³/(eqd), whose positive focusing magnitude is mv²/(2eβ|q|d). If the undefined c in the supplied text is the proportionality constant in f = cv², then c = −m/(2eβqd), or m/(2eβ|q|d) for a focusing lens. For a slender conducting torus, λ = q/(2πR) and the leading surface potential is Φ_s ≈ [λ/(2πε₀)]ln(8R/a) = [q/(4π²ε₀R)]ln(8R/a), giving C ≈ 4π²ε₀R/ln(8R/a); at leading logarithmic accuracy ln(8R/a) may be replaced by ln(R/a). For discharge after switching to ground, q(t) = q₀e^(−t/τ), where q₀ = CV₀ and τ = R₀C. Since d/v is comparable to τ, the exponential cannot be expanded, and the impulse is determined by ∫₀^(d/v)q(t)dt = q₀τ[1 − e^(−d/(vτ))]. For infinitesimal reversible Carnot cycles, the total entropy change of the two reservoirs is zero: C ln(Tf/T1)+C ln(Tf/T2)=0, giving Tf=√(T1T2); energy conservation then gives the maximum engine work W=C(T1+T2−2Tf)=C(√T2−√T1)². For T1=100 K and T2=300 K, Tf=100√3 K≈173.2 K and W=(400−200√3)C K≈53.59C K. For the thermodynamic maximum temperature of the third body, the process must be reversible and the first two bodies must finish at a common low-side temperature TL; otherwise their remaining temperature difference could be used to raise the third body further. Energy and entropy conservation give 2TL+TH=700 K and ln(TL/100)+ln(TL/300)+ln(TH/300)=0, so TL²TH=9,000,000 K³. Substituting TH=700−2TL gives TL²(700−2TL)=9,000,000, whose physical root that raises the third body above 300 K is TL=150 K, yielding TH=400 K. Because the first body initially has T1=100 K, it is actually warmed to 150 K rather than lowered; if “the first object” is meant literally, its minimum attainable temperature without external work is its initial 100 K. Merely dissipating the separately obtained work W in the third body would give 300 K+W/C≈353.6 K, but that irreversible procedure is not the global thermodynamic maximum. Final answer: Tf=√(T1T2), W=C(T1+T2−2√(T1T2)); numerically Tf≈173.2 K and W≈53.59C K; TL=150 K as the common final low-side temperature, and TH=400 K, while the literal minimum of the initially 100 K first object is 100 K.

The return to x=0 requires a cyclotron angle 4π/3 and takes 4πm/(3eB₀), so if T is prescribed the full time condition gives B₀,min=max{√3mv₀/(ed),8πm/(3eT)}; the commonly intended geometrical minimum √3mv₀/(ed) is attainable when T≥8π√3d/(9v₀). Final answer: entry speed 2v₀/√3 directed 30° above +x; geometrical B₀,min=√3mv₀/(ed), or max{√3mv₀/(ed),8πm/(3eT)} for prescribed T; first-period M-exit values B₀=4√3mv₀/(3ed) and T=π√3d/(6v₀).

The image shows an approximately spherical water drop of radius r hanging from a downward metallic tube of internal diameter d, with d ≪ r and the tube held at potential φ; the Kelvin-dropper capacitance, drop rate, bowl distance, and bowl geometry are not shown, so these must be represented parametrically. The separation line has length l=πd, so the limiting condition (4πr_max^3/3)ρg=πdσ gives r_max=(3σd/(4ρg))^(1/3). Treating the water drop as an isolated conducting sphere, its capacitance is 4πε₀r, hence Q=4πε₀rφ, with the sign of Q equal to that of φ. The electric field immediately outside is E=φ/r, so the pressure difference is p_in−p_atm=2σ/r−ε₀φ²/(2r²); setting this to zero gives |φ_max|=2√(σr/ε₀), equivalently |Q|=8π√(ε₀σr^3). For a symmetric Kelvin dropper, let C be the capacitance between electrodes, U=q/C their voltage, and their potentials relative to the surroundings be ±U/2; then a separating drop has magnitude Q₀=4πε₀r_max(U/2)=2πε₀r_max|q|/C. If ν is the number of drop pairs produced per unit time, each pair increases the magnitude of the capacitor charge by Q₀, so dq/dt=νQ₀=(2πε₀r_maxν/C)q and q(t)=q₀exp(2πε₀r_maxνt/C). For example, if each electrode is approximately a distant sphere of radius R, then C=2πε₀R, Q₀=(r_max/R)|q|, and q(t)=q₀exp(νr_maxt/R). For the repulsion limit, write the upward bowl field at the drop as E_b=βU, where β is fixed by the omitted geometry; balancing Q₀E_b against the drop weight gives U_push=r_max√(2ρg/(3ε₀β)). In a uniform-field approximation over a fall distance H, β=1/H and U_push=r_max√(2ρgH/(3ε₀)); if instead the bowl is approximated as a point charge q=CU at distance H, β=C/(4πε₀H²) and U_push=Hr_max√(8πρg/(3C)). The instability from the pressure condition separately limits the symmetric electrode voltage to U_R=2φ_max=4√(σr_max/ε₀), so the attainable voltage is the smaller of U_R and the geometry-dependent repulsion limit. Final answer: r_max=(3σd/(4ρg))^(1/3); Q=4πε₀rφ; |φ_max|=2√(σr/ε₀); Q₀=2πε₀r_max|q|/C; q(t)=q₀exp(2πε₀r_maxνt/C); U_max=min[4√(σr_max/ε₀), r_max√(2ρg/(3ε₀β))], with β=1/H giving U_push=r_max√(2ρgH/(3ε₀)).
